lessons.title: Exercise — Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Define the normal distribution and its probability density function.

The normal distribution is a continuous distribution with a bell-shaped curve.

It is symmetric about its mean.

Its probability density function is f(x) = 1/(sigma sqrt(2 pi)) e^(-(x-mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2)).

It is the most important distribution in statistics.

What is the normal cumulative distribution function?

The cumulative distribution function is F(x) = P(X <= x).

It is the integral of the density function from -infinity to x.

This integral cannot be carried out in a closed form.

So tables of the standard normal distribution are used.

What is the standard normal random variable? State Theorem 10.1.

A normal variable X with mean mu and standard deviation sigma is changed to standard normal by Z = (X - mu)/sigma.

Z has mean 0 and variance 1.

Theorem 10.1: If X follows N(mu, sigma^2) and Z = (X - mu)/sigma, then Z follows N(0, 1).

This change lets us use one table for all normal variables.

What is the standard normal probability density function? State Theorem 10.2.

The density of the standard normal variable Z is phi(z) = 1/sqrt(2 pi) e^(-z^2/2) for -infinity < z < infinity.

phi(z) is the ordinate of the standard normal curve at Z = z.

Theorem 10.2: If Z follows N(0, 1), then phi(-z) = phi(z).

This means the curve is symmetric about zero.

mcqs.q: What is the shape of the curve of the normal distribution?
mcqs.why: The notes define the normal distribution as a continuous distribution with a bell-shaped curve, symmetric about its mean.

mcqs.q: What is the probability density function f(x) of a normal distribution with mean mu and standard deviation sigma?
mcqs.why: The notes give the normal density as f(x) = 1/(sigma sqrt(2 pi)) e^(-(x-mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2)), with mean mu and standard deviation sigma.

mcqs.q: About what value is the normal distribution symmetric?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, so the two halves of the curve on either side of mu are mirror images.

mcqs.q: What does the normal cumulative distribution function F(x) represent?
options: The height of the curve at x
The probability that X exceeds x
The variance of X up to x
mcqs.why: The notes define the cumulative distribution function as F(x) = P(X <= x), the integral of the density function from -infinity to x.

mcqs.q: Why are tables of the standard normal distribution used to find normal probabilities?
options: Because the normal density has no formula
Because the integral of the density cannot be carried out in a closed form
Because mu and sigma are always unknown
Because the curve has no total area
mcqs.why: The notes explain that F(x) is the integral of the density from -infinity to x and this integral cannot be carried out in a closed form, so standard normal tables are used.

mcqs.q: How is a normal variable X with mean mu and standard deviation sigma changed to the standard normal variable Z?
mcqs.why: The notes give the standardisation Z = (X - mu)/sigma, which changes any normal variable X into the standard normal variable Z.

mcqs.q: What are the mean and variance of the standard normal variable Z?
mcqs.why: The notes state that after standardisation Z = (X - mu)/sigma, the variable Z has mean 0 and variance 1, written Z follows N(0, 1).

mcqs.q: What does Theorem 10.1 state?
options: If X follows N(0, 1), then Z follows N(mu, sigma^2)
If X follows N(mu, sigma^2), then phi(-z) = phi(z)
If Z follows N(0, 1), then Z has variance sigma^2
If X follows N(mu, sigma^2) and Z = (X - mu)/sigma, then Z follows N(0, 1)
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.1 in the notes says: if X follows N(mu, sigma^2) and Z = (X - mu)/sigma, then Z follows N(0, 1), so one table serves all normal variables.

mcqs.q: What is the probability density function phi(z) of the standard normal variable Z?
options: phi(z) = 1/sqrt(2 pi) e^(-z^2/2) for -infinity < z < infinity
mcqs.why: The notes give the standard normal density as phi(z) = 1/sqrt(2 pi) e^(-z^2/2) for -infinity < z < infinity, where phi(z) is the ordinate at Z = z.

mcqs.q: Theorem 10.2 states that phi(-z) = phi(z). What does this mean?
options: The standard normal curve has no symmetry
The standard normal curve is symmetric about zero
The standard normal curve is symmetric about mu
The ordinate at -z is the negative of the ordinate at z
mcqs.why: The notes state Theorem 10.2 as phi(-z) = phi(z) for Z following N(0, 1), and explain that this means the curve is symmetric about zero.

lessons.title: Exercise — True or False
lessons.notes_html:
The shape of a normal distribution depends upon its parameters, namely mu and sigma.

True

The normal distribution is a bell-shaped symmetrical distribution.

True

In a normal distribution, the mean, median and mode are equal.

True

In a normal distribution, mean and variance are always equal.

False

The expected value of a normal distribution is mu.

True

The two points containing the middle 95.45% area under a normal curve are mu plus-minus sigma.

False

The points of inflexion of the normal curve lie at mu plus-minus 2 sigma.

False

mcqs.q: The shape of a normal distribution depends upon which parameters?
mcqs.why: The lesson marks as True the statement that the shape of a normal distribution depends upon its parameters, namely mu and sigma.

mcqs.q: Which description of the normal distribution is correct?
options: A skewed distribution with a long right tail
A discrete distribution on whole numbers
A uniform distribution on a fixed interval
mcqs.why: The lesson marks as True the statement that the normal distribution is a bell-shaped symmetrical distribution.

mcqs.q: In a normal distribution, what is the relationship between the mean, median and mode?
options: The mean is greater than the median and mode
The mean, median and mode are all equal
The mode is greater than the mean and median
The median is twice the mean
mcqs.why: The lesson marks as True the statement that in a normal distribution the mean, median and mode are equal, all at the centre of the symmetric curve.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the mean and variance of a normal distribution is correct?
options: The mean and variance are always equal
The mean and variance are not always equal
mcqs.why: The lesson marks as False the claim that in a normal distribution the mean and variance are always equal, so they are not always equal.

mcqs.q: What is the expected value of a normal distribution?
mcqs.why: The lesson marks as True the statement that the expected value of a normal distribution is mu, the mean of the distribution.

mcqs.q: Is the statement 'The two points containing the middle 95.45% area under a normal curve are mu plus-minus sigma' true or false?
mcqs.why: The lesson marks this statement as False: the points mu plus-minus sigma do not contain the middle 95.45% area under a normal curve.

mcqs.q: Is the statement 'The points of inflexion of the normal curve lie at mu plus-minus 2 sigma' true or false?
options: True only for the standard normal curve
mcqs.why: The lesson marks this statement as False: the points of inflexion of the normal curve do not lie at mu plus-minus 2 sigma.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements about the normal distribution is TRUE?
options: Its mean and variance are always equal
Its points of inflexion lie at mu plus-minus 2 sigma
Its middle 95.45% area lies between mu - sigma and mu + sigma
mcqs.why: Of the four statements, only 'the expected value is mu' is marked True in the lesson; the other three statements are each marked False.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements about the normal distribution is FALSE?
options: It is a bell-shaped symmetrical distribution
Its shape depends upon mu and sigma
Its mean and variance are always equal
Its mean, median and mode are equal
mcqs.why: The lesson marks 'mean and variance are always equal' as False, while the bell shape, dependence on mu and sigma, and equality of mean, median and mode are all True.

mcqs.q: A student says the normal curve is bell-shaped and symmetrical, with mean, median and mode all equal. How is this claim judged in the lesson?
options: False, because the curve is skewed
False, because only the mean and mode are equal
True only for the standard normal distribution
mcqs.why: The lesson marks both parts as True: the normal distribution is a bell-shaped symmetrical distribution, and in it the mean, median and mode are equal.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3 — Objective Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Note: 7 items already in the earlier Q. 4 block above

Q. 1 (i) The normal distribution is a continuous distribution that ranges from -infinity to infinity.

Q. 1 (ii) The value of the parameter sigma of a normal distribution is always positive

Q. 1 (iii) The normal distribution is a bell shaped symmetrical distribution.

Q. 1 (iv) If X ~ N(50, 25), then sigma = 5

Q. 1 (v) The maximum ordinate of the standard normal curve is at Z = 0

Q. 1 (vi) In a standard normal distribution, if P(Z < z0.975) = 0.975, then z0.975 = 1.96

Q. 1 (vii) The maximum ordinate of a normal curve is at X = mu

Q. 1 (viii) The total area under a normal curve is unity

Q. 1 (ix) The mean of a normal distribution corresponds to z = 0 in the standard normal distribution.

Q. 1 (x) In a normal distribution, the mean, median and mode are equal

Q. 2 (i) In a normal distribution, Q1 = mu - 0.6745 sigma.

Q. 2 (ii) In a normal distribution, Q3 = mu + 0.6745 sigma.

Q. 2 (iii) In a normal distribution, Q.D. is approximately 2/3 sigma.

Q. 2 (iv) In a normal distribution, M.D. is approximately 4/5 sigma.

Q. 2 (v) The limits mu ± 0.6745 sigma include 50 percent area under the normal curve.

Q. 2 (vi) The limits mu ± sigma include 68.27 percent area under the normal curve.

Q. 2 (vii) The limits mu ± 2 sigma include 95.45 percent area under the normal curve.

Q. 2 (viii) The limits mu ± 3 sigma include 99.73 percent area under the normal curve.

Q. 2 (ix) In a normal distribution, all odd ordered moments about mean are zero

Q. 2 (x) In a normal distribution, beta1 = 0 and beta2 = 3

Q. 2 (xi) The normal distribution is neither platykurtic nor leptokurtic but mesokurtic

Q. 2 (xii) The points of inflexion of a normal curve are equidistant from mean.

Q. 3 (i) Normal distribution has two parameters namely mu and sigma-squared.

True

Q. 3 (ii) If X is normally distributed with mean mu and variance sigma-squared then it is denoted by X ~ N(mu, sigma-squared).

True

Q. 3 (iii) The standard normal distribution has mean 0 and variance 1.

True

Q. 3 (iv) The maximum ordinate of a standard normal curve is at Z = 1.

False

Q. 3 (v) The standard normal distribution is symmetrical about Z = 0.

True

Q. 3 (vi) In a standard normal distribution, if P(Z < z0.025) = 0.025, then z0.025 = -1.96.

True

Q. 3 (vii) In a standard normal distribution, if P(Z < z0.975) = 0.975, then z0.975 = 1.96.

True

Q. 3 (viii) In a standard normal distribution, if P(|Z| < a) = 0.95, then a = 1.96.

True

Q. 3 (ix) The normal curve has maximum ordinate at X = 0.

False

Q. 4 (ii) The parameter sigma controls the relative flatness of the normal curve.

True

Q. 4 (v) In a normal distribution, Q1 = mu - 0.6745 sigma and Q3 = mu + 0.6745 sigma.

True

Q. 4 (viii) The standard deviation of a normal distribution is sigma.

True

Q. 4 (ix) The quartile deviation of a normal distribution is 0.6745 sigma.

True

Q. 4 (x) The mean deviation of a normal distribution is 0.7979 sigma.

True

Q. 4 (xii) In a normal distribution, all even ordered moments about mean are zero.

False

Q. 4 (xiii) In a normal distribution, all odd ordered moments about mean are zero.

True

Q. 4 (xiv) In a normal distribution, beta1 = 0 and beta2 = 3.

True

Q. 4 (xvi) The normal curve gets closer and closer to the x-axis but never touches it.

True

mcqs.q: Over what range does the normal distribution extend?
options: From mu - sigma to mu + sigma
mcqs.why: The objective questions state that the normal distribution is a continuous distribution that ranges from -infinity to infinity.

mcqs.q: If X ~ N(50, 25), what is the value of sigma?
mcqs.why: In the notation X ~ N(mu, sigma^2), the second number is the variance. Working: sigma = sqrt(sigma^2) = sqrt(25) = 5, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: In a standard normal distribution, if P(Z < z0.975) = 0.975, what is z0.975?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that in a standard normal distribution, if P(Z < z0.975) = 0.975, then z0.975 = 1.96.

mcqs.q: What is the total area under a normal curve?
mcqs.why: The objective questions state that the total area under a normal curve is unity, because the total probability over the whole range must equal 1.

mcqs.q: In a normal distribution, what is the first quartile Q1?
mcqs.why: The notes give Q1 = mu - 0.6745 sigma and Q3 = mu + 0.6745 sigma, so the first quartile lies 0.6745 sigma below the mean.

mcqs.q: What percentage of the area under the normal curve lies within the limits mu plus-minus 2 sigma?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the limits mu plus-minus 2 sigma include 95.45 percent area under the normal curve, while mu plus-minus sigma gives 68.27 percent.

mcqs.q: In a normal distribution, what are the values of beta1 and beta2?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a normal distribution beta1 = 0 and beta2 = 3, showing zero skewness and the standard peakedness of the normal curve.

mcqs.q: How is the normal distribution described in terms of kurtosis?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the normal distribution is neither platykurtic nor leptokurtic but mesokurtic, consistent with beta2 = 3.

mcqs.q: What is the mean deviation (M.D.) of a normal distribution, in terms of sigma?
mcqs.why: The notes state the mean deviation of a normal distribution is 0.7979 sigma, approximately 4/5 sigma, while 0.6745 sigma is the quartile deviation.

mcqs.q: In a standard normal distribution, if P(|Z| < a) = 0.95, what is the value of a?
mcqs.why: The notes mark as True that in a standard normal distribution, if P(|Z| < a) = 0.95, then a = 1.96, the central 95% limit on each side.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2 — Numerical Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) If X is a normal random variable with mu = 24 and sigma = 4, write down its probability density function. Find the ordinate of its normal curve at x = 21. Also find its maximum ordinate. (Book answers: 0.075285, 0.099735)

Step 1: The normal density is f(x) = 1 / (sigma x sqrt(2 x pi)) x e^(-(x - mu)^2 / (2 x sigma^2)).

Step 2: Put mu = 24 and sigma = 4, so f(x) = 1 / (4 x sqrt(2 x pi)) x e^(-(x - 24)^2 / 32).

Step 3: At x = 21, the exponent is -(21 - 24)^2 / 32 = -9 / 32 = -0.28125.

Step 4: So f(21) = 1 / (4 x 2.5066) x e^(-0.28125) = 0.099735 x 0.754840 = 0.075285.

Step 5: The maximum ordinate is at x = mu = 24, where the exponent is 0.

Step 6: Maximum ordinate = 1 / (4 x sqrt(2 x pi)) = 1 / 10.0265 = 0.099735.

Answer: ordinate at x = 21 is 0.075285; maximum ordinate is 0.099735.

Q. 1 (b) During transcendental meditation, the reduction of a person's oxygen consumption is normal with mu = 37.6 c.c. per minute and sigma = 4.6 c.c. per minute. Find the probabilities that the oxygen will be reduced by (i) at most 35.0, (ii) at least 44.5, (iii) anywhere from 30.0 to 40.0 c.c. per minute. (Book answers: 0.28604, 0.06681, 0.64900)

Step 1: Standardize with Z = (X - mu) / sigma = (X - 37.6) / 4.6.

Step 2: (i) For X = 35.0, Z = (35.0 - 37.6) / 4.6 = -2.6 / 4.6 = -0.57 (to two places, -0.565).

Step 3: From the standard normal table, Phi(-0.57) = 0.2843; with the table value used in the book this is 0.28604.

Step 4: (ii) For X = 44.5, Z = (44.5 - 37.6) / 4.6 = 6.9 / 4.6 = 1.50.

Step 5: P(X >= 44.5) = 1 - Phi(1.50) = 1 - 0.93319 = 0.06681.

Step 6: (iii) For X = 30.0, Z = (30.0 - 37.6) / 4.6 = -1.65; for X = 40.0, Z = (40.0 - 37.6) / 4.6 = 0.52.

Step 7: P(30.0 <= X <= 40.0) = Phi(0.52) - Phi(-1.65) = 0.69847 - 0.04947 = 0.64900.

Answer: (i) 0.28604, (ii) 0.06681, (iii) 0.64900.

Q. 1 (c) Let X ~ N(20, 25). Find the area under the normal curve (i) below 30, (ii) above 30, (iii) between 30 and 42. (Book answers: 0.97725, 0.02275, 0.02274)

Step 1: Here mu = 20 and sigma^2 = 25, so sigma = 5.

Step 2: Standardize with Z = (X - 20) / 5.

Step 3: (i) For X = 30, Z = (30 - 20) / 5 = 2.00, so P(X < 30) = Phi(2.00) = 0.97725.

Step 4: (ii) P(X > 30) = 1 - Phi(2.00) = 1 - 0.97725 = 0.02275.

Step 5: (iii) For X = 42, Z = (42 - 20) / 5 = 4.40, and Phi(4.40) = 1.00000 to five places.

Step 6: P(30 < X < 42) = Phi(4.40) - Phi(2.00) = 1.00000 - 0.97725 = 0.02275, printed in the book as 0.02274.

Answer: (i) 0.97725, (ii) 0.02275, (iii) 0.02274.

Q. 2 (a) IQ scores for adult Pakistanis are normal with mu = 100 and sigma = 10. If a person with an IQ of 130 or above is classed as a genius, what is the probability that a random selection yields a genius? (Book answer: 0.00135)

Step 1: Standardize with Z = (X - mu) / sigma = (X - 100) / 10.

Step 2: For X = 130, Z = (130 - 100) / 10 = 3.00.

Step 3: P(X >= 130) = 1 - Phi(3.00).

Step 4: From the table, Phi(3.00) = 0.99865.

Step 5: Hence P(X >= 130) = 1 - 0.99865 = 0.00135.

Answer: 0.00135.

Q. 2 (b) The mean inside diameter of a sample of 250 washers is 5.05 mm with standard deviation 0.05 mm. The allowed tolerance is 4.95 mm to 5.10 mm; otherwise a washer is defective. Find the percentage of defective washers, assuming a normal distribution. (Book answer: 18.14%)

Step 1: Here mu = 5.05 mm and sigma = 0.05 mm; standardize with Z = (X - 5.05) / 0.05.

Step 2: For X = 4.95, Z = (4.95 - 5.05) / 0.05 = -2.00, so P(X < 4.95) = Phi(-2.00) = 0.02275.

Step 3: For X = 5.10, Z = (5.10 - 5.05) / 0.05 = 1.00, so P(X > 5.10) = 1 - Phi(1.00) = 1 - 0.84134 = 0.15866.

Step 4: A washer is defective if it is below 4.95 mm or above 5.10 mm.

Step 5: P(defective) = 0.02275 + 0.15866 = 0.18141.

Step 6: As a percentage, 0.18141 x 100 = 18.14%.

Answer: 18.14% defective.

Q. 3 (a) The length of life of a washing machine is approximately normal with mean 3.5 years and standard deviation 1.0 year. If the machine is guaranteed for 12 months, what percentage of sales will require replacement? (Book answer: 0.62%)

Step 1: Here mu = 3.5 years and sigma = 1.0 year; 12 months = 1 year.

Step 2: Standardize with Z = (X - 3.5) / 1.0.

Step 3: For X = 1, Z = (1 - 3.5) / 1.0 = -2.50.

Step 4: P(X < 1) = Phi(-2.50) = 0.00621.

Step 5: As a percentage, 0.00621 x 100 = 0.62%.

Answer: 0.62% of sales.

Q. 3 (b) The time X for a runner to run a mile is normal with mu = 4 minutes 1 second and sigma = 2 seconds. Find the probability that he runs the mile (i) in less than 4 minutes, (ii) in more than 3 minutes 55 seconds. (Book answers: 0.3085, 0.9987)

Step 1: Work in seconds: mu = 241 seconds and sigma = 2 seconds.

Step 2: (i) 4 minutes = 240 seconds, so Z = (240 - 241) / 2 = -0.50.

Step 3: P(X < 240) = Phi(-0.50) = 0.30854, i.e. 0.3085.

Step 4: (ii) 3 minutes 55 seconds = 235 seconds, so Z = (235 - 241) / 2 = -3.00.

Step 5: P(X > 235) = 1 - Phi(-3.00) = 1 - 0.00135 = 0.99865, i.e. 0.9987.

Answer: (i) 0.3085, (ii) 0.9987.

Q. 3 (c) The distance X a shot-putter puts the shot is normal with mu = 50 feet and sigma = 5 feet. Find the probability that he tosses it not less than 55 feet, and the probability that his toss travels between 50 feet and 60 feet. (Book answers: 0.1587, 0.4773)

Step 1: Standardize with Z = (X - 50) / 5.

Step 2: For X = 55, Z = (55 - 50) / 5 = 1.00.

Step 3: P(X >= 55) = 1 - Phi(1.00) = 1 - 0.84134 = 0.15866, i.e. 0.1587.

Step 4: For X = 60, Z = (60 - 50) / 5 = 2.00; for X = 50, Z = 0.

Step 5: P(50 < X < 60) = Phi(2.00) - Phi(0) = 0.97725 - 0.50000 = 0.47725, i.e. 0.4773.

Answer: 0.1587 and 0.4773.

Q. 3 (d) If X is normal with parameters mu and sigma, find the area under the curve between (i) (mu - sigma) and (mu + sigma), (ii) mu and (mu + 2 sigma). (Book answers: 0.68268, 0.47725)

Step 1: Standardize with Z = (X - mu) / sigma.

Step 2: (i) X = mu - sigma gives Z = -1; X = mu + sigma gives Z = 1.

Step 3: P(mu - sigma < X < mu + sigma) = Phi(1) - Phi(-1) = 0.84134 - 0.15866 = 0.68268.

Step 4: (ii) X = mu gives Z = 0; X = mu + 2 sigma gives Z = 2.

Step 5: P(mu < X < mu + 2 sigma) = Phi(2) - Phi(0) = 0.97725 - 0.50000 = 0.47725.

Answer: (i) 0.68268, (ii) 0.47725.

Q. 4 (a) FLAG - BOOK ANSWERS DO NOT FOLLOW FROM THE STATED DATA. The heights of boys are normal with mean 150.3 cm and standard deviation 5.0 cm. Find the probability that a boy picked at random has height (i) less than 153 cm, (ii) more than 145 cm, (iii) between 146 cm and 152 cm. (Book prints: 0.67003, 0.83147, 0.5015)

Step 1: Standardize with Z = (X - 150.3) / 5.0.

Step 2: (i) For X = 153, Z = (153 - 150.3) / 5.0 = 2.7 / 5.0 = 0.54.

Step 3: P(X < 153) = Phi(0.54) = 0.70540, NOT the book's printed 0.67003.

Step 4: (ii) For X = 145, Z = (145 - 150.3) / 5.0 = -5.3 / 5.0 = -1.06.

Step 5: P(X > 145) = 1 - Phi(-1.06) = 1 - 0.14457 = 0.85543, NOT the book's printed 0.83147.

Step 6: (iii) For X = 146, Z = -0.86; for X = 152, Z = 0.34.

Step 7: P(146 < X < 152) = Phi(0.34) - Phi(-0.86) = 0.63307 - 0.19489 = 0.43818, NOT the book's printed 0.5015.

Answer (correct from the stated data): (i) 0.70540, (ii) 0.85543, (iii) 0.43818. The book's printed answers are kept above for comparison but do not follow from mu = 150.3, sigma = 5.0.

Q. 4 (b) Weekly incomes X are normal with mean 10.06 Rs. and variance 2.64 Rs-squared. Find P(8 <= X <= 12), assuming incomes are recorded to the nearest rupee. (Book answer: 0.87569)

Step 1: sigma = sqrt(2.64) = 1.6248 Rs.; standardize with Z = (X - 10.06) / 1.6248.

Step 2: Recorded to the nearest rupee, 8 <= X <= 12 means 7.5 <= X <= 12.5 (continuity correction).

Step 3: For X = 7.5, Z = (7.5 - 10.06) / 1.6248 = -2.56 / 1.6248 = -1.58.

Step 4: For X = 12.5, Z = (12.5 - 10.06) / 1.6248 = 2.44 / 1.6248 = 1.50.

Step 5: P(7.5 <= X <= 12.5) = Phi(1.50) - Phi(-1.58) = 0.93319 - 0.05705 = 0.87614, printed in the book as 0.87569.

Answer: 0.87569 (0.87614 by exact calculation; difference is table rounding).

Q. 5 (a) Find the value of X which corresponds to a standardized value of -2.05 and 0.86 for (i) X ~ N(62.3, 38), (ii) X ~ N(mu, sigma-squared), (iii) X ~ N(a, b). (Book answers: 49.66, 67.60; mu - 2.05 sigma, mu + 0.86 sigma; a - 2.05 sqrt(b), a + 0.86 sqrt(b))

Step 1: Use X = mu + Z x sigma.

Step 2: (i) Here sigma = sqrt(38) = 6.1644.

Step 3: For Z = -2.05, X = 62.3 - 2.05 x 6.1644 = 62.3 - 12.637 = 49.66.

Step 4: For Z = 0.86, X = 62.3 + 0.86 x 6.1644 = 62.3 + 5.301 = 67.60.

Step 5: (ii) In general, X = mu - 2.05 sigma for Z = -2.05, and X = mu + 0.86 sigma for Z = 0.86.

Step 6: (iii) Here sigma = sqrt(b), so X = a - 2.05 sqrt(b) and X = a + 0.86 sqrt(b).

Answer: (i) 49.66, 67.60; (ii) mu - 2.05 sigma, mu + 0.86 sigma; (iii) a - 2.05 sqrt(b), a + 0.86 sqrt(b).

Q. 5 (b) If X ~ N(100, 64), find the value of a such that P(X < a) = 0.95. (Book answer: 113.16)

Step 1: Here mu = 100 and sigma = sqrt(64) = 8.

Step 2: P(X < a) = 0.95 means Phi((a - 100) / 8) = 0.95.

Step 3: From the table, the Z value with Phi(Z) = 0.95 is Z = 1.645.

Step 4: So (a - 100) / 8 = 1.645.

Step 5: Hence a = 100 + 1.645 x 8 = 100 + 13.16 = 113.16.

Answer: a = 113.16.

Q. 5 (c) If X ~ N(60, 25), find the value of a such that P(X > a) = 0.837. (Book answer: 55.09)

Step 1: Here mu = 60 and sigma = sqrt(25) = 5.

Step 2: P(X > a) = 0.837 means P(X <= a) = 1 - 0.837 = 0.163.

Step 3: So Phi((a - 60) / 5) = 0.163, and from the table (a - 60) / 5 = -0.98.

Step 4: Hence a = 60 - 0.98 x 5 = 60 - 4.91 = 55.09.

Answer: a = 55.09.

Q. 6 (a) In a normal distribution mu = 30 and sigma = 5. Find (i) a point that has 15% area below it, (ii) a point that has 28% area above it, (iii) two points containing the middle 95% area. (Book answers: 24.8; 32.9; 20.2 and 39.8)

Step 1: Use X = mu + Z x sigma = 30 + 5Z.

Step 2: (i) 15% below means Phi(Z) = 0.15, so Z = -1.04 (table value).

Step 3: X = 30 - 1.04 x 5 = 30 - 5.2 = 24.8.

Step 4: (ii) 28% above means Phi(Z) = 0.72, so Z = 0.58 (table value).

Step 5: X = 30 + 0.58 x 5 = 30 + 2.9 = 32.9.

Step 6: (iii) The middle 95% leaves 2.5% in each tail, so Z = -1.96 and Z = +1.96.

Step 7: X = 30 - 1.96 x 5 = 20.2 and X = 30 + 1.96 x 5 = 39.8.

Answer: (i) 24.8, (ii) 32.9, (iii) 20.2 and 39.8.

Q. 6 (b) The time for a nurse to inject a shot of penicillin is normal with mu = 30 seconds and sigma = 10 seconds. Find (i) the 10th percentile, (ii) the 90th percentile. (Book answers: 17.2 sec, 42.8 sec)

Step 1: Use X = mu + Z x sigma = 30 + 10Z.

Step 2: (i) The 10th percentile has Phi(Z) = 0.10, so Z = -1.28 (table value).

Step 3: X = 30 - 1.28 x 10 = 30 - 12.8 = 17.2 seconds.

Step 4: (ii) The 90th percentile has Phi(Z) = 0.90, so Z = 1.28.

Step 5: X = 30 + 1.28 x 10 = 30 + 12.8 = 42.8 seconds.

Answer: (i) 17.2 sec, (ii) 42.8 sec.

Q. 6 (c) Scores on a national education achievement test are normal with mu = 500 and sigma = 100. Find (i) the 95th percentile, (ii) the lower and upper quartiles, (iii) the score separating the successful applicants if the university takes the top 40 percent. (Book answers: 664.5; 432.55, 567.45; 525.33)

Step 1: Use X = 500 + 100Z.

Step 2: (i) The 95th percentile has Phi(Z) = 0.95, so Z = 1.645.

Step 3: X = 500 + 1.645 x 100 = 500 + 164.5 = 664.5.

Step 4: (ii) Quartiles use Z = -0.6745 and Z = +0.6745.

Step 5: Lower quartile = 500 - 0.6745 x 100 = 500 - 67.45 = 432.55.

Step 6: Upper quartile = 500 + 0.6745 x 100 = 500 + 67.45 = 567.45.

Step 7: (iii) Taking the top 40 percent means 60 percent are below the cut-off, so Phi(Z) = 0.60 and Z = 0.2533.

Step 8: Cut-off = 500 + 0.2533 x 100 = 500 + 25.33 = 525.33.

Answer: (i) 664.5, (ii) 432.55 and 567.45, (iii) 525.33.

Q. 7 (a) A high jumper's cleared height is normal with mean 6 feet and standard deviation 2.4 inches. Find (i) the greatest height he will jump with probability 0.95, (ii) the height he will clear only 10% of the time. (Book answers: 68.06 inches, 75 inches)

Step 1: Work in inches: mean = 6 feet = 72 inches, sigma = 2.4 inches.

Step 2: (i) 'With probability 0.95' here means the height exceeded 95% of the time is not intended; the book's value is the 5th percentile: Phi(Z) = 0.05 gives Z = -1.645.

Step 3: X = 72 - 1.645 x 2.4 = 72 - 3.948 = 68.05 inches, i.e. 68.06 inches.

Step 4: (ii) Clearing a height only 10% of the time means 90% are below it: Phi(Z) = 0.90 gives Z = 1.28.

Step 5: X = 72 + 1.28 x 2.4 = 72 + 3.07 = 75.07 inches, i.e. 75 inches.

Answer: (i) 68.06 inches, (ii) 75 inches.

Q. 7 (b) The amount of vaccine needed to immunize against smallpox is normal with mu = 0.250 ounce and sigma = 0.040 ounce. Increasing the dosage increases the chance of success. What is the minimum dosage required to produce success in 99 percent of cases? (Book answer: 0.34304 ounces)

Step 1: Success in 99 percent of cases means the dosage must cover the 99th percentile.

Step 2: Phi(Z) = 0.99 gives Z = 2.326 (table value).

Step 3: Dosage = mu + Z x sigma = 0.250 + 2.326 x 0.040.

Step 4: 2.326 x 0.040 = 0.09304.

Step 5: Dosage = 0.250 + 0.09304 = 0.34304 ounces.

Answer: 0.34304 ounces.

Q. 8 (a) If X ~ N(70, 25), find the value of a such that P(|X - 70| < a) = 0.8. Hence find the limits within which the central 80% of the distribution lies. (Book answers: 6.41; 63.59, 76.41)

Step 1: Here mu = 70 and sigma = sqrt(25) = 5.

Step 2: P(|X - 70| < a) = 0.8 means the central 80% lies between 70 - a and 70 + a.

Step 3: The central 80% leaves 10% in each tail, so a / 5 = 1.282 (the Z value with 0.90 below it).

Step 4: Hence a = 1.282 x 5 = 6.41.

Step 5: Lower limit = 70 - 6.41 = 63.59; upper limit = 70 + 6.41 = 76.41.

Answer: a = 6.41; limits 63.59 to 76.41.

Q. 8 (b) Bags of flour have masses normal with mean 500 g and standard deviation 20 g. 2% of bags are rejected for being underweight and 1% for being overweight.

Between what values should the mass of a bag lie to be accepted? (Book answers: 458.92, 546.52)

Step 1: Acceptance means the mass is above the 2nd percentile and below the 99th percentile.

Step 2: For the 2nd percentile, Phi(Z) = 0.02 gives Z = -2.054.

Step 3: Lower limit = 500 - 2.054 x 20 = 500 - 41.08 = 458.92 g.

Step 4: For the 99th percentile, Phi(Z) = 0.99 gives Z = 2.326.

Step 5: Upper limit = 500 + 2.326 x 20 = 500 + 46.52 = 546.52 g.

Answer: between 458.92 g and 546.52 g.

Q. 9 (a) The lengths of items are normal with mean mu cm and standard deviation 12 cm. It is known that 4.78% of items have a length greater than 92 cm. Find mu.

(Book answer: 72)

Step 1: P(X > 92) = 0.0478 means P(X <= 92) = 1 - 0.0478 = 0.9522.

Step 2: Phi(Z) = 0.9522 gives Z = 1.67 (table value).

Step 3: So (92 - mu) / 12 = 1.67.

Step 4: Hence 92 - mu = 1.67 x 12 = 20.04.

Step 5: Therefore mu = 92 - 20.04 = 71.96, i.e. 72 cm.

Answer: mu = 72 cm.

Q. 9 (b) Rod lengths in a workshop are normal with mean mu and variance 4. If 10% of rods are less than 17.4 cm long, find the probability that a rod chosen at random will be between 18 cm and 23 cm long. (Book answer: 0.7725)

Step 1: sigma = sqrt(4) = 2 cm.

Step 2: P(X < 17.4) = 0.10 gives (17.4 - mu) / 2 = -1.282.

Step 3: Hence 17.4 - mu = -2.564, so mu = 17.4 + 2.564 = 19.964 cm.

Step 4: For X = 18, Z = (18 - 19.964) / 2 = -0.982; for X = 23, Z = (23 - 19.964) / 2 = 1.518.

Step 5: P(18 < X < 23) = Phi(1.518) - Phi(-0.982) = 0.9355 - 0.1630 = 0.7725.

Answer: 0.7725.

Q. 10 (a) Tea is sold in packages marked 750 g. Package masses are normal with mean 760 g and standard deviation sigma. What is the maximum value of sigma if less than 1% of packages are underweight? (Book answer: 4.299)

Step 1: Underweight means X < 750 g; we need P(X < 750) = 0.01 at the maximum sigma.

Step 2: P(X < 750) = 0.01 gives (750 - 760) / sigma = -2.326.

Step 3: So -10 / sigma = -2.326.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 10 / 2.326 = 4.299.

Answer: maximum sigma = 4.299 g.

Q. 10 (b) The life in hours of an electric tube is normal with mu = 160 hours and standard deviation sigma hours. What is the maximum allowable value of sigma if the life X of a tube is to have probability 0.80 of being between 120 and 200 hours?

(Book answer: 31.21)

Step 1: The interval 120 to 200 is symmetric about mu = 160, with half-width 40 hours.

Step 2: P(120 < X < 200) = 0.80 means the central 80%, so (200 - 160) / sigma = 1.282.

Step 3: Hence 40 / sigma = 1.282.

Step 4: Therefore sigma = 40 / 1.282 = 31.20, i.e. 31.21 by the table value used in the book.

Answer: maximum sigma = 31.21 hours.

Q. 11 (a) A large number of students have average weight 150 lb and weights are normally distributed. If 36.4% of students have weights between 137 lb and 163 lb, what is the standard deviation of the weights? (Book answer: 27.47)

Step 1: The interval 137 to 163 is symmetric about the mean 150, with half-width 13 lb.

Step 2: P(137 < X < 163) = 0.364 means Phi(Z) - Phi(-Z) = 0.364, where Z = 13 / sigma.

Step 3: Hence Phi(Z) = 0.5 + 0.364 / 2 = 0.682, so Z = 0.473 (table value).

Step 4: So 13 / sigma = 0.473.

Step 5: Therefore sigma = 13 / 0.473 = 27.48, i.e. 27.47 lb by the table value used in the book.

Answer: sigma = 27.47 lb.

Q. 11 (b) In a normal distribution mu = 40 and P(25 < X < 55) = 0.8662. Find P(20 < X < 60). (Book answer: 0.9545)

Step 1: The interval 25 to 55 is symmetric about mu = 40, with half-width 15.

Step 2: P(25 < X < 55) = 0.8662 means Phi(Z) - Phi(-Z) = 0.8662 with Z = 15 / sigma.

Step 3: Hence Phi(Z) = 0.5 + 0.8662 / 2 = 0.9331, so Z = 1.50.

Step 4: So 15 / sigma = 1.50, giving sigma = 10.

Step 5: For the interval 20 to 60, Z = (60 - 40) / 10 = 2 and Z = -2.

Step 6: P(20 < X < 60) = Phi(2) - Phi(-2) = 0.97725 - 0.02275 = 0.95450.

Answer: 0.9545.

Q. 12 (a) In a normal distribution 31% of items are under 45 and 8% are over 64.

Find the mean and standard deviation. (Book answers: 50, 10)

Step 1: P(X < 45) = 0.31 gives (45 - mu) / sigma = -0.496 (table value).

Step 2: P(X > 64) = 0.08 gives P(X <= 64) = 0.92, so (64 - mu) / sigma = 1.405 (table value).

Step 3: Subtract the two equations: (64 - 45) / sigma = 1.405 - (-0.496) = 1.901.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 19 / 1.901 = 9.995, i.e. 10.

Step 5: From the first equation, mu = 45 + 0.496 x 10 = 45 + 4.96 = 49.96, i.e. 50.

Answer: mean = 50, standard deviation = 10.

Q. 12 (b) If X ~ N(mu, sigma-squared) and P(X < 35) = 0.20 and P(35 < X < 45) = 0.65, find mu and sigma. (Book answers: 39.5, 5.32)

Step 1: P(X < 35) = 0.20 gives (35 - mu) / sigma = -0.842 (table value).

Step 2: P(35 < X < 45) = 0.65, so P(X < 45) = 0.20 + 0.65 = 0.85, giving (45 - mu) / sigma = 1.036 (table value).

Step 3: Subtract: (45 - 35) / sigma = 1.036 - (-0.842) = 1.878.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 10 / 1.878 = 5.32.

Step 5: From the first equation, mu = 35 + 0.842 x 5.32 = 35 + 4.48 = 39.48, i.e. 39.5.

Answer: mu = 39.5, sigma = 5.32.

Q. 13 (a) Marks are normally distributed. The number of first-class students (60% or more) is 25, the number of failed students (less than 30% marks) is 90, and the total number of candidates is 450. Find the mean and standard deviation. (Book answers: 40.37, 12.32)

Step 1: P(X >= 60) = 25 / 450 = 0.0556, so P(X < 60) = 0.9444 and (60 - mu) / sigma = 1.593.

Step 2: P(X < 30) = 90 / 450 = 0.20, so (30 - mu) / sigma = -0.842.

Step 3: Subtract: (60 - 30) / sigma = 1.593 - (-0.842) = 2.435.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 30 / 2.435 = 12.32.

Step 5: From the second equation, mu = 30 + 0.842 x 12.32 = 30 + 10.37 = 40.37.

Answer: mean = 40.37, standard deviation = 12.32.

Q. 13 (b) A marketing organization grades apples: small (diameter less than 60 mm), medium (60 to 80 mm), large (more than 80 mm). A grower finds 61% of his crop is small and 14% is large. Assuming the diameter X is normal, calculate the standard deviation and mean. (Book answers: 24.97, 53.03)

Step 1: P(X < 60) = 0.61 gives (60 - mu) / sigma = 0.279 (table value).

Step 2: P(X > 80) = 0.14 gives P(X <= 80) = 0.86, so (80 - mu) / sigma = 1.080 (table value).

Step 3: Subtract: (80 - 60) / sigma = 1.080 - 0.279 = 0.801.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 20 / 0.801 = 24.97 mm.

Step 5: From the first equation, mu = 60 - 0.279 x 24.97 = 60 - 6.97 = 53.03 mm.

Answer: standard deviation = 24.97 mm, mean = 53.03 mm.

Q. 13 (c) The maximum temperature on June 1 in a locality is normally distributed over years. About 15% of the time it has exceeded 30 degrees C, and about 5% of the time it has been less than 20 degrees C. What are the mean and variance?

(Book answers: 26.13 degrees C, 13.91 degrees C)

Step 1: P(X > 30) = 0.15 gives P(X <= 30) = 0.85, so (30 - mu) / sigma = 1.036.

Step 2: P(X < 20) = 0.05 gives (20 - mu) / sigma = -1.645.

Step 3: Subtract: (30 - 20) / sigma = 1.036 - (-1.645) = 2.681.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 10 / 2.681 = 3.73 degrees C.

Step 5: From the second equation, mu = 20 + 1.645 x 3.73 = 20 + 6.13 = 26.13 degrees C.

Step 6: Variance = sigma-squared = 3.73 x 3.73 = 13.91 (square degrees C; the book prints degrees C).

Answer: mean = 26.13 degrees C, variance = 13.91.

Q. 14 (a) A man cuts hazel twigs for bean poles, saying a stick is 240 cm long. In fact the length is normal, 10% are 250 cm or more, while 55% are over 240 cm. Find the probability that a stick picked at random is less than 235 cm long. (Book answer: 0.203)

Step 1: P(X >= 250) = 0.10 gives (250 - mu) / sigma = 1.282.

Step 2: P(X > 240) = 0.55 gives P(X <= 240) = 0.45, so (240 - mu) / sigma = -0.126.

Step 3: Subtract: (250 - 240) / sigma = 1.282 - (-0.126) = 1.408.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 10 / 1.408 = 7.10 cm.

Step 5: From the second equation, mu = 240 + 0.126 x 7.10 = 240 + 0.89 = 240.89 cm.

Step 6: For X = 235, Z = (235 - 240.89) / 7.10 = -5.89 / 7.10 = -0.83.

Step 7: P(X < 235) = Phi(-0.83) = 0.2033, i.e. 0.203.

Answer: 0.203.

Q. 14 (b) The 90th percentile of a normal distribution is 50 while the 15th percentile is 25. Find (i) mu and sigma, (ii) the 40th percentile. (Book answers: 36.17, 10.79, 33.44)

Step 1: (50 - mu) / sigma = 1.282 (90th percentile) and (25 - mu) / sigma = -1.036 (15th percentile).

Step 2: Subtract: (50 - 25) / sigma = 1.282 - (-1.036) = 2.318.

Step 3: Hence sigma = 25 / 2.318 = 10.79.

Step 4: From the second equation, mu = 25 + 1.036 x 10.79 = 25 + 11.18 = 36.18, i.e. 36.17 by the table value used in the book.

Step 5: (ii) The 40th percentile has Phi(Z) = 0.40, so Z = -0.253.

Step 6: 40th percentile = 36.17 - 0.253 x 10.79 = 36.17 - 2.73 = 33.44.

Answer: (i) mu = 36.17, sigma = 10.79; (ii) 40th percentile = 33.44.

Q. 15 (a) The masses of articles in a workshop are normal with mean mu and standard deviation sigma. 5% of articles have a mass greater than 85 g and 10% have a mass less than 25 g. Find mu and sigma, and find the range symmetrical about the mean within which 75% of the masses lie. (Book answers: 51.3, 20.5, 26.72, 73.88)

Step 1: P(X > 85) = 0.05 gives (85 - mu) / sigma = 1.645.

Step 2: P(X < 25) = 0.10 gives (25 - mu) / sigma = -1.282.

Step 3: Subtract: (85 - 25) / sigma = 1.645 - (-1.282) = 2.927.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 60 / 2.927 = 20.50 g.

Step 5: From the second equation, mu = 25 + 1.282 x 20.50 = 25 + 26.28 = 51.28, i.e. 51.3 g.

Step 6: The middle 75% leaves 12.5% in each tail, so Z = 1.150 (since Phi(1.150) = 0.875).

Step 7: Half-width = 1.150 x 20.50 = 23.58 g.

Step 8: Range = 51.3 - 23.58 to 51.3 + 23.58 = 27.72 g to 74.88 g.

Answer: mu = 51.3 g, sigma = 20.5 g, 75% range 27.72 g to 74.88 g. FLAG: the book's printed range 26.72 to 73.88 is centred at 50.3, not at mu = 51.3, so it does not follow from the book's own mu; the corrected range above is used.

Q. 15 (b) In a certain examination, the percentages of passes and distinctions were 80 and 10 respectively. Estimate the average marks, the minimum pass and distinction marks being 40 and 75 respectively, assuming marks are normal. (Book answers: 53.87, 16.48)

Step 1: Pass means X >= 40 with probability 0.80, so P(X < 40) = 0.20 and (40 - mu) / sigma = -0.842.

Step 2: Distinction means X >= 75 with probability 0.10, so P(X < 75) = 0.90 and (75 - mu) / sigma = 1.282.

Step 3: Subtract: (75 - 40) / sigma = 1.282 - (-0.842) = 2.124.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 35 / 2.124 = 16.48.

Step 5: From the first equation, mu = 40 + 0.842 x 16.48 = 40 + 13.87 = 53.87.

Answer: average marks = 53.87, standard deviation = 16.48.

Q. 16 (a) What is the importance of the normal distribution in statistical theory?

Describe its properties.

The normal distribution is the most important continuous distribution in statistics.

It describes many natural measurements, such as heights, weights and examination marks.

It is the limiting form of many other distributions, including the binomial for large n.

Its properties are: it is bell-shaped and symmetrical about its mean.

Its mean, median and mode are all equal.

Its total area under the curve is 1.

Its points of inflexion are at mu - sigma and mu + sigma.

Its odd moments about the mean are zero, and beta1 = 0 and beta2 = 3.

Its quartile deviation is 0.6745 sigma and its mean deviation is 0.7979 sigma.

Q. 16 (b) Suppose X is normally distributed with mu = 25 and sigma = 5. Find (i) the lower and upper quartiles, (ii) the median, (iii) the mean deviation. (Book answers: 21.6, 28.4, 25, 4)

Step 1: Quartiles use Z = -0.6745 for Q1 and Z = +0.6745 for Q3.

Step 2: Q1 = mu - 0.6745 x sigma = 25 - 0.6745 x 5 = 25 - 3.3725 = 21.6275, i.e. 21.6.

Step 3: Q3 = mu + 0.6745 x sigma = 25 + 0.6745 x 5 = 25 + 3.3725 = 28.3725, i.e. 28.4.

Step 4: In a normal distribution the median equals the mean, so median = 25.

Step 5: Mean deviation = 0.7979 x sigma = 0.7979 x 5 = 3.9895, i.e. 4.

Answer: lower quartile 21.6, upper quartile 28.4, median 25, mean deviation 4.

Q. 16 (c) In a normal distribution, the lower and upper quartiles are respectively 8 and 17. Find the mean and standard deviation. (Book answers: 12.5, 6.67)

Step 1: For a normal distribution, Q1 = mu - 0.6745 sigma = 8 and Q3 = mu + 0.6745 sigma = 17.

Step 2: Add the two equations: 2 mu = 8 + 17 = 25, so mu = 12.5.

Step 3: Subtract the two equations: Q3 - Q1 = 2 x 0.6745 sigma = 1.349 sigma = 17 - 8 = 9.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 9 / 1.349 = 6.67.

Answer: mean = 12.5, standard deviation = 6.67.

Q. 16 (d) The continuous random variable X is normally distributed with mean mu and standard deviation sigma. Given P(X < 53) = 0.04 and P(X < 65) = 0.97, find the interquartile range. (Book answer: 4.46)

Step 1: P(X < 53) = 0.04 gives (53 - mu) / sigma = -1.751 (table value).

Step 2: P(X < 65) = 0.97 gives (65 - mu) / sigma = 1.881 (table value).

Step 3: Subtract: (65 - 53) / sigma = 1.881 - (-1.751) = 3.632.

Step 4: Hence sigma = 12 / 3.632 = 3.304.

Step 5: Interquartile range = Q3 - Q1 = 1.349 x sigma = 1.349 x 3.304 = 4.457, i.e. 4.46.

Answer: interquartile range = 4.46.

Q. 17 (a) The value of the second moment about the mean in a normal distribution is 4. Find the third and fourth moments about the mean. (Book answers: 0, 48)

Step 1: The second moment about the mean is mu2 = sigma-squared = 4, so sigma = 2.

Step 2: In a normal distribution all odd moments about the mean are zero, so mu3 = 0.

Step 3: The fourth moment about the mean is mu4 = 3 sigma^4.

Step 4: sigma^4 = 4 x 4 = 16, so mu4 = 3 x 16 = 48.

Answer: third moment = 0, fourth moment = 48.

Q. 17 (b) Find the proportion of the area under the normal curve included between the limits mu +/- sigma, mu +/- 2 sigma and mu +/- 3 sigma. (Book answers: 0.6827, 0.9545, 0.9973)

Step 1: Standardize with Z = (X - mu) / sigma, so the limits become Z = -1 to 1, -2 to 2, and -3 to 3.

Step 2: For mu +/- sigma: Phi(1) - Phi(-1) = 0.84134 - 0.15866 = 0.68268, i.e. 0.6827.

Step 3: For mu +/- 2 sigma: Phi(2) - Phi(-2) = 0.97725 - 0.02275 = 0.95450, i.e. 0.9545.

Step 4: For mu +/- 3 sigma: Phi(3) - Phi(-3) = 0.99865 - 0.00135 = 0.99730, i.e. 0.9973.

Answer: 0.6827, 0.9545, 0.9973.

Q. 17 (c) If X is a random variable with distribution N(12.5, 9) and Y = g(X) = 2X + 5, find P(-infinity <= Y <= 21) and P(45 <= Y <= infinity). (Book answers: 0.06681, 0.00621)

Step 1: For X ~ N(12.5, 9), mu_X = 12.5 and sigma_X = 3.

Step 2: A linear function of a normal variable is normal: Y = 2X + 5 has mean 2 x 12.5 + 5 = 30.

Step 3: The standard deviation of Y is 2 x sigma_X = 2 x 3 = 6, so Y ~ N(30, 36).

Step 4: For Y = 21, Z = (21 - 30) / 6 = -1.50, so P(Y <= 21) = Phi(-1.50) = 0.06681.

Step 5: For Y = 45, Z = (45 - 30) / 6 = 2.50, so P(Y >= 45) = 1 - Phi(2.50) = 1 - 0.99379 = 0.00621.

Answer: 0.06681 and 0.00621.

mcqs.q: X is normal with mu = 24 and sigma = 4. What is the ordinate of its normal curve at x = 21?
Boys' heights are normal with mu = 150.3 cm and sigma = 5.0 cm. What is P(X < 153), the probability that a boy picked at random is less than 153 cm tall?
mcqs.why: Working: Z = (X - mu)/sigma = (153 - 150.3)/5.0 = 2.7/5.0 = 0.54, so P(X < 153) = Phi(0.54) = 0.70540. The book prints 0.67003, but that value does not follow from mu = 150.3 and sigma = 5.0, so the corrected value 0.70540 is used.

mcqs.q: During meditation, oxygen reduction is normal with mu = 37.6 and sigma = 4.6 c.c. per minute. What is the probability that the reduction is at least 44.5 c.c. per minute?
Let X ~ N(20, 25). What is the area under the normal curve below 30?
IQ scores are normal with mu = 100 and sigma = 10. A person with IQ 130 or above is classed as a genius. What is the probability that a random selection yields a genius?
Washer diameters are normal with mu = 5.05 mm and sigma = 0.05 mm. Washers outside 4.95 mm to 5.10 mm are defective. What percentage of washers are defective?
The life of a washing machine is normal with mean 3.5 years and standard deviation 1.0 year. It is guaranteed for 12 months. What percentage of sales will require replacement?
A runner's mile time is normal with mu = 4 minutes 1 second and sigma = 2 seconds. What is the probability that he runs the mile in less than 4 minutes?
mcqs.why: Working: in seconds mu = 241 and sigma = 2; 4 minutes = 240 seconds. Z = (240 - 241)/2 = -0.50. Then P(X < 240) = Phi(-0.50) = 0.30854, i.e. 0.3085.

mcqs.q: A shot-putter's distance is normal with mu = 50 feet and sigma = 5 feet. What is the probability that his toss travels between 50 feet and 60 feet?
If X ~ N(100, 64), what is the value of a such that P(X < a) = 0.95?

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Sampling Techniques and Sampling Distributions

lessons.title: Exercise — Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
What is sampling? Why is it used?

Sampling means selecting a part of the population for study.

It is used because studying the whole population is often costly, slow or impossible.

A well-chosen sample gives reliable information about the population.

What is a sampling distribution? What is the standard error?

The sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic computed from samples.

Its standard deviation is called the standard error of that statistic.

The standard error measures how much the statistic varies from sample to sample.

mcqs.q: What does sampling mean?
options: Selecting a part of the population for study
Studying every unit of the population
Listing only the largest units of a population
Recording the results of a complete census
mcqs.why: Sampling means selecting a part of the population for study, instead of examining the whole population.

mcqs.q: Why is sampling used instead of studying the whole population?
options: Because a sample always contains every population unit
Because studying the whole population is often costly, slow or impossible
Because population values are never needed in statistics
Because samples never vary from one another
mcqs.why: Studying the whole population is often costly, slow or impossible, so a part of it is selected and studied instead.

mcqs.q: What can a well-chosen sample provide?
options: Exact values for every unit in the population
A guarantee that no error of any kind can occur
The complete list of all sampling units
mcqs.why: The notes state that a well-chosen sample gives reliable information about the population it was drawn from.

mcqs.q: What is a sampling distribution?
options: The list of all sampling units in a population
The distribution of values within a single sample
The difference between a statistic and a parameter
The probability distribution of a statistic computed from samples
mcqs.why: A sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic computed from samples drawn from a population.

mcqs.q: What is the standard error of a statistic?
options: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of that statistic
The mean of the sampling distribution of that statistic
The difference between the sample mean and the population mean
The number of samples that can be drawn from a population
mcqs.why: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic is called the standard error of that statistic.

mcqs.q: What does the standard error measure?
options: How large the population is compared with the sample
How much the statistic varies from sample to sample
How many units were left out of the sample
How costly it was to collect the sample data
mcqs.why: The standard error measures how much the statistic varies from sample to sample, because it is the spread of its sampling distribution.

mcqs.q: Which statement about sampling is correct?
options: Sampling examines every unit of the population
Sampling is used only when the population is very small
Sampling selects a part of the population for study
Sampling removes the need to choose the sample carefully
mcqs.why: Sampling is the selection of a part of the population for study; examining every unit would be a complete enumeration, not sampling.

mcqs.q: The probability distribution of which quantity is a sampling distribution?
options: A single observation from the population
mcqs.why: A sampling distribution belongs to a statistic computed from samples; a parameter is a fixed population value, not a distribution over samples.

mcqs.q: If a statistic varies very little from sample to sample, what does that imply about its standard error?
options: Its standard error equals the population size
Its standard error cannot be defined
mcqs.why: The standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution, so little variation from sample to sample means a small standard error.

mcqs.q: Which pair of ideas is correctly matched?
options: Sampling distribution - a list of sampling units
Standard error - the standard deviation of a sampling distribution
Statistic - a value that never changes between samples
mcqs.why: The standard error is defined as the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic, so this pair is correctly matched.

lessons.title: Exercise — True or False
lessons.notes_html:
A sample survey provides results which are more accurate than those obtained from a census.

False

A sample design is a procedure for obtaining a sample from a given population prior to collecting any data.

True

In sampling with replacement, the sample size may be greater than the population size.

True

In sampling without replacement, the sample size can be greater than population size.

False

The standard deviation of a sampling distribution of a statistic is called the standard error of that statistic.

True

We can decrease both sampling error and standard error by increasing the sample size.

True

mcqs.q: The statement 'A sample survey provides results which are more accurate than those obtained from a census' is:
options: True, for every population and every survey
True, only when the sample is larger than the population
True, only when sampling is without replacement
mcqs.why: The notes mark this statement False: a sample survey does not provide results more accurate than those obtained from a census.

mcqs.q: A sample design is a procedure for obtaining a sample from a given population. When is this procedure fixed?
options: After all the data have been collected
Only after the first sample is drawn
At the time the results are published
mcqs.why: The notes mark this True: a sample design is a procedure for obtaining a sample, decided prior to collecting any data.

mcqs.q: In sampling with replacement, can the sample size be greater than the population size?
options: No, it can never exceed the population size
Yes, only if the population is infinite
No, because each unit is used at most once
Yes, because units are returned and may be drawn again
mcqs.why: The notes mark this True: with replacement a unit is returned before the next draw, so the sample size may be greater than the population size.

mcqs.q: In sampling without replacement, can the sample size be greater than the population size?
options: Yes, if the draws are made quickly
Yes, whenever the population is finite
mcqs.why: The notes mark this False: without replacement each unit can be used only once, so the sample size cannot exceed the population size.

mcqs.q: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic is called its:
mcqs.why: The notes mark this True: the standard deviation of a sampling distribution of a statistic is called the standard error of that statistic.

mcqs.q: How can both sampling error and standard error be decreased?
options: By using a smaller sampling frame
mcqs.why: The notes mark this True: increasing the sample size decreases both the sampling error and the standard error.

mcqs.q: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the notes?
options: A census is always less accurate than any sample survey
Without replacement, the sample size can exceed the population size
With replacement, the sample size may exceed the population size
Increasing the sample size increases the standard error
mcqs.why: With replacement is the true statement: returned units may be drawn again, so the sample size may be greater than the population size.

mcqs.q: Which of the following statements is FALSE according to the notes?
options: A sample design is fixed prior to collecting any data
The standard error is the standard deviation of a sampling distribution
Increasing the sample size decreases the standard error
A sample survey is always more accurate than a census
mcqs.why: The false statement is the claim about the sample survey: the notes mark 'a sample survey is more accurate than a census' as False.

mcqs.q: As the sample size increases, what happens to the standard error?
options: It becomes equal to the population mean
mcqs.why: The notes state that we can decrease both sampling error and standard error by increasing the sample size.

mcqs.q: In sampling with replacement, why may more draws be made than there are units in the population?
options: Because new units are added to the population during sampling
Because each selected unit is returned before the next draw and can be selected again
Because the population size is not counted in this method
Because every unit is selected exactly twice
mcqs.why: With replacement, the selected unit is returned to the population before the next draw, so draws can continue beyond the population size.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.5 — Objective Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (i) A population is the totality of the observations made on all the objects possessing some common specific characteristics.

Q. 1 (ii) A sample is a part of the population which is selected with the expectation that it will represent the characteristics of the population.

Q. 1 (iii) Sampling is a procedure of selecting a representative sample from a given population.

Q. 1 (iv) The descriptive measures of a population are called parameters

Q. 1 (v) A descriptive measure on the sample observations is called statistic

Q. 1 (vi) A population is called finite if it includes a limited number of sampling units.

Q. 1 (vii) A population is called infinite if it includes an unlimited number of sampling units.

Q. 1 (viii) Sampling frame is a complete list of the sampling units.

Q. 1 (ix) A non-probability sampling is a procedure in which we cannot assign to an element of the population the probability of its being included in the sample.

Q. 1 (x) A probability sampling is a process in which the sample is selected in such a way that every element of a population has a known nonzero probability of being included in the sample.

Q. 1 (xi) Another name of a probability sampling is random sampling.

Q. 1 (xii) Random sampling provides reliable estimates

Q. 1 (xiii) The sampling is said to be with replacement when the unit selected at random is returned to the population before the next unit is selected.

Q. 1 (xiv) The sampling is said to be without replacement when the unit selected at random is returned to the population before the next unit is selected. (Book misprint: the sense is 'is NOT returned'.)

Q. 1 (xv) A sample is usually selected by without replacement.

Q. 1 (xvi) In sampling with replacement, a sampling unit can be selected more than once.

Q. 2 (ii) In sampling with replacement, a finite population becomes infinite

Q. 2 (iii) Simple random sampling is a procedure of selecting a sample from the population in such a way that every unit available for sampling has an equal probability of being selected.

Q. 2 (iv) The sampling error decreases by increasing the sample size

Q. 2 (v) The non-sampling errors may be present both in sample survey and census.

Q. 2 (vi) The bias increases by increasing the sample size

Q. 2 (vii) A sample which is free from bias is called an unbiased sample.

Q. 2 (viii) Non-sampling errors may arise due to faulty sampling frames, non-responses and processing of data.

Q. 2 (ix) Non-sampling errors can be controlled by the proper training of the investigators and following up the non-responses.

Q. 2 (x) The probability distribution of a sample statistic is called sampling distribution of that statistic.

Q. 2 (xi) The standard deviation of sampling distribution of a sample statistic is called the standard error of that statistic.

Q. 2 (xii) The standard error can be reduced by increasing the sample size

Q. 2 (xiii) The number of all possible samples of size n taken with replacement from a population of size N is N to the power n

Q. 2 (xiv) The number of all possible samples of size n taken without replacement from a population of size N is N P n

Q. 3 (i) A descriptive measure on the sample observations is called parameter and a descriptive measure of a population is called statistic.

False

Q. 3 (ii) A sample statistic is a random variable whereas the parameter being estimated is constant.

True

Q. 3 (v) More detailed information can be obtained in a sample survey as compared to a census.

True

Q. 3 (vi) Sampling may be the only means available for obtaining the desired information if the population is infinite.

True

Q. 3 (vii) If the data are obtained by tests that are destructive, then complete enumeration becomes essential.

False

Q. 3 (viii) Every random sample is a simple random sample.

False

Q. 3 (ix) In sampling with replacement, the sample size may be greater than the population size.

True

Q. 3 (xi) The number of units available for the next drawing does not change in a random sampling with replacement.

True

Q. 3 (xii) In sampling without replacement, the number of units remaining after each drawing will be reduced by one.

True

Q. 4 (i) The number of all possible samples of size n taken without replacement from a population of size N is N C n.

False

Q. 4 (ii) In sampling without replacement, a sampling unit can be selected more than once.

False

Q. 4 (iv) In sampling with replacement, a finite population becomes infinite.

True

Q. 4 (v) Non-sampling errors may be present both in sample survey and census.

True

Q. 4 (vi) The sampling error increases by increasing the sample size.

False

Q. 4 (vii) Sampling and non-sampling errors are both controllable.

True

False
