True

mcqs.q: The descriptive measures of a population are called:
mcqs.why: Descriptive measures of a population are called parameters, while a descriptive measure computed from sample observations is called a statistic.

mcqs.q: A population is called finite when it:
options: Includes an unlimited number of sampling units
Has no sampling units at all
Includes a limited number of sampling units
mcqs.why: A population is finite if it includes a limited number of sampling units; an unlimited number of units makes it infinite.

mcqs.q: What is a sampling frame?
options: A complete list of the sampling units
The probability distribution of a statistic
A measure computed from a sample
mcqs.why: The sampling frame is a complete list of the sampling units from which the sample is to be drawn.

mcqs.q: In probability sampling, every element of the population has:
options: Zero probability of being included in the sample
An unknown probability of being included in the sample
A probability of inclusion equal to one
A known nonzero probability of being included in the sample
mcqs.why: Probability sampling selects the sample so that every element has a known nonzero probability of being included; it is also called random sampling.

mcqs.q: Sampling is said to be WITHOUT replacement when the unit selected at random:
options: Is returned to the population before the next unit is selected
Is NOT returned to the population before the next unit is selected
Is selected more than once in the sample
Is chosen by the investigator's judgement
mcqs.why: Corrected value: the book misprints this as 'is returned', but the sense is 'is NOT returned' - without replacement the drawn unit is kept out, so it cannot be drawn again.

mcqs.q: The number of all possible samples of size n taken WITH replacement from a population of size N is:
mcqs.why: With replacement each of the n draws has N choices, giving N x N x ... (n times) = N to the power n possible samples, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, the number of all possible samples of size n taken WITHOUT replacement from a population of size N is:
mcqs.why: The notes give the number of samples without replacement as N P n (ordered samples), and mark the statement that it is N C n as False.

mcqs.q: Which statement about non-sampling errors is correct?
options: They occur only in a sample survey and never in a census
They can arise from faulty sampling frames, non-responses and processing of data
They disappear when the sample size is increased
They are the same as the standard error of a statistic
mcqs.why: Non-sampling errors may be present both in a sample survey and a census, and they may arise due to faulty sampling frames, non-responses and processing of data.

mcqs.q: The statement 'Standard error is the difference of a statistic from the parameter being estimated' is:
options: True, by the definition of standard error
True, only for the sample mean
True, only in sampling without replacement
mcqs.why: The notes mark this False: the standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the statistic, not its difference from the parameter.

mcqs.q: A sample statistic, compared with the parameter it estimates, is:
options: A constant, while the parameter is a random variable
A random variable, while the parameter being estimated is constant
Always exactly equal to the parameter
mcqs.why: The notes mark this True: a sample statistic is a random variable because it changes from sample to sample, whereas the parameter being estimated is constant.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1 — Sampling Techniques
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) Explain the terms: Population; Sample; Sampling frame; Sampling unit.

Step 1: Population: the totality of the observations made on all the objects (or elementary units) possessing some common specific characteristics, which are of particular interest to researchers.

Step 2: Sample: a part of the population which is selected with the expectation that it will represent the characteristics of the population.

Step 3: Sampling frame: the list of all the sampling units of the population from which the sample is to be drawn (for example, a list of voters, or a list of households).

Answer: Sampling unit: the basic unit of the population in terms of which the sample design is planned, for example a student, a household, a field or a bulb.

Q. 1 (b) Define suitable populations from which the following samples are selected: (i) One thousand homes are called by telephone in the city of Karachi and asked to name the T.V. programme that they are now watching. (ii) A coin is flipped 53 times and 32 heads are recorded. (iii) Two hundred pairs of a new type of combat boots were tested for durability in Vietnam and, on the average, lasted two months.

Step 1: (i) The population is the homes in Karachi city having telephones and T.V.

sets: only such homes could be reached by telephone and could be watching a programme.

Step 2: (ii) The population is an infinite number of tosses of the coin: the 53 tosses are a sample from all the tosses that could be made.

Answer: (iii) The population is the total production of the new type of combat boots during a particular period: the 200 pairs tested are a sample from that production.

Q. 1 (c) In each of the following situations, determine whether the sampling is done from a finite population or an infinite population and then define the population. (i) A coin is tossed 20 times and 12 heads are recorded. (ii) Ten employees of a large manufacturing company are selected as representatives of labour to serve as a labour management committee. (iii) A sample of bulbs is selected periodically to determine the number of defective bulbs produced by a production unit. (iv) A coin is weighed 15 times to estimate its true weight.

Step 1: (i) Infinite: the population is all the potential tosses of the coin.

Step 2: (ii) Finite: the population is all the employees of the company.

Step 3: (iii) Infinite: the population is all the bulbs produced by the production unit.

Answer: (iv) Infinite: the population is all the potential weights (weighings) of the coin.

Q. 2 (a) What is meant by sampling? Describe the advantages of sampling over complete enumeration.

Step 1: Sampling is the procedure of selecting a representative sample from a given population, instead of examining every unit of the population.

Step 2: Time saving: a sample survey involves less time in execution and analysis than a complete enumeration, which matters when information is urgently needed.

Step 3: Economy: a sample survey costs less in money and labour, because only a fraction of the population is covered.

Step 4: Accuracy: a sample survey can give results almost as accurate as a complete census, and a properly designed sample survey will often provide even better results, because a small trained staff can be used.

Answer: Feasibility: sometimes sampling is the only possible method, for example when the population is infinite or inaccessible, or when testing destroys the unit (as in testing the life of electric bulbs).

Q. 2 (b) For each of the following reasons, give an example of a situation for which a census would be less desirable than a sample. In each case, explain why this is so.

(i) Economy (ii) Timeliness (iii) Size of population (iv) Inaccessibility (v) Accuracy (vi) Destructive observations.

Step 1: (i) Economy: estimating the average life of electric bulbs. Testing every bulb would cost far more than testing a sample, and the information from a sample is enough.

Step 2: (ii) Timeliness: an election-day opinion poll. A census of all voters could not be completed before the result is needed, while a sample gives a quick estimate.

Step 3: (iii) Size of population: the heights of all the students enrolled in a university in a year. A census is a huge operation; a sample gives the required information with far less work.

Step 4: (iv) Inaccessibility: households scattered over a large or remote area.

Reaching every household is impracticable, while a sample of areas can be reached.

Step 5: (v) Accuracy: a census uses a large, less-trained staff, so non-sampling errors grow. A small, well-trained sample team can collect and check data more carefully, giving better results.

Answer: (vi) Destructive observations: testing the life of electric bulbs, or the bursting strength of a product. The test destroys the unit, so testing the whole lot would leave nothing to sell.

Q. 2 (c) Distinguish between the following: (i) Population and sample, (ii) Sampling with and without replacement.

Step 1: (i) Population and sample: the population is the whole collection of units under study; the sample is only a part of it, selected to represent the population.

Step 2: (ii) Sampling with replacement: a unit drawn is returned to the population before the next draw, so the same unit can be drawn again and the population size stays N at every draw.

Answer: Sampling without replacement: a unit drawn is not returned, so it cannot be drawn again and the number of units remaining falls by one after each draw.

Q. 3 (a) Distinguish between probability and non-probability sampling, giving examples. Describe the advantages of using a probability sample.

Step 1: Probability sampling: every unit of the population has a known, non-zero probability of selection, for example simple random sampling by lottery or by random digits.

Step 2: Non-probability sampling: units are selected by judgement, convenience or quota, with no known probability of selection, for example choosing the first ten students met in a corridor.

Step 3: Advantage of a probability sample: because selection is by chance, the sample is free from personal bias, and the sampling error can be measured.

Answer: Only a probability sample lets us use the theory of sampling distributions to judge how close a sample estimate is likely to be to the population value.

Q. 3 (b) What do you understand by a simple random sample? By taking some artificial example, explain the method of drawing a simple random sample.

Step 1: A simple random sample is a sample in which every possible sample of the given size has the same probability of selection, so every unit has an equal chance of being included.

Step 2: Artificial example: to draw 10 households from a list of 250, number the households from 1 to 250 (or 001 to 250).

Step 3: Lottery method: write each number on a slip, mix the slips thoroughly in a container, and draw 10 slips blindly; the households with those numbers form the sample.

Answer: Random-digits method: read three-digit groups from a table of random digits, discard numbers above 250 and repeats (for sampling without replacement), and take the first 10 numbers that remain.

Q. 3 (c) Distinguish between the following: (i) Random sampling and simple random sampling. (ii) Simple random sampling and stratified random sampling. (iii) Sampling and non-sampling errors.

Step 1: (i) Random sampling is any sampling in which chance decides selection; simple random sampling is the special case in which every possible sample of the size has an equal probability.

Step 2: (ii) Simple random sampling draws directly from the whole population; stratified random sampling first divides a heterogeneous population into homogeneous strata and then draws a simple random sample separately from each stratum.

Answer: (iii) Sampling errors arise because only a part of the population is observed (the difference between a statistic and the parameter); non-sampling errors arise from wrong population, response bias, or mistakes in collecting, analysing and reporting the data, and they occur in a census as well.

Q. 4 (a) Explain how would you select a random sample of 10 households from a list of 250 households, by using a table of random digits.

Step 1: Number the 250 households in the list from 001 to 250, so that every household has a distinct three-digit number.

Step 2: Choose a starting point in the table of random digits at random, and read the digits in groups of three.

Step 3: Keep a three-digit group if it lies between 001 and 250 and has not occurred before; discard any group above 250 and any repeat (sampling without replacement).

Answer: Continue until 10 distinct numbers are obtained; the households bearing those numbers form the required random sample of 10.

Q. 4 (b) A poll is to be conducted to determine the voting preference of the voters in a certain city. Design a sampling plan such that the sample would be representative of the population of all the voters.

Step 1: Take the list of all registered voters in the city as the sampling frame.

Step 2: Stratify the frame by area (and, if available, by sex or age group), so that every part of the city is represented in proportion to its number of voters.

Step 3: Draw a simple random sample (by lottery or random digits) separately from each stratum, with the stratum sample sizes proportional to the stratum sizes.

Answer: Interview the voters so selected; because every stratum contributes in proportion and selection within each stratum is random, the sample represents the population of all the voters.

Q. 4 (c) In a certain locality, there are 300 households. We wish to select a sample of 50 households. How would you select this sample using Random Numbers?

Step 1: Number the 300 households from 001 to 300.

Step 2: Choose a random starting point in a table of random numbers and read the numbers in groups of three digits.

Step 3: Accept a group if it is between 001 and 300 and has not been accepted before; discard groups above 300 and repeats.

Answer: Stop when 50 distinct numbers have been accepted; the households with those numbers form the sample of 50.

Q. 5 (a) What is the difference between precision and accuracy of a result? Explain with some examples.

Step 1: Accuracy is closeness to the true value: the smaller the difference between the sample result and the population true value, the greater the accuracy.

Step 2: Precision is closeness of repeated results to one another, that is, how well a result can be reproduced from sample to sample; it is measured by the sampling error, a smaller sampling error meaning greater precision.

Step 3: Example: weighing a coin many times on a faulty scale may give nearly the same weight every time (precise) but all the readings may be away from the true weight (inaccurate), because of a constant bias.

Answer: A result can therefore be precise without being accurate, and accurate on average without being precise; a good survey aims at both, by reducing bias and by increasing the sample size.

Q. 5 (b) What are two broad categories of errors in data collected by sample surveys? What are the methods for reducing sampling error?

Step 1: The two broad categories are (i) sampling (random) errors and (ii) non-sampling (non-random) errors.

Step 2: Sampling error is the difference between a statistic from a sample and the corresponding population parameter; non-sampling error comes from a wrong population, response bias, or mistakes in collection and analysis.

Step 3: Sampling error can be reduced (i) by increasing the sample size, (ii) by improving the sampling design, for example by stratification, and (iii) by using supplementary information.

Answer: Non-sampling error is reduced by careful planning, trained staff, and careful checking of the data at every stage.

mcqs.q: In a telephone survey, 1000 homes in Karachi are called and asked which T.V. programme they are watching. The population is:
options: Homes in Karachi city having telephones and T.V. sets
All T.V. programmes shown in Karachi
mcqs.why: Only homes that could be reached by telephone and could be watching a programme belong to the population: homes in Karachi having telephones and T.V. sets.

mcqs.q: A coin is flipped 53 times and 32 heads are recorded. This is a sample from which population?
options: An infinite number of tosses of the coin
All coins of the same denomination
mcqs.why: The 53 tosses are a sample from all the tosses that could be made, which is an infinite population of tosses of the coin.

mcqs.q: Ten employees of a large manufacturing company are selected to serve on a labour management committee. The sampling here is from:
options: An infinite population of all workers everywhere
A finite population: all the employees of the company
A finite population: the ten selected employees
mcqs.why: The population is all the employees of the company, a limited number of units, so the population is finite.

mcqs.q: Which is an advantage of sampling over complete enumeration in terms of cost and effort?
options: Economy: a sample survey costs less in money and labour because only a fraction of the population is covered
A sample survey covers more units than a census
A sample survey needs a larger staff than a census
A sample survey takes longer than complete enumeration
mcqs.why: Sampling is economical: only a fraction of the population is covered, so a sample survey costs less in money and labour than complete enumeration.

mcqs.q: When testing destroys the unit, as in testing the life of electric bulbs, sampling is preferred because:
options: A census would be cheaper than a sample
Testing the whole lot would leave nothing to sell
Destructive tests give no information from a sample
A census of bulbs is always inaccurate
mcqs.why: The test destroys the unit, so testing the whole lot would leave nothing to sell; a sample gives the needed information while the rest survive.

mcqs.q: To draw a random sample of 10 households from a list of 250 using random digits, the households should be numbered:
options: Only the even numbers from 2 to 500
mcqs.why: Number the 250 households from 001 to 250 so every household has a distinct three-digit number, then read the random digits in groups of three.

mcqs.q: In that random-digits procedure (10 households from 250), a three-digit group should be discarded when it:
options: Lies between 001 and 250 and has not occurred before
Is the first group read from the table
Is above 250 or is a repeat of a number already taken
Contains the digit zero anywhere in it
mcqs.why: Groups above 250 and repeats are discarded (sampling without replacement); groups between 001 and 250 that have not occurred before are kept until 10 numbers are obtained.

mcqs.q: How does stratified random sampling differ from simple random sampling?
options: It never uses random selection within any group
It first divides a heterogeneous population into homogeneous strata and draws a simple random sample from each stratum
It selects units by convenience from the whole population
It draws the sample only from the largest group in the population
mcqs.why: Simple random sampling draws directly from the whole population; stratified random sampling first divides a heterogeneous population into homogeneous strata and samples each stratum separately.

mcqs.q: Repeated weighings of a coin on a faulty scale give nearly the same weight every time, but all readings are away from the true weight. This result is:
mcqs.why: Precision is closeness of repeated results to one another and accuracy is closeness to the true value, so consistent readings away from the true weight are precise but not accurate.

mcqs.q: Which is a method of reducing SAMPLING error?
options: Choosing a wrong population for the study
mcqs.why: Sampling error can be reduced by increasing the sample size, by improving the sampling design such as stratification, and by using supplementary information.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.2 — Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) How do you define a population and a sample? Differentiate between parameter and statistic. Why a parameter is said to be a constant and statistic a variable?

Step 1: Population: the totality of observations on all the units possessing the characteristic under study. Sample: a part of the population selected to represent it.

Step 2: Parameter: a numerical quantity that describes a characteristic of the population, for example the population mean mu or variance sigma-squared.

Statistic: a function of the observations of a random sample which does not contain any unknown parameter, for example the sample mean X-bar or sample variance s-squared.

Answer: A parameter is a constant because it describes the fixed, whole population; a statistic is a variable (a random variable) because its value changes from one sample to another, since different samples give different values.

Q. 1 (b) A labour union has 1000 members. A random sample of 50 members of the union gave an average age of 40 years. The average age of the members of the labour union was, therefore, estimated to be 40 years. A complete enumeration of all the members indicated that the true mean age was 43 years. Answer the following: (i) Which figure is a parameter? (ii) Which figure is a statistic? (Book answers: (i) Population size N = 1000, and population mean age mu = 43 years; (ii) Sample size n, and sample mean X-bar = 40 years.)

Step 1: The population is the 1000 members of the union, so N = 1000.

Step 2: The true mean age from the complete enumeration is 43 years; it describes the whole population, so it is the parameter mu = 43 years.

Answer: (i) The parameter is 43 years (with N = 1000). (ii) The statistic is the sample mean X-bar = 40 years, computed from the sample of n = 50 members; it is an estimate of mu.

Q. 2 (a) What is meant by a sampling distribution and a standard error? Describe the properties of the sampling distribution of sample mean.

Step 1: Sampling distribution of a statistic: the probability distribution of the statistic obtained from all possible samples of a specified size that can be drawn from a given population.

Step 2: Standard error of a statistic: the standard deviation of its sampling distribution; it measures how much the statistic varies from sample to sample.

Step 3: Properties of the sampling distribution of the sample mean X-bar: (i) its mean equals the population mean, mu_X-bar = mu, for sampling with or without replacement.

Step 4: (ii) Its variance is sigma_X-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n for an infinite population (or sampling with replacement).

Answer: (iii) For a finite population sampled without replacement, sigma_X-bar-squared = (sigma-squared / n) x ((N - n) / (N - 1)), where (N - n) / (N - 1) is the finite population correction; if the population is normal, X-bar is normal, and for large n it is approximately normal by the Central Limit Theorem.

Q. 2 (b) What is meant by standard error and what are its practical uses?

Step 1: The standard error of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution.

Step 2: Practical use 1: it measures the precision of an estimate; a smaller standard error means the estimate is likely to be closer to the true value.

Step 3: Practical use 2: it is used to form confidence intervals for a parameter and to test hypotheses about it.

Answer: Practical use 3: it tells us how large a sample is needed for a required precision, since the standard error falls as the sample size grows (as 1 / sqrt(n)).

Q. 2 (c) What is the finite population correction factor? When is it appropriately used in sampling applications and when can it, without too great an undesirable consequence, be ignored?

Step 1: The finite population correction (f.p.c.) factor for the variance is (N - n) / (N - 1), and for the standard error it is sqrt((N - n) / (N - 1)).

Step 2: It is used when a sample of size n is drawn without replacement from a finite population of size N, because the draws are then not independent.

Step 3: As N tends to infinity (or n is very small compared with N), (N - n) / (N - 1) tends to 1, so the correction tends to 1.

Answer: It can therefore be ignored, without too great an undesirable consequence, when the population is infinite, when sampling is with replacement, or when the sampling fraction n / N is very small (in practice, below about 5 percent).

Q. 3 (a) A finite population consists of the numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Calculate the sample means for all possible random samples of size n = 2, that can be drawn from this population, with replacement. Assuming the 36 possible samples equally likely, make the sampling distribution of sample means and find the mean and variance of this distribution. Calculate mean and variance of the population and verify that (i) mu_X-bar = mu, (ii) sigma_X-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n. (Book answers: mu = 7, sigma-squared = 11.667, mu_X-bar = 7, sigma_X-bar-squared = 5.833.)

Step 1: Population: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12; N = 6; sample size n = 2 with replacement, so the number of possible samples is 6 x 6 = 36.

Step 2: Population mean: mu = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12) / 6 = 42 / 6 = 7.

Step 3: Population variance: sum of squares = 4 + 16 + 36 + 64 + 100 + 144 = 364; sigma-squared = 364 / 6 - 7-squared = 60.667 - 49 = 11.667.

Step 4: Sampling distribution of X-bar (value: frequency out of 36): 2: 1, 3: 2, 4: 3, 5: 4, 6: 5, 7: 6, 8: 5, 9: 4, 10: 3, 11: 2, 12: 1. Probabilities are frequency / 36.

Step 5: Mean of the distribution: mu_X-bar = E(X-bar) = sum X-bar x p(X-bar) = 7.

Step 6: Variance: E(X-bar-squared) = 54.833, so sigma_X-bar-squared = 54.833 - 7-squared = 5.833.

Answer: (i) mu_X-bar = 7 = mu, verified. (ii) sigma-squared / n = 11.667 / 2 = 5.833 = sigma_X-bar-squared, verified.

Q. 3 (b) A finite population consists of the numbers 2, 4, 6, 6, 8 and 10. Calculate the sample means for all possible random samples of size n = 2, that can be drawn from this population, with replacement. Assuming the 36 possible samples equally likely, form the sampling distribution of sample means and find the mean and variance of this distribution. Calculate mean and variance of the population and verify that (i) mu_X-bar = mu, (ii) sigma_X-bar = sigma / sqrt(n). (Book answers: mu = 6, mu_X-bar = 6, sigma = 2.582, sigma_X-bar = 1.826.)

Step 1: Population: 2, 4, 6, 6, 8, 10; N = 6 (the value 6 occurs twice); n = 2 with replacement, so the number of possible samples is 6 x 6 = 36.

Step 2: Population mean: mu = (2 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 8 + 10) / 6 = 36 / 6 = 6.

Step 3: Population variance: sum of squares = 4 + 16 + 36 + 36 + 64 + 100 = 256; sigma-squared = 256 / 6 - 6-squared = 42.667 - 36 = 6.667; sigma = sqrt(6.667) = 2.582.

Step 4: Sampling distribution of X-bar (value: frequency out of 36): 2: 1, 3: 2, 4: 5, 5: 6, 6: 8, 7: 6, 8: 5, 9: 2, 10: 1.

Step 5: Mean: mu_X-bar = E(X-bar) = 6.

Step 6: Variance: sigma_X-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n = 6.667 / 2 = 3.333, so sigma_X-bar = sqrt(3.333) = 1.826.

Answer: (i) mu_X-bar = 6 = mu, verified. (ii) sigma_X-bar = 1.826 = sigma / sqrt(n) = 2.582 / sqrt(2), verified.

Q. 3 (c) Draw all possible samples of size n = 3 with replacement from the population 3, 6, 9 and 12. Assuming the 64 possible samples equally likely, form a sampling distribution of the sample means. Hence state and verify the relation between (i) the mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean and the population mean; (ii) the variance of the sampling distribution of the sample mean and the population variance. (Book answers: mu = 7.5, mu_X-bar = 7.5, sigma-squared = 11.25, sigma_X-bar-squared = 3.75.)

Step 1: Population: 3, 6, 9, 12; N = 4; n = 3 with replacement, so the number of possible samples is 4 x 4 x 4 = 64.

Step 2: Population mean: mu = (3 + 6 + 9 + 12) / 4 = 30 / 4 = 7.5.

Step 3: Population variance: sum of squares = 9 + 36 + 81 + 144 = 270; sigma-squared = 270 / 4 - 7.5-squared = 67.5 - 56.25 = 11.25.

Step 4: Sampling distribution of X-bar (value: frequency out of 64): 3: 1, 4: 3, 5: 6, 6: 10, 7: 12, 8: 12, 9: 10, 10: 6, 11: 3, 12: 1.

Step 5: Mean: mu_X-bar = E(X-bar) = 7.5.

Step 6: Variance: sigma_X-bar-squared = 3.75.

Answer: (i) mu_X-bar = 7.5 = mu, verified. (ii) sigma_X-bar-squared = 3.75 = sigma-squared / n = 11.25 / 3, verified; hence sigma_X-bar = sqrt(3.75) = 1.936.

Q. 4 (a) A finite population consists of the numbers 2, 4, 6, 6, 8 and 10. Calculate the sample means for all possible random samples of size n = 2, that can be drawn from this population, without replacement. Assuming the 30 possible samples equally likely, make the sampling distribution of sample mean. Find the mean and variance of this distribution. Calculate mean and variance of the population and verify that (i) mu_X-bar = mu, (ii) sigma_X-bar = (sigma / sqrt(n)) x sqrt((N - n) / (N - 1)). (Book answers: mu = 6, mu_X-bar = 6, sigma = 2.582, sigma_X-bar = 1.633.)

Step 1: Population: 2, 4, 6, 6, 8, 10; N = 6; n = 2 without replacement (the two 6s are distinct units), so the number of ordered samples is 6 x 5 = 30.

Step 2: Population mean: mu = 36 / 6 = 6.

Step 3: Population variance: sigma-squared = 6.667, so sigma = 2.582 (as in Q. 3 (b)).

Step 4: Sampling distribution of X-bar (value: frequency out of 30): 3: 2, 4: 4, 5: 6, 6: 6, 7: 6, 8: 4, 9: 2.

Step 5: Mean: mu_X-bar = E(X-bar) = 6.

Step 6: Variance: sigma_X-bar-squared = (sigma-squared / n) x ((N - n) / (N - 1)) = (6.667 / 2) x (4 / 5) = 3.333 x 0.8 = 2.667, so sigma_X-bar = sqrt(2.667) = 1.633.

Answer: (i) mu_X-bar = 6 = mu, verified. (ii) sigma_X-bar = 1.633 = (2.582 / sqrt(2)) x sqrt(4 / 5), verified.

Q. 4 (b) A finite population consists of the values 6, 6, 9, 15 and 18. Calculate the sample means for all possible random samples of size n = 3, that can be drawn from this population, without replacement. Assuming the 60 possible samples equally likely, make the sampling distribution of sample mean and find the mean and variance of this distribution. Calculate mean and variance of the population and show that (i) mu_X-bar = mu, (ii) sigma_X-bar-squared = (sigma-squared / n) x ((N - n) / (N - 1)). (Book answers: mu = 10.8, sigma-squared = 23.76, mu_X-bar = 10.8, sigma_X-bar-squared = 3.96.)

Step 1: Population: 6, 6, 9, 15, 18; N = 5; n = 3 without replacement, so the number of ordered samples is 5 x 4 x 3 = 60.

Step 2: Population mean: mu = (6 + 6 + 9 + 15 + 18) / 5 = 54 / 5 = 10.8.

Step 3: Population variance: sum of squares = 36 + 36 + 81 + 225 + 324 = 702; sigma-squared = 702 / 5 - 10.8-squared = 140.4 - 116.64 = 23.76.

Step 4: Sampling distribution of X-bar (value: frequency out of 60): 7: 6, 9: 6, 10: 18, 11: 12, 13: 12, 14: 6.

Step 5: Mean: mu_X-bar = E(X-bar) = 10.8.

Step 6: Variance: sigma_X-bar-squared = (23.76 / 3) x ((5 - 3) / (5 - 1)) = 7.92 x 0.5 = 3.96.

Answer: (i) mu_X-bar = 10.8 = mu, verified. (ii) sigma_X-bar-squared = 3.96, as required.

Q. 4 (c) Find the mean mu and variance sigma-squared of the finite population 1, 4, 7 and 8. Take all possible samples of size 2, that can be drawn at random without replacement from this population. Assuming the 12 possible samples equally likely, make the sampling distribution of sample mean and find the mean and variance of this distribution. Verify that (i) E(X-bar) = mu, (ii) Var(X-bar) = (sigma-squared / n) x ((N - n) / (N - 1)). (Book answers: mu = 5, sigma-squared = 7.5, E(X-bar) = 5, Var(X-bar) = 2.5, (N - n) / (N - 1) tends to 1 as N tends to infinity.)

Step 1: Population: 1, 4, 7, 8; N = 4; n = 2 without replacement, so the number of ordered samples is 4 x 3 = 12.

Step 2: Population mean: mu = (1 + 4 + 7 + 8) / 4 = 20 / 4 = 5.

Step 3: Population variance: sum of squares = 1 + 16 + 49 + 64 = 130; sigma-squared = 130 / 4 - 5-squared = 32.5 - 25 = 7.5.

Step 4: Sampling distribution of X-bar (value: frequency out of 12): 2.5: 2, 4: 2, 4.5: 2, 5.5: 2, 6: 2, 7.5: 2.

Step 5: Mean: E(X-bar) = 5.

Step 6: Variance: Var(X-bar) = (7.5 / 2) x ((4 - 2) / (4 - 1)) = 3.75 x (2 / 3) = 2.5.

Answer: (i) E(X-bar) = 5 = mu, verified. (ii) Var(X-bar) = 2.5, as required. Note: as N tends to infinity, (N - n) / (N - 1) tends to 1, so the finite population correction disappears.

Q. 5 (a) In an infinite population mu = 50 and sigma-squared = 250, find the mean and variance for the distribution of X-bar if: (i) n = 25, (ii) n = 100, (iii) n = 1250.

(Book answers: (i) mu_X-bar = 50, sigma_X-bar-squared = 10; (ii) mu_X-bar = 50, sigma_X-bar-squared = 2.5; (iii) mu_X-bar = 50, sigma_X-bar-squared = 0.2.)

Step 1: For an infinite population, mu_X-bar = mu = 50 for every n, and sigma_X-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n.

Step 2: (i) n = 25: sigma_X-bar-squared = 250 / 25 = 10.

Step 3: (ii) n = 100: sigma_X-bar-squared = 250 / 100 = 2.5.

Answer: (iii) n = 1250: sigma_X-bar-squared = 250 / 1250 = 0.2; in all three cases mu_X-bar = 50.

Q. 5 (b) A large number of samples of size 50 were selected at random from a normal population with mean mu and variance sigma-squared. The mean and standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean were obtained 2500 and 4 respectively. Find the mean and variance of the population. (Book answer: 2500, 800.)

Step 1: The mean of the sampling distribution of X-bar is mu_X-bar = mu, so mu = 2500.

Step 2: The standard error is sigma_X-bar = sigma / sqrt(n) = 4, with n = 50.

Step 3: So sigma = 4 x sqrt(50), and sigma-squared = 16 x 50 = 800.

Answer: The population mean is 2500 and the population variance is 800.

Q. 6 (a) If the size of the simple random sample from an infinite population is 55, the variance of sample mean is 27, what must be the standard error of sample mean if n = 165? (Book answer: sigma_X-bar = 3.)

Step 1: sigma_X-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n, so with n = 55 and variance 27, sigma-squared = 27 x 55 = 1485.

Step 2: For n = 165, sigma_X-bar-squared = 1485 / 165 = 9.

Answer: Hence sigma_X-bar = sqrt(9) = 3.

Q. 6 (b) If the size of the simple random sample from an infinite population is 36 and the standard error of the mean is 2, what must the size of the sample become if the standard error is to be reduced to 1.2? (Book answer: n = 100.)

Step 1: sigma_X-bar = sigma / sqrt(n), so sigma = 2 x sqrt(36) = 2 x 6 = 12, and sigma-squared = 144.

Step 2: For the new standard error 1.2, we need sqrt(n) = sigma / 1.2 = 12 / 1.2 = 10.

Answer: Hence n = 10-squared = 100.

Q. 7 (a) The random variable X has the following probability distribution: x_j: 4, 5, 6, 7; p(x_j): 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1. Find the mean mu_X-bar, variance sigma_X-bar-squared and standard error sigma_X-bar of the mean X-bar for a random sample of size 36.

(Book answers: mu_X-bar = 5.3, sigma_X-bar-squared = 0.0225, sigma_X-bar = 0.15.)

Step 1: Population mean: mu = sum x_j p(x_j) = 4 x 0.2 + 5 x 0.4 + 6 x 0.3 + 7 x 0.1 = 0.8 + 2.0 + 1.8 + 0.7 = 5.3.

Step 2: E(X-squared) = 16 x 0.2 + 25 x 0.4 + 36 x 0.3 + 49 x 0.1 = 3.2 + 10.0 + 10.8 + 4.9 = 28.9.

Step 3: Population variance: sigma-squared = 28.9 - 5.3-squared = 28.9 - 28.09 = 0.81.

Step 4: For n = 36, mu_X-bar = mu = 5.3.

Step 5: sigma_X-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n = 0.81 / 36 = 0.0225.

Answer: sigma_X-bar = sqrt(0.0225) = 0.15.

Q. 7 (b) A random sample of 36 cases is drawn from a negatively skewed probability distribution with a mean of 2 and a standard deviation of 3. Find the mean and standard error of the sampling distribution of X-bar. (Book answers: mu_X-bar = 2, sigma_X-bar = 0.5.)

Step 1: mu_X-bar = mu = 2.

Step 2: sigma_X-bar = sigma / sqrt(n) = 3 / sqrt(36) = 3 / 6 = 0.5.

Answer: The mean is 2 and the standard error is 0.5. (For n = 36 the distribution of X-bar is approximately normal by the Central Limit Theorem, even though the parent distribution is skewed.)

Q. 7 (c) A random sample of 100 is taken from a population with mean 30 and standard deviation 5. The probability distribution of the parent population is unknown, find the mean and standard error of the sampling distribution of X-bar.

(Book answers: mu_X-bar = 30, sigma_X-bar = 0.5.)

Step 1: mu_X-bar = mu = 30.

Step 2: sigma_X-bar = sigma / sqrt(n) = 5 / sqrt(100) = 5 / 10 = 0.5.

Answer: The mean is 30 and the standard error is 0.5.

mcqs.q: A labour union has 1000 members. A random sample of 50 members gave an average age of 40 years, while complete enumeration showed the true mean age was 43 years. Which figure is the PARAMETER?
options: The true mean age of 43 years
The number of members sampled twice
mcqs.why: A parameter describes the whole population: N = 1000 and the true mean age mu = 43 years from complete enumeration is the parameter; 40 years is the statistic x-bar from n = 50.

mcqs.q: For the population 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, what are the mean mu and variance sigma-squared?
For that same population (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12), samples of size n = 2 are drawn WITH replacement. How many possible samples are there, and what is the variance of the sampling distribution of x-bar?
mcqs.why: Working: with replacement the number of samples is 6 x 6 = 36. sigma_x-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n = 11.667 / 2 = 5.833, and mu_x-bar = mu = 7.

mcqs.q: A population consists of 2, 4, 6, 6, 8, 10 (sigma = 2.582). For samples of size n = 2 drawn WITH replacement, the standard error of x-bar is:
mcqs.why: Working: sigma-squared = 256/6 - 6^2 = 42.667 - 36 = 6.667. sigma_x-bar = sigma / sqrt(n) = 2.582 / sqrt(2) = 1.826, since sigma_x-bar-squared = 6.667/2 = 3.333.

mcqs.q: For the same population (2, 4, 6, 6, 8, 10), samples of size n = 2 are drawn WITHOUT replacement. The standard error of x-bar is:
mcqs.why: Working: sigma_x-bar-squared = (sigma-squared / n) x ((N - n)/(N - 1)) = (6.667/2) x (4/5) = 3.333 x 0.8 = 2.667, so sigma_x-bar = sqrt(2.667) = 1.633.

mcqs.q: Samples of size n = 3 are drawn with replacement from the population 3, 6, 9, 12. The variance of the sampling distribution of x-bar is:
mcqs.why: Working: mu = 30/4 = 7.5 and sigma-squared = 270/4 - 7.5^2 = 67.5 - 56.25 = 11.25. sigma_x-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n = 11.25 / 3 = 3.75 (the number of possible samples is 4^3 = 64).

mcqs.q: In an infinite population with mu = 50 and sigma-squared = 250, what is the variance of the sampling distribution of x-bar when n = 100?
mcqs.why: Working: mu_x-bar = mu = 50 for every n. sigma_x-bar-squared = sigma-squared / n = 250 / 100 = 2.5. (For n = 25 it is 10 and for n = 1250 it is 0.2.)

mcqs.q: Samples of size 50 from a normal population gave mean of x-bar = 2500 and standard error = 4. The population variance sigma-squared is:
mcqs.why: Working: mu = mu_x-bar = 2500. Standard error sigma / sqrt(n) = 4 with n = 50, so sigma-squared = 4^2 x 50 = 16 x 50 = 800.

mcqs.q: From an infinite population, a sample of size 36 has standard error of the mean = 2. What sample size will reduce the standard error to 1.2?
mcqs.why: Working: sigma = 2 x sqrt(36) = 2 x 6 = 12. For standard error 1.2, sqrt(n) = sigma / 1.2 = 12 / 1.2 = 10, so n = 10^2 = 100.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.3 — Sampling Distribution of the Difference Between Two Sample Means
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) What is meant by the sampling distribution of the difference between two sample means. Describe the properties of the sampling distribution of the differences between two sample means.

Step 1: The sampling distribution of the difference between two sample means, X-bar_1 - X-bar_2, is the probability distribution of all possible differences between the means X-bar_1 and X-bar_2 obtained from all possible independent simple random samples of sizes n_1 and n_2 drawn from two given populations.

Step 2: Property 1 (mean): the mean of the distribution equals the difference between the population means, mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = mu_1 - mu_2. This holds regardless of the sample sizes and whether sampling is with or without replacement.

Step 3: Property 2 (variance, infinite populations or with replacement): sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2.

Step 4: Property 3 (variance, finite populations without replacement): sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = (sigma_1-squared / n_1) x ((N_1 - n_1) / (N_1 - 1)) + (sigma_2-squared / n_2) x ((N_2 - n_2) / (N_2 - 1)).

Answer: Property 4: if the two populations are normal, the difference X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 is normal; for large samples it is approximately normal by the Central Limit Theorem, and Z = ((X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) - (mu_1 - mu_2)) / sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) is standard normal.

Q. 1 (b) Let X-bar_1 represent the mean of a sample of size n_1 = 2, selected with replacement from a finite population -2, 0, 2, and 4. Similarly, let X-bar_2 represent the mean of a sample of size n_2 = 2, selected with replacement from the population -1 and 1. (i) Assuming that the 64 possible differences X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 are equally likely to occur, construct the sampling distribution of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2.

(ii) Verify that sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2. (Book answers: mu_1 = 1, mu_2 = 0, mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 1, sigma_1-squared = 5, sigma_2-squared = 1, sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 3.)

Step 1: Population I: -2, 0, 2, 4; N_1 = 4. Population II: -1, 1; N_2 = 2. Sample sizes n_1 = 2, n_2 = 2, both with replacement.

Step 2: mu_1 = (-2 + 0 + 2 + 4) / 4 = 4 / 4 = 1. sigma_1-squared = (4 + 0 + 4 + 16) / 4 - 1-squared = 6 - 1 = 5.

Step 3: mu_2 = (-1 + 1) / 2 = 0. sigma_2-squared = (1 + 1) / 2 - 0 = 1.

Step 4: Number of possible differences: (4 x 4) x (2 x 2) = 16 x 4 = 64. Sampling distribution of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 (value: frequency out of 64): -3: 1, -2: 4, -1: 8, 0: 12, 1: 14, 2: 12, 3: 8, 4: 4, 5: 1.

Step 5: Mean: mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 1 = mu_1 - mu_2.

Step 6: Variance: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 5 / 2 + 1 / 2 = 2.5 + 0.5 = 3.

Answer: (ii) Verified: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 3 = sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2; the standard error is sqrt(3) = 1.732.

Q. 2 (a) Let the variable X-bar_1 represent the mean of random samples of size n_1 = 2, with replacement drawn from the finite population 3, 4, 5. Similarly, let X-bar_2 represent the means of random samples of size n_2 = 3, with replacement, drawn from the population 0, 3. Assuming that the 72 possible differences X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 are equally likely to occur, construct the sampling distribution of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2. Show that (i) mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = mu_1 - mu_2, (ii) sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2. (Book answers: mu_1 = 4, mu_2 = 1.5, mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 2.5, sigma_1-squared = 0.667, sigma_2-squared = 2.25, sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 1.083.)

Step 1: Population I: 3, 4, 5; N_1 = 3. Population II: 0, 3; N_2 = 2. n_1 = 2, n_2 = 3, both with replacement.

Step 2: mu_1 = (3 + 4 + 5) / 3 = 4. sigma_1-squared = (9 + 16 + 25) / 3 - 16 = 16.667 - 16 = 0.667.

Step 3: mu_2 = (0 + 3) / 2 = 1.5. sigma_2-squared = (0 + 9) / 2 - 2.25 = 4.5 - 2.25 = 2.25.

Step 4: Number of possible differences: (3 x 3) x (2 x 2 x 2) = 9 x 8 = 72. Sampling distribution of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 (value: frequency out of 72): 0: 1, 0.5: 2, 1: 6, 1.5: 8, 2: 13, 2.5: 12, 3: 13, 3.5: 8, 4: 6, 4.5: 2, 5: 1.

Step 5: Mean: mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 2.5 = 4 - 1.5 = mu_1 - mu_2.

Step 6: Variance: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 0.667 / 2 + 2.25 / 3 = 0.333 + 0.75 = 1.083.

Answer: (i) and (ii) both verified; the standard error is sqrt(1.083) = 1.041.

Q. 2 (b) Let the variable X-bar_1 represent the means of random samples of size 2 without replacement, drawn from the finite population 5, 7, 9. Similarly, let X-bar_2 represent the means of random sample of size 2, without replacement from another finite population 4, 6, 8. Assuming the 36 possible differences X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 are equally likely to occur, construct the sampling distribution of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 and verify that (i) mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = mu_1 - mu_2, (ii) sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = (sigma_1-squared / n_1) x ((N_1 - n_1) / (N_1 - 1)) + (sigma_2-squared / n_2) x ((N_2 - n_2) / (N_2 - 1)). (Book answers: mu_1 = 7, mu_2 = 6, mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 1, sigma_1-squared = 2.667, sigma_2-squared = 2.667, sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 1.333.)

Step 1: Population I: 5, 7, 9; N_1 = 3. Population II: 4, 6, 8; N_2 = 3. n_1 = 2, n_2 = 2, both without replacement.

Step 2: mu_1 = (5 + 7 + 9) / 3 = 7. sigma_1-squared = (25 + 49 + 81) / 3 - 49 = 51.667 - 49 = 2.667.

Step 3: mu_2 = (4 + 6 + 8) / 3 = 6. sigma_2-squared = (16 + 36 + 64) / 3 - 36 = 38.667 - 36 = 2.667.

Step 4: Number of possible differences: (3 x 2) x (3 x 2) = 6 x 6 = 36. Sampling distribution of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 (value: frequency out of 36): -1: 4, 0: 8, 1: 12, 2: 8, 3: 4.

Step 5: Mean: mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 1 = 7 - 6 = mu_1 - mu_2.

Step 6: Variance: (2.667 / 2) x ((3 - 2) / (3 - 1)) + (2.667 / 2) x ((3 - 2) / (3 - 1)) = 1.333 x 0.5 + 1.333 x 0.5 = 0.667 + 0.667 = 1.333.

Answer: (i) and (ii) both verified; the standard error is sqrt(1.333) = 1.155.

Q. 3 (a) The television picture tubes of manufacturer A have a mean lifetime of 6.5 years and a standard deviation of 0.9 years, while those of manufacturer B have a mean lifetime of 6.0 years and a standard deviation of 0.8 years. A random sample of size 36 tubes is selected from manufacturer A and its mean X-bar_1 is calculated.

Another random sample of size 49 tubes is selected from manufacturer B and its mean X-bar_2 is calculated. Find the mean and standard error of the sampling distribution of the difference X-bar_1 - X-bar_2. (Book answers: mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 0.5, sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 0.1886.)

Step 1: mu_1 = 6.5, sigma_1 = 0.9, n_1 = 36; mu_2 = 6.0, sigma_2 = 0.8, n_2 = 49.

Step 2: Mean of the difference: mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = mu_1 - mu_2 = 6.5 - 6.0 = 0.5 years.

Step 3: Variance: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 0.81 / 36 + 0.64 / 49 = 0.0225 + 0.01306 = 0.03556.

Answer: Standard error: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = sqrt(0.03556) = 0.1886 years.

Q. 3 (b) Random samples of each size 100 are drawn from two independent probability distributions and their means X-bar_1 and X-bar_2 computed. If the means and standard deviations of the two populations are mu_1 = 10, sigma_1 = 2, mu_2 = 8, sigma_2 = 1, find the mean and standard error of the sampling distribution of the difference X-bar_1 - X-bar_2. (Book answers: mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 2, sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 0.2236.)

Step 1: mu_1 = 10, sigma_1 = 2, n_1 = 100; mu_2 = 8, sigma_2 = 1, n_2 = 100.

Step 2: Mean of the difference: mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = 10 - 8 = 2.

Step 3: Variance: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 4 / 100 + 1 / 100 = 0.05.

Answer: Standard error: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = sqrt(0.05) = 0.2236.

options: The distribution of a single sample mean X-bar_1
The probability distribution of all possible differences X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 from all possible independent samples of sizes n_1 and n_2
The distribution of the population values in the two populations
The distribution of the difference between two single observations
mcqs.q: What is the sampling distribution of the difference between two sample means, X-bar_1 - X-bar_2?
mcqs.why: By definition it is the probability distribution of all possible differences between the means obtained from all possible independent simple random samples of sizes n_1 and n_2 drawn from the two given populations.

mcqs.q: What is the mean of the sampling distribution of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2?
mcqs.why: Property 1 states mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) = mu_1 - mu_2, and this holds regardless of the sample sizes and whether sampling is with or without replacement.

mcqs.q: For infinite populations, or sampling with replacement, what is the variance of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2?
mcqs.why: Property 2 gives sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2 for infinite populations or sampling with replacement; the two variances are added, not subtracted.

options: Factors n_1 / N_1 and n_2 / N_2 are multiplied in
No extra factors appear at all
Factors (N_1 + n_1) / (N_1 - 1) and (N_2 + n_2) / (N_2 - 1) are multiplied in
Finite population corrections (N_1 - n_1) / (N_1 - 1) and (N_2 - n_2) / (N_2 - 1) are multiplied in
mcqs.q: In the variance formula for X-bar_1 - X-bar_2 when sampling without replacement from finite populations, what extra factors appear?
mcqs.why: Property 3 multiplies the first term by (N_1 - n_1) / (N_1 - 1) and the second term by (N_2 - n_2) / (N_2 - 1), the finite population correction for each population.

mcqs.q: Samples of size n_1 = 2 with replacement are drawn from -2, 0, 2, 4 and samples of size n_2 = 2 with replacement from -1, 1. What is mu_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)?
For the same two populations (-2, 0, 2, 4 and -1, 1) with n_1 = n_2 = 2 with replacement, what is sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared, given sigma_1-squared = 5 and sigma_2-squared = 1?
mcqs.why: Working: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2 = 5 / 2 + 1 / 2 = 2.5 + 0.5 = 3. The value 1.732 is the standard error sqrt(3), not the variance.

mcqs.q: Samples of size n_1 = 2 are drawn from 3, 4, 5 (sigma_1-squared = 0.667) and samples of size n_2 = 3 from 0, 3 (sigma_2-squared = 2.25), both with replacement. What is sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared?
mcqs.why: Working: sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared = 0.667 / 2 + 2.25 / 3 = 0.333 + 0.75 = 1.083. The value 1.041 is the standard error sqrt(1.083), not the variance.

mcqs.q: Samples of size 2 without replacement are drawn from 5, 7, 9 and from 4, 6, 8, where N_1 = N_2 = 3 and sigma_1-squared = sigma_2-squared = 2.667. What is sigma_(X-bar_1 - X-bar_2)-squared?
mcqs.why: Working: (2.667 / 2) x ((3 - 2) / (3 - 1)) + (2.667 / 2) x ((3 - 2) / (3 - 1)) = 1.333 x 0.5 + 1.333 x 0.5 = 0.667 + 0.667 = 1.333, using the finite population correction for each term.

mcqs.q: Manufacturer A tubes have mu_1 = 6.5, sigma_1 = 0.9, n_1 = 36 and manufacturer B tubes have mu_2 = 6.0, sigma_2 = 0.8, n_2 = 49. What is the standard error of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2?
mcqs.why: Working: variance = sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2 = 0.81 / 36 + 0.64 / 49 = 0.0225 + 0.01306 = 0.03556, so the standard error = sqrt(0.03556) = 0.1886 years.

mcqs.q: Two populations have mu_1 = 10, sigma_1 = 2 and mu_2 = 8, sigma_2 = 1, with samples of size n_1 = n_2 = 100. What are the mean and standard error of X-bar_1 - X-bar_2?
mcqs.why: Working: mean = mu_1 - mu_2 = 10 - 8 = 2; variance = 4 / 100 + 1 / 100 = 0.05, so the standard error = sqrt(0.05) = 0.2236. The value 0.05 is the variance, not the standard error.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.4 — Sampling Distributions
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) A fair coin is tossed 50 times and the number of heads recorded is 27. The proportion of heads was therefore estimated to be 0.54. Answer: (i) Which figure is a parameter? (ii) Which figure is a statistic? (Book answers: (i) pi = 0.5; (ii) n = 50, p = 0.54)

Step 1: A parameter describes the POPULATION; a statistic describes the SAMPLE.

Step 2: (i) For a fair coin, the population probability of a head in a single trial is pi = 0.5.

Step 3: This 0.5 does not come from the 50 tosses; it is a property of the coin itself, so it is the parameter.

Step 4: (ii) The sample size is n = 50 tosses.

Step 5: The number of heads in the sample is x = 27, so the sample proportion is p = x / n = 27 / 50 = 0.54.

Step 6: Both n = 50 and p = 0.54 are computed from the sample, so they are statistics.

Answer: (i) parameter: pi = 0.5; (ii) statistics: n = 50 and p = 0.54. FLAG: the book's printed solution writes x = 30, but 30 / 50 = 0.60, not 0.54; the question's own figure x = 27 gives 27 / 50 = 0.54, and is used here.

Q. 1 (b) What is meant by the sampling distribution of sample proportion? Describe the properties of the sampling distribution of sample proportion.

The sampling distribution of a sample proportion is the probability distribution of the values of the sample proportion P obtained from all possible samples of a given size from a population.

Its properties are: its mean is the population proportion, mu_P = pi.

Its variance for sampling with replacement (or an infinite population) is sigma_P-squared = pi (1 - pi) / n.

For sampling without replacement from a finite population of size N, the variance is multiplied by the finite population correction (N - n) / (N - 1).

Its standard deviation sigma_P is called the standard error of the proportion.

For large samples it is approximately normal by the central limit theorem.

Q. 2 (a) A finite population consists of the numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8. Find the proportion P of even numbers in all possible random samples of size n = 2 drawn with replacement. Assuming the 36 possible samples equally likely, make the sampling distribution of sample proportions and find its mean and variance. Verify (i) E(P) = pi, (ii) Var(P) = pi (1 - pi) / n. (Book answers: pi = 2/3, mu_P = 2/3, sigma_P-squared = 1/9)

Step 1: Even numbers in the population are 2, 4, 6, 8, i.e. 4 out of 6, so pi = 4 / 6 = 2/3.

Step 2: Number of possible samples with replacement = 6 x 6 = 36.

Step 3: Count samples by the number of even values: both odd (odd values are 3, 5): 2 x 2 = 4 samples give P = 0.

Step 4: One even and one odd: 4 x 2 x 2 = 16 samples give P = 1/2.

Step 5: Both even: 4 x 4 = 16 samples give P = 1.

Step 6: Sampling distribution: P = 0 with frequency 4 (probability 4/36); P = 1/2 with frequency 16 (16/36); P = 1 with frequency 16 (16/36).

Step 7: Mean mu_P = (0 x 4 + (1/2) x 16 + 1 x 16) / 36 = 24 / 36 = 2/3.

Step 8: E(P-squared) = (0 x 4 + (1/4) x 16 + 1 x 16) / 36 = 20 / 36 = 5/9.

Step 9: Variance = E(P-squared) - mu_P-squared = 5/9 - 4/9 = 1/9.

Step 10: Verify (i): E(P) = 2/3 = pi. Verify (ii): pi (1 - pi) / n = (2/3)(1/3) / 2 = 1/9.

Answer: distribution 0: 4/36, 1/2: 16/36, 1: 16/36; mean 2/3; variance 1/9. Both results verified.

Q. 2 (b) A population consists of N = 4 numbers 1, 3, 4 and 5. Find the proportion P of odd numbers in all possible samples of size n = 3 drawn without replacement.

Assuming the 24 possible samples equally likely, construct the sampling distribution and find its mean and variance. Verify (i) mu_P = pi, (ii) sigma_P-squared = pi (1 - pi) / n x (N - n) / (N - 1). (Book answers: pi = 3/4, mu_P = 3/4, sigma_P-squared = 1/48)

Step 1: Odd numbers in the population are 1, 3, 5, i.e. 3 out of 4, so pi = 3/4.

Step 2: Number of possible ordered samples without replacement = 4 x 3 x 2 = 24.

Step 3: The 4 unordered triples are: {1, 3, 4} (odd proportion 2/3), {1, 3, 5} (1), {1, 4, 5} (2/3), {3, 4, 5} (2/3).

Step 4: Each unordered triple has 6 orderings, so P = 2/3 occurs in 18 samples (18/24) and P = 1 occurs in 6 samples (6/24).

Step 5: Mean mu_P = ((2/3) x 18 + 1 x 6) / 24 = 18 / 24 = 3/4.

Step 6: E(P-squared) = ((4/9) x 18 + 1 x 6) / 24 = 14 / 24 = 7/12.

Step 7: Variance = 7/12 - (3/4)-squared = 7/12 - 9/16 = 28/48 - 27/48 = 1/48.

Step 8: Verify (i): mu_P = 3/4 = pi. Verify (ii): pi (1 - pi) / n x (N - n) / (N - 1) = (3/4)(1/4) / 3 x 1/3 = 1/48.

Answer: distribution 2/3: 18/24, 1: 6/24; mean 3/4; variance 1/48. Both results verified.

Q. 3 (a) Suppose 60% of a city population favours public funding for a proposed recreational facility. If 150 persons are randomly selected and interviewed, what are the mean and standard error of the sample proportion favouring this issue? (Book answers: mu_P = 0.60, sigma_P = 0.04)

Step 1: Population proportion pi = 0.60 and sample size n = 150.

Step 2: Mean of the sample proportion mu_P = pi = 0.60.

Step 3: Standard error sigma_P = sqrt(pi (1 - pi) / n) = sqrt(0.60 x 0.40 / 150).

Step 4: 0.60 x 0.40 = 0.24; 0.24 / 150 = 0.0016.

Step 5: sqrt(0.0016) = 0.04.

Answer: mean = 0.60, standard error = 0.04.

Q. 3 (b) A small professional society has N = 4500 members. The president mailed n = 400 questionnaires to a random sample asking whether they wish to affiliate with a large group. Assuming the proportion of the entire membership favouring consolidation is pi = 0.7, find the mean and standard error of the sample proportion P. (Book answers: mu_P = 0.7, sigma_P = 0.022)

Step 1: Population proportion pi = 0.7, sample size n = 400, population size N = 4500.

Step 2: Mean of the sample proportion mu_P = pi = 0.7.

Step 3: With the finite population correction, sigma_P = sqrt(pi (1 - pi) / n x (N - n) / (N - 1)).

Step 4: pi (1 - pi) / n = 0.7 x 0.3 / 400 = 0.21 / 400 = 0.000525.

Step 5: (N - n) / (N - 1) = 4100 / 4499 = 0.9113.

Step 6: sigma_P = sqrt(0.000525 x 0.9113) = sqrt(0.000478) = 0.02187, i.e. 0.022.

Answer: mean = 0.7, standard error = 0.022.

Q. 4 (a) What is meant by the sampling distribution of the difference between two sample proportions? Describe its properties. Explain its usefulness in statistical inference.

The sampling distribution of the difference between two sample proportions is the probability distribution of P1 - P2, where P1 and P2 are the sample proportions from two independent populations.

Its properties are: its mean is the difference of the population proportions, mu_(P1 - P2) = pi1 - pi2.

Its variance is the sum of the two variances: sigma-squared_(P1 - P2) = pi1 (1 - pi1) / n1 + pi2 (1 - pi2) / n2, with the finite population correction for each part when sampling without replacement from finite populations.

Its standard deviation is the standard error of the difference of proportions.

For large samples it is approximately normal.

Its usefulness in statistical inference is: it lets us compare two populations, for example two cities or two groups, by testing whether pi1 = pi2 and by building confidence intervals for pi1 - pi2.

Q. 4 (b) Let P1 be the proportion of odd numbers in a random sample of size n1 = 3 with replacement from the population {4, 5}. Let P2 be the proportion of odd numbers in a random sample of size n2 = 2 with replacement from the population {2, 3, 6}. Assuming the 72 possible differences P1 - P2 equally likely, construct the sampling distribution of P1 - P2 and verify (i) mu_(P1 - P2) = pi1 - pi2, (ii) sigma-squared_(P1 - P2) = pi1 (1 - pi1) / n1 + pi2 (1 - pi2) / n2. (Book answers: pi1 = 1/2, pi2 = 1/3, mu = 1/6, sigma-squared = 7/36)

Step 1: Population 1: odd value is 5 only, so pi1 = 1/2. Population 2: odd value is 3 only, so pi2 = 1/3.

Step 2: P1 distribution (8 samples of size 3 from {4, 5}): P1 = 0 in 1 sample, 1/3 in 3 samples, 2/3 in 3 samples, 1 in 1 sample.

Step 3: P2 distribution (9 samples of size 2 from {2, 3, 6}): P2 = 0 in 4 samples, 1/2 in 4 samples, 1 in 1 sample.

Step 4: The 72 differences P1 - P2 occur with frequencies: -1: 1, -2/3: 3, -1/2: 4, -1/3: 3, -1/6: 12, 0: 5, 1/6: 12, 1/3: 12, 1/2: 4, 2/3: 12, 1: 4.

Step 5: Check the total: 1 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 12 + 5 + 12 + 12 + 4 + 12 + 4 = 72.

Step 6: Mean = sum of (difference x frequency) / 72 = 12 / 72 = 1/6.

Step 7: E((P1 - P2)-squared) = sum of (difference-squared x frequency) / 72 = 16 / 72 = 2/9.

Step 8: Variance = E((P1 - P2)-squared) - mean-squared = 2/9 - (1/6)-squared = 8/36 - 1/36 = 7/36.

Step 9: Using the formula: pi1 (1 - pi1) / n1 = (1/2)(1/2) / 3 = 1/12; pi2 (1 - pi2) / n2 = (1/3)(2/3) / 2 = 1/9.

Step 10: Sum = 1/12 + 1/9 = 3/36 + 4/36 = 7/36, which equals the variance computed from the distribution.

Step 11: Verify (i): mu_(P1 - P2) = 1/6 = 1/2 - 1/3 = pi1 - pi2.

Answer: distribution as in Step 4; mean 1/6; variance 7/36. Both results verified.

Q. 5 (a) Let P1 be the proportion of even numbers in a random sample of size n1 = 2 without replacement from the population {4, 6, 9}. Let P2 be the proportion of even numbers in a random sample of size n2 = 2 without replacement from the population {2, 3, 5}. Assuming the 36 possible differences P1 - P2 equally likely, construct the sampling distribution of P1 - P2 and verify (i) mu_(P1 - P2) = pi1 - pi2, (ii) sigma-squared_(P1 - P2) = pi1 (1 - pi1) / n1 x (N1 - n1) / (N1 - 1) + pi2 (1 - pi2) / n2 x (N2 - n2) / (N2 - 1). (Book answers: pi1 = 2/3, pi2 = 1/3, mu = 1/3, sigma-squared = 1/9)

Step 1: Population 1 evens are 4, 6, so pi1 = 2/3, N1 = 3. Population 2 evens are 2 only, so pi2 = 1/3, N2 = 3.

Step 2: Ordered samples without replacement: 3 x 2 = 6 samples for each population.

Step 3: P1 distribution: the ordered pairs are (4, 6), (6, 4) giving P1 = 1 (2 samples), and (4, 9), (6, 9), (9, 4), (9, 6) giving P1 = 1/2 (4 samples).

Step 4: P2 distribution: the ordered pairs are (2, 3), (2, 5), (3, 2), (5, 2) giving P2 = 1/2 (4 samples), and (3, 5), (5, 3) giving P2 = 0 (2 samples).

Step 5: Differences: P1 - P2 = 0 in 4 x 4 = 16 cases; = 1/2 in (2 x 4) + (4 x 2) = 16 cases; = 1 in 2 x 2 = 4 cases.

Step 6: Check the total: 16 + 16 + 4 = 36.

Step 7: Mean = (0 x 16 + (1/2) x 16 + 1 x 4) / 36 = 12 / 36 = 1/3.

Step 8: E((P1 - P2)-squared) = (0 x 16 + (1/4) x 16 + 1 x 4) / 36 = 8 / 36 = 2/9.

Step 9: Variance = 2/9 - (1/3)-squared = 2/9 - 1/9 = 1/9.

Step 10: Verify (i): mu = 1/3 = 2/3 - 1/3 = pi1 - pi2.

Step 11: Verify (ii): first term = (2/3)(1/3) / 2 x (3 - 2) / (3 - 1) = (1/9) x (1/2) = 1/18; second term is the same, 1/18; sum = 1/9.

Answer: distribution 0: 16/36, 1/2: 16/36, 1: 4/36; mean 1/3; variance 1/9. Both results verified.

Q. 5 (b) The percentage of families with a monthly income of Rs. 1,000 or more in city A and city B is 25% and 20% respectively. If a random sample of 100 families is selected from each city and the proportions are compared, what are the mean and standard error of P1 - P2? (Book answers: mu = 0.05, sigma = 0.059)

Step 1: pi1 = 0.25, pi2 = 0.20, n1 = n2 = 100.

Step 2: Mean mu_(P1 - P2) = pi1 - pi2 = 0.25 - 0.20 = 0.05.

Step 3: Variance = pi1 (1 - pi1) / n1 + pi2 (1 - pi2) / n2 = 0.25 x 0.75 / 100 + 0.20 x 0.80 / 100.

Step 4: = 0.001875 + 0.0016 = 0.003475.

Step 5: Standard error = sqrt(0.003475) = 0.05895, i.e. 0.059.

Answer: mean = 0.05, standard error = 0.059.

Q. 6 (a) A finite population consists of five values 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Take all possible samples of size 2 drawn with replacement. Assuming the 25 possible samples equally likely, construct the sampling distributions of sample means and sample variances and find the mean of these distributions. Calculate the mean and variance of the population and verify (i) mu_(x-bar) = mu, (ii) mu_(S-squared) = (n - 1) / n x sigma-squared, where x-bar = sum X_i / n and S-squared = sum (X_i - x-bar)-squared / n. (Book answers: mu = 6, sigma-squared = 8, mu_(x-bar) = 6, mu_(S-squared) = 4)

Step 1: Population mean mu = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10) / 5 = 30 / 5 = 6.

Step 2: Population variance sigma-squared = (4 + 16 + 36 + 64 + 100) / 5 - 6-squared = 220 / 5 - 36 = 44 - 36 = 8.

Step 3: Number of samples with replacement = 5 x 5 = 25.

Step 4: Sample means distribution: mean 2 in 1 sample, 3 in 2, 4 in 3, 5 in 4, 6 in 5, 7 in 4, 8 in 3, 9 in 2, 10 in 1.

Step 5: Mean of the sample means = (2 x 1 + 3 x 2 + 4 x 3 + 5 x 4 + 6 x 5 + 7 x 4 + 8 x 3 + 9 x 2 + 10 x 1) / 25 = 150 / 25 = 6.

Step 6: For n = 2, S-squared = (X1 - X2)-squared / 4. Sample variances distribution: 0 in 5 samples, 1 in 8, 4 in 6, 9 in 4, 16 in 2.

Step 7: Mean of the sample variances = (0 x 5 + 1 x 8 + 4 x 6 + 9 x 4 + 16 x 2) / 25 = 100 / 25 = 4.

Step 8: Verify (i): mu_(x-bar) = 6 = mu. Verify (ii): (n - 1) / n x sigma-squared = (1/2) x 8 = 4 = mu_(S-squared).

Answer: means distribution as in Step 4; variances distribution as in Step 6; mu_(x-bar) = 6, mu_(S-squared) = 4. Both results verified.

Q. 6 (b) A finite population consists of five values 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Take all possible samples of size 2 drawn with replacement. Assuming the 25 possible samples equally likely, construct the sampling distributions of sample means and sample variances and find the mean of these distributions. Calculate the mean and variance of the population. Discuss the results. (Book answers: mu = 5, sigma-squared = 8, mu_(x-bar) = 5, mu_(S-squared) = 4, mu_(x-bar) = mu, mu_(S-squared) = (n - 1) / n x sigma-squared)

Step 1: Population mean mu = (1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9) / 5 = 25 / 5 = 5.

Step 2: Population variance sigma-squared = (1 + 9 + 25 + 49 + 81) / 5 - 5-squared = 165 / 5 - 25 = 33 - 25 = 8.

Step 3: Number of samples with replacement = 5 x 5 = 25.

Step 4: Sample means distribution: mean 1 in 1 sample, 2 in 2, 3 in 3, 4 in 4, 5 in 5, 6 in 4, 7 in 3, 8 in 2, 9 in 1.

Step 5: Mean of the sample means = (1 x 1 + 2 x 2 + 3 x 3 + 4 x 4 + 5 x 5 + 6 x 4 + 7 x 3 + 8 x 2 + 9 x 1) / 25 = 125 / 25 = 5.

Step 6: Sample variances distribution (same differences as Q. 6 (a)): 0 in 5 samples, 1 in 8, 4 in 6, 9 in 4, 16 in 2.

Step 7: Mean of the sample variances = (0 x 5 + 1 x 8 + 4 x 6 + 9 x 4 + 16 x 2) / 25 = 100 / 25 = 4.

Step 8: Discussion: mu_(x-bar) = 5 = mu, so the sample mean is unbiased for mu.

Step 9: mu_(S-squared) = 4 = (1/2) x 8 = (n - 1) / n x sigma-squared, so S-squared with divisor n is biased downwards; dividing by n - 1 would remove the bias.

Answer: means distribution as in Step 4; variances distribution as in Step 6; mu_(x-bar) = 5, mu_(S-squared) = 4.

Q. 7 (a) A finite population consists of 5 values 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Take all possible samples of size 2 drawn without replacement. Assuming the 20 possible samples equally likely, construct the sampling distributions of sample means and sample variances and find the mean of these distributions. Calculate the mean and variance of the population and verify (i) mu_(x-bar) = mu, (ii) mu_(S-squared) = N / (N - 1) x (n - 1) / n x sigma-squared, where x-bar and S-squared are as in Q. 6 (a). (Book answers: mu = 5, sigma-squared = 8, mu_(x-bar) = 5, mu_(S-squared) = 5)

Step 1: Population mean mu = 5 and variance sigma-squared = 8, as in Q. 6 (b).

Step 2: Number of ordered samples without replacement = 5 x 4 = 20.

Step 3: Sample means distribution: mean 2 in 2 samples, 3 in 2, 4 in 4, 5 in 4, 6 in 4, 7 in 2, 8 in 2.

Step 4: Mean of the sample means = (2 x 2 + 3 x 2 + 4 x 4 + 5 x 4 + 6 x 4 + 7 x 2 + 8 x 2) / 20 = 100 / 20 = 5.

Step 5: Sample variances distribution (S-squared = (X1 - X2)-squared / 4): 1 in 8 samples, 4 in 6, 9 in 4, 16 in 2.

Step 6: Mean of the sample variances = (1 x 8 + 4 x 6 + 9 x 4 + 16 x 2) / 20 = 100 / 20 = 5.

Step 7: Verify (i): mu_(x-bar) = 5 = mu.

Step 8: Verify (ii): N / (N - 1) x (n - 1) / n x sigma-squared = (5/4) x (1/2) x 8 = 5 = mu_(S-squared).

Answer: means distribution as in Step 3; variances distribution as in Step 5; mu_(x-bar) = 5, mu_(S-squared) = 5. Both results verified.

Q. 7 (b) Take all possible samples of 2 distinct values from the population 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Assuming the 20 possible samples equally likely, construct the sampling distributions of sample means and sample variances and find the mean of these distributions. Calculate the mean and variance of the population. Discuss the results. (Book answers: mu = 6, sigma-squared = 8, mu_(x-bar) = 6, mu_(S-squared) = 5, mu_(x-bar) = mu, mu_(S-squared) = N / (N - 1) x (n - 1) / n x sigma-squared)

Step 1: Population mean mu = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10) / 5 = 30 / 5 = 6.

Step 2: Population variance sigma-squared = 220 / 5 - 36 = 8, as in Q. 6 (a).

Step 3: Number of ordered samples of 2 distinct values = 5 x 4 = 20.

Step 4: Sample means distribution: mean 3 in 2 samples, 4 in 2, 5 in 4, 6 in 4, 7 in 4, 8 in 2, 9 in 2.

Step 5: Mean of the sample means = (3 x 2 + 4 x 2 + 5 x 4 + 6 x 4 + 7 x 4 + 8 x 2 + 9 x 2) / 20 = 120 / 20 = 6.

Step 6: Sample variances distribution (same gaps as Q. 7 (a)): 1 in 8 samples, 4 in 6, 9 in 4, 16 in 2.

Step 7: Mean of the sample variances = (1 x 8 + 4 x 6 + 9 x 4 + 16 x 2) / 20 = 100 / 20 = 5.

Step 8: Discussion: mu_(x-bar) = 6 = mu, and mu_(S-squared) = 5 = (5/4) x (1/2) x 8, the without-replacement form.

Step 9: Without replacement the mean of S-squared is larger than with replacement (5 instead of 4), because no sample has variance 0.

Answer: means distribution as in Step 4; variances distribution as in Step 6; mu_(x-bar) = 6, mu_(S-squared) = 5.

options: pi = 0.5, the population probability of a head for a fair coin
p = 0.54, the proportion of heads in the sample
n = 50, the number of tosses in the sample
x = 27, the number of heads in the sample
mcqs.q: A fair coin is tossed 50 times and 27 heads are recorded. Which figure is the parameter?
mcqs.why: A parameter describes the population. For a fair coin pi = 0.5 is a property of the coin itself and does not come from the 50 tosses, while n, x and p are all computed from the sample and are statistics.

options: p = 0.27, from x = 27 heads out of 100
p = 0.54, from x = 27 heads; the book wrongly writes x = 30
mcqs.q: In the fair coin example (50 tosses, 27 heads), what is the sample proportion p, and what correction do the notes make to the book?
mcqs.why: Working: p = x / n = 27 / 50 = 0.54. The notes flag a book misprint: the printed solution writes x = 30, but 30 / 50 = 0.60, not 0.54; the question's own figure x = 27 gives the correct 0.54.

options: Mean 0 and variance pi (1 - pi) / n
Mean pi and variance pi (1 - pi) / n
Mean pi and variance pi / n
Mean n x pi and variance pi (1 - pi)
mcqs.q: What are the mean and variance of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion P for sampling with replacement?
mcqs.why: The properties state mu_P = pi and, for sampling with replacement or an infinite population, sigma_P-squared = pi (1 - pi) / n. The standard deviation sigma_P is called the standard error of the proportion.

mcqs.q: For the population 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 with samples of size n = 2 with replacement, what are pi and Var(P) for the proportion of even numbers?
mcqs.why: Working: even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, so pi = 4 / 6 = 2/3. Var(P) = pi (1 - pi) / n = (2/3)(1/3) / 2 = (2/9) / 2 = 1/9, which also equals E(P-squared) - mu_P-squared = 5/9 - 4/9.

mcqs.q: For the population 1, 3, 4, 5 (N = 4) with samples of size n = 3 without replacement, what is Var(P) for the proportion of odd numbers, where pi = 3/4?
mcqs.why: Working: Var(P) = pi (1 - pi) / n x (N - n) / (N - 1) = (3/4)(1/4) / 3 x (4 - 3) / (4 - 1) = (1/16) x (1/3) = 1/48. The finite population correction must be included because sampling is without replacement.

mcqs.q: If 60% of a city population favours public funding and 150 persons are sampled, what are the mean and standard error of the sample proportion P?
mcqs.why: Working: mu_P = pi = 0.60. Standard error = sqrt(pi (1 - pi) / n) = sqrt(0.60 x 0.40 / 150) = sqrt(0.24 / 150) = sqrt(0.0016) = 0.04. The value 0.0016 is the variance, not the standard error.

mcqs.q: A society has N = 4500 members, n = 400 are sampled, and pi = 0.7. What is the standard error of P, using the finite population correction?
What is the mean of the sampling distribution of the difference between two sample proportions, P1 - P2?
mcqs.why: The property states mu_(P1 - P2) = pi1 - pi2, the difference of the two population proportions, and its variance is the sum pi1 (1 - pi1) / n1 + pi2 (1 - pi2) / n2, with corrections when needed.

mcqs.q: P1 is the proportion of odd numbers in samples of size n1 = 3 from {4, 5} (pi1 = 1/2) and P2 in samples of size n2 = 2 from {2, 3, 6} (pi2 = 1/3). What is Var(P1 - P2)?
In city A 25% and in city B 20% of families have income Rs. 1,000 or more, with samples of 100 families from each city. What are the mean and standard error of P1 - P2?

lessons.title: Exercise — Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
What is the difference between point estimation and interval estimation?

Point estimation gives a single value as the estimate of a population parameter.

Interval estimation gives a range of values with a stated confidence level.

An interval estimate also shows how precise the estimate is.

What is a confidence interval?

A confidence interval is a range computed from sample data.

It is expected to contain the unknown true value of the parameter with a given confidence.

Its width depends on the sample size and the confidence coefficient.

Only a confidence level, with no value
