lessons.title: Exercise 12.1 — Point Estimation
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) Explain what is meant by statistical inference?

Step 1: Statistical inference is the field concerned with drawing conclusions about distributions, or about the unknown parameters of a population, by using the observed values of random variables governed by these distributions.

Step 2: It uses only a limited amount of information contained in an observed sample taken from the population at random.

Answer: Its two most important types are (i) estimation of parameters and (ii) testing of hypotheses.

Q. 1 (b) What is meant by estimation? Differentiate between estimator and estimate?

Step 1: Estimation is a procedure of making a judgment about the unknown value of a population parameter by using the sample observations.

Step 2: An estimator is a statistic, that is, a function of the sample observations, used to estimate a parameter; it is a random variable because it varies from sample to sample.

Answer: An estimate is the particular numerical value taken by the estimator for the observed sample; it is a fixed number, not a random variable.

Q. 2 (a) Specify the estimator and the estimate in each of the following: (i) A sample of 35 students gave an average height of 62 inches. (ii) A sample of 50 households having television sets showed that 85 percent of them liked a particular programme. (iii) A sample of 25 bolts produced by a company showed that 20 of them were according to specifications. (iv) A sample of 30 houses showed an average consumption of electricity as 65 units.

Step 1: (i) Estimator: sample mean height X-bar; estimate: x-bar = 62 inches.

Step 2: (ii) Estimator: sample proportion of households who liked a particular programme P; estimate: p = 0.85.

Step 3: (iii) Estimator: sample number of bolts according to specification X, with estimate x = 20; or sample proportion P, with estimate p = 20 / 25 = 0.80.

Answer: (iv) Estimator: sample mean consumption of electricity X-bar; estimate: x-bar = 65 units.

Q. 2 (b) Suppose I choose a random sample of three observations from a population and obtain the values 2, 5, 3. From these values I estimate the centre of the population by ranking the observations and taking the middle one. What estimator am I using and what is my estimate? (Book answer: Sample median X_0.5 = X_((n+1)/2); x_0.5 = x_((n+1)/2) = 3.)

Step 1: Ranking the observations 2, 5, 3 in ascending order gives 2, 3, 5.

Step 2: The middle observation, the second one, is 3.

Answer: The estimator used is the sample median X_0.5 = X_((n+1)/2), and the estimate is x_0.5 = 3.

Q. 3 (a) Is an estimator a random variable? Why or why not? (Book answer: Yes. An estimator is a random variable having its own probability distribution.)

Step 1: An estimator is a function of the sample observations X_1, X_2, ..., X_n, which are themselves random variables.

Step 2: Different random samples give different values of the estimator, so the estimator has its own probability distribution, namely its sampling distribution.

Answer: Yes, an estimator is a random variable.

Q. 3 (b) Why do we call the standard deviation of a sample statistic as standard error of the statistic? (Book answer: In the context of estimation, the deviation of a sample statistic T from its target theta (parameter to be estimated) must be considered as error. So the standard deviation of the sample statistic is commonly called the standard error of the sample statistic.)

Step 1: A sample statistic T is used to estimate a parameter theta, and T differs from theta because only a sample is observed.

Step 2: This difference is regarded as the error of the estimate.

Answer: The standard deviation of T measures the size of this error from sample to sample, so it is called the standard error of the statistic.

Q. 4 (a) What is meant by unbiasedness? Differentiate between an unbiased and a biased estimator.

Step 1: Unbiasedness: an estimator T of a parameter theta is unbiased if the mean of its sampling distribution is equal to the parameter, that is, E(T) = theta.

Step 2: An unbiased estimator is centred at the parameter it estimates, so on average it neither over-estimates nor under-estimates theta.

Answer: A biased estimator has E(T) not equal to theta; the amount of bias is Bias = E(T) - theta, so it tends to give estimates systematically above or below theta.

Q. 4 (b) A finite population consists of the numbers 3, 5, 7 and 9. Take all possible samples of size 2 which can be drawn with replacement from this population. By forming the sampling distributions of X-bar and S-squared show that (i) the sample mean X-bar = sum X_i / n is an unbiased estimator of the population mean mu. (ii) the sample variance S-squared = sum (X_i - X-bar)-squared / n is a biased estimator of the population variance sigma-squared. (Book answers: (i) mu = 6, E(X-bar) = 6, E(X-bar) = mu. (ii) sigma-squared = 5, E(S-squared) = 2.5, E(S-squared) not equal to sigma-squared.)

Step 1: Population: 3, 5, 7, 9; N = 4. Population mean: mu = (3 + 5 + 7 + 9) / 4 = 24 / 4 = 6.

Step 2: Population variance: sum of squares = 9 + 25 + 49 + 81 = 164; sigma-squared = 164 / 4 - 6-squared = 41 - 36 = 5.

Step 3: Samples of size n = 2 with replacement: 4 x 4 = 16 samples, all equally likely. The sample means have mean E(X-bar) = 6.

Step 4: The sample variances S-squared = sum (X_i - X-bar)-squared / n over the 16 samples have mean E(S-squared) = 2.5.

Answer: (i) E(X-bar) = 6 = mu, so X-bar is an unbiased estimator of mu. (ii) E(S-squared) = 2.5, which is not equal to sigma-squared = 5, so S-squared is a biased estimator of sigma-squared.

Q. 4 (c) Draw all possible samples of size 3 taken without replacement from the population 7, 10, 13 and 16. By forming the sampling distributions, show that both sample mean X-bar and sample median X_0.5 are unbiased estimators.

Step 1: Population: 7, 10, 13, 16; N = 4. Population mean: mu = (7 + 10 + 13 + 16) / 4 = 46 / 4 = 11.5.

Step 2: Samples of size n = 3 without replacement: the 4 unordered samples are (7, 10, 13), (7, 10, 16), (7, 13, 16), (10, 13, 16), all equally likely.

Step 3: Their sample means are 10, 11, 12, 13; the mean of these is (10 + 11 + 12 + 13) / 4 = 46 / 4 = 11.5.

Step 4: Their sample medians (middle values) are 10, 10, 13, 13; the mean of these is (10 + 10 + 13 + 13) / 4 = 46 / 4 = 11.5.

Answer: E(X-bar) = 11.5 = mu and E(X_0.5) = 11.5 = mu, so both the sample mean and the sample median are unbiased estimators of mu.

Q. 5 (a) A finite population consists of the numbers 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Consider all possible samples of size two which can be drawn with replacement from this population. By forming the sampling distributions of X-bar, S-squared and S-hat-squared show that (i) the sample mean X-bar = sum X_i / n is an unbiased estimator of the population mean mu. (ii) the sample variance S-squared = sum (X_i - X-bar)-squared / n is a biased estimator of the population variance sigma-squared.

(iii) the sample variance S-hat-squared = sum (X_i - X-bar)-squared / (n - 1) is an unbiased estimator of the population variance sigma-squared. (Book answers: (i) mu = 5, E(X-bar) = 5, E(X-bar) = mu. (ii) sigma-squared = 8, E(S-squared) = 4, E(S-squared) not equal to sigma-squared. (iii) sigma-squared = 8, E(S-hat-squared) = 8, E(S-hat-squared) = sigma-squared.)

Step 1: Population: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; N = 5. Population mean: mu = (1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9) / 5 = 25 / 5 = 5.

Step 2: Population variance: sum of squares = 1 + 9 + 25 + 49 + 81 = 165; sigma-squared = 165 / 5 - 5-squared = 33 - 25 = 8.

Step 3: Samples of size n = 2 with replacement: 5 x 5 = 25 samples, all equally likely. The sample means have mean E(X-bar) = 5.

Step 4: The values of S-squared over the 25 samples have mean E(S-squared) = 4.

Step 5: The values of S-hat-squared = sum (X_i - X-bar)-squared / (n - 1) over the 25 samples have mean E(S-hat-squared) = 8.

Answer: (i) E(X-bar) = 5 = mu, so X-bar is unbiased. (ii) E(S-squared) = 4, not equal to 8, so S-squared is biased. (iii) E(S-hat-squared) = 8 = sigma-squared, so S-hat-squared is unbiased.

Q. 5 (b) A finite population consists of the numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8. Find the proportion P of even numbers in all possible random samples of size n = 2 that can be drawn with replacement from this population. By forming the sampling distribution of sample proportions show that sample proportion is an unbiased estimator of the population proportion. Also verify the relation Var(P) = pi (1 - pi) / n, where P and pi are sample and population proportions respectively. (Book answers: pi = 2/3, mu_P = 2/3, sigma_P-squared = 1/9.)

Step 1: Population: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8; N = 6. Even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, that is 4 out of 6, so the population proportion is pi = 4 / 6 = 2/3.

Step 2: Samples of size n = 2 with replacement: 6 x 6 = 36 samples, all equally likely. For each sample, P = (number of even numbers) / 2, taking values 0, 1/2, 1.

Step 3: Mean of the sampling distribution: mu_P = E(P) = 2/3.

Step 4: Variance: Var(P) = pi (1 - pi) / n = (2/3) x (1/3) / 2 = (2/9) / 2 = 1/9.

Answer: mu_P = 2/3 = pi, so the sample proportion P is an unbiased estimator of pi, and Var(P) = 1/9, as required.

Q. 5 (c) A finite population consists of the numbers 4, 5, 6 and 8. Find the proportion P of even numbers in all possible random samples of size n = 3 that can be drawn without replacement from this population. By forming the sampling distribution of sample proportions show that sample proportion is an unbiased estimator of the population proportion. Also verify the relation Var(P) = (pi (1 - pi) / n) x ((N - n) / (N - 1)), where P and pi are sample and population proportions respectively. (Book answers: pi = 3/4, mu_P = 3/4, sigma_P-squared = 1/48.)

Step 1: Population: 4, 5, 6, 8; N = 4. Even numbers are 4, 6, 8, that is 3 out of 4, so pi = 3/4.

Step 2: Samples of size n = 3 without replacement: the 4 unordered samples are (4, 5, 6), (4, 5, 8), (4, 6, 8), (5, 6, 8), all equally likely.

Step 3: Their sample proportions of even numbers are 2/3, 2/3, 1, 2/3; the mean is (2/3 + 2/3 + 1 + 2/3) / 4 = 3 / 4.

Step 4: Variance: Var(P) = (pi (1 - pi) / n) x ((N - n) / (N - 1)) = ((3/4) x (1/4) / 3) x ((4 - 3) / (4 - 1)) = (1/16) x (1/3) = 1/48.

Answer: mu_P = 3/4 = pi, so P is an unbiased estimator of pi, and Var(P) = 1/48, as required.

mcqs.q: What is statistical inference, and what are its two most important types?
mcqs.why: Statistical inference draws conclusions about distributions, or about the unknown parameters of a population, using the limited information in a random sample. Its two most important types are estimation of parameters and testing of hypotheses.

mcqs.why: For an average, the estimator is the sample mean height X-bar, and the estimate is the value it takes for this sample, x-bar = 62 inches. The sample size 35 is neither the estimator nor the estimate.

mcqs.why: For a percentage who liked the programme, the estimator is the sample proportion P of households who liked it, and the estimate is p = 0.85, the value taken in this sample of 50 households.

mcqs.q: A sample of 25 bolts showed that 20 were according to specifications. Expressed as a proportion, what is the estimate p?
mcqs.why: Working: the sample proportion is p = x / n = 20 / 25 = 0.80. The estimator is the sample proportion P (or the sample number X, whose estimate is x = 20); as a proportion the estimate is 0.80.

options: Sample median X_0.5 = X_((n+1)/2); estimate x_0.5 = 3
mcqs.q: A sample gives the values 2, 5, 3, and the centre is estimated by ranking them and taking the middle one. What estimator is used and what is the estimate?
mcqs.why: Working: ranking 2, 5, 3 in ascending order gives 2, 3, 5, and the middle (second) observation is 3. Taking the middle ranked value is the sample median X_0.5 = X_((n+1)/2), and the estimate is x_0.5 = 3.

options: Yes, because it is a function of the random sample observations, so different samples give it different values and it has its own sampling distribution
No, because it always takes one fixed value

mcqs.why: An estimator is a function of X_1, X_2, ..., X_n, which are themselves random variables. Different random samples give different values, so the estimator has its own probability distribution, its sampling distribution, and is a random variable.

options: Because the statistic is always wrong by that amount
Because it is computed with an error in the formula
Because it measures the standard deviation of the population

mcqs.q: Why is the standard deviation of a sample statistic called its standard error?
mcqs.why: In estimation, the deviation of a sample statistic T from the parameter theta it estimates must be considered as error. The standard deviation of T measures the size of this error from sample to sample, so it is called the standard error.

options: When Var(T) = theta; bias = Var(T) - theta

mcqs.why: Unbiasedness means the mean of the sampling distribution equals the parameter: E(T) = theta, so on average T neither over-estimates nor under-estimates theta. A biased estimator has E(T) not equal to theta, with Bias = E(T) - theta.

mcqs.why: Working: sigma-squared = 165 / 5 - 25 = 33 - 25 = 8. Over the 25 samples, E(S-hat-squared) = 8 = sigma-squared, so S-hat-squared with divisor (n - 1) is unbiased, unlike S-squared with divisor n, whose mean is only E(S-squared) = 4.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.2 — Confidence Interval for Population Mean
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) What is meant by estimation? Distinguish between point estimate and interval estimate. Why is an interval estimate more useful?

Step 1: Estimation is a procedure of making a judgment about the unknown value of a population parameter by using the sample observations.

Step 2: A point estimate is a single number computed from the sample, used as an estimate of the parameter.

Step 3: An interval estimate is an interval computed from the sample, which is likely to include the unknown true value of the parameter.

Answer: An interval estimate is more useful because a point estimate alone gives no information about its precision, that is, about how close it is likely to be to the true value, while an interval estimate expresses the estimate together with its measure of variation.

Q. 1 (b) Distinguish between the following: (i) Estimator and estimate, (ii) Point and interval estimation.

Step 1: (i) An estimator is a statistic (a function of the sample observations) used to estimate a parameter; it is a random variable. An estimate is the particular numerical value of the estimator for the observed sample.

Answer: (ii) Point estimation gives a single number as the estimate of a parameter; interval estimation gives an interval of values, with a stated confidence coefficient, which is likely to contain the parameter.

Q. 2 (a) Explain what is meant by (i) Confidence interval, (ii) Confidence limits, (iii) Confidence coefficient.

Step 1: (i) Confidence interval: an interval (L, U) computed from the sample observations such that, prior to sampling, it includes the unknown true value of the parameter theta with a specified high probability 1 - alpha, that is, P(L < theta < U) = 1 - alpha.

Step 2: (ii) Confidence limits: the end points L and U that bound the confidence interval; L is the lower confidence limit and U is the upper confidence limit. They are functions of the sample observations and so are random variables.

Answer: (iii) Confidence coefficient: the probability 1 - alpha that the random interval includes the parameter; commonly used values are 90 percent, 95 percent, 98 percent and 99 percent.

Q. 2 (b) When would a confidence interval be preferred over point estimation for a parameter? (Book answer: When the reliability of a point estimator is needed, the confidence interval conveniently expresses the estimator along with its measure of variation. Reliability is reported through the confidence coefficient and the variation is reflected by the length of the interval.)

Step 1: A point estimate alone does not show how reliable it is.

Step 2: A confidence interval gives the point estimate together with its measure of variation, in the form of the length of the interval.

Answer: A confidence interval is therefore preferred when the reliability of the estimate must be reported: the confidence coefficient states the reliability, and the length of the interval reflects the variation.

Q. 3 (a) Find a 90% confidence interval for the mean of a normal distribution with sigma = 3, given the sample as 2.3, -0.2, -0.4, -0.9. (Book answer: -2.268 < mu < 2.668.)

Step 1: Sample size n = 4. Sample mean: x-bar = (2.3 - 0.2 - 0.4 - 0.9) / 4 = 0.8 / 4 = 0.2.

Step 2: sigma = 3 is known, so the 90% confidence interval is x-bar +/- z_0.95 x (sigma / sqrt(n)), with z_0.95 = 1.645.

Step 3: Standard error: sigma / sqrt(n) = 3 / sqrt(4) = 3 / 2 = 1.5.

Step 4: Margin of error: 1.645 x 1.5 = 2.468.

Answer: The interval is 0.2 +/- 2.468, that is, -2.268 < mu < 2.668.

Q. 3 (b) The standard deviation of the amounts poured into bottles by an automatic filling machine is 1.8 ml (millilitre). The amounts of fill in a random sample of bottles, in ml, were 481, 479, 482, 480, 477, 478, 481 and 482. Suppose the population of amounts of fill is normal. Construct a 90% confidence interval for the mean amount in all bottles filled by the machine. (Book answer: 478.95 < mu < 481.05.)

Step 1: Sample size n = 8. Sample mean: x-bar = (481 + 479 + 482 + 480 + 477 + 478 + 481 + 482) / 8 = 3840 / 8 = 480 ml.

Step 2: sigma = 1.8 ml is known, so the 90% interval is x-bar +/- 1.645 x (sigma / sqrt(n)).

Step 3: Standard error: 1.8 / sqrt(8) = 1.8 / 2.828 = 0.636 ml.

Step 4: Margin of error: 1.645 x 0.636 = 1.047 ml.

Answer: The interval is 480 +/- 1.047, that is, 478.95 < mu < 481.05 ml.

Q. 4 (a) A random sample of size 36 is taken from a normal population with a known variance sigma-squared = 25. If the mean of the sample is 42.6, find 95% confidence limits for the population mean. (Book answer: 40.967 < mu < 44.233.)

Step 1: n = 36, x-bar = 42.6, sigma-squared = 25, so sigma = 5.

Step 2: The 95% interval is x-bar +/- z_0.975 x (sigma / sqrt(n)), with z_0.975 = 1.960.

Step 3: Standard error: 5 / sqrt(36) = 5 / 6 = 0.833.

Step 4: Margin of error: 1.960 x 0.833 = 1.633.

Answer: The interval is 42.6 +/- 1.633, that is, 40.967 < mu < 44.233.

Q. 4 (b) A school wishes to estimate the average weight of students in the sixth grade. A random sample of n = 25 is selected and the sample mean is found to be x-bar = 100 lbs. The standard deviation of the population is known to be 15 lbs.

Compute 90% confidence interval for the population mean. (Book answer: 95.065 < mu < 104.935.)

Step 1: n = 25, x-bar = 100 lbs, sigma = 15 lbs (known).

Step 2: The 90% interval is x-bar +/- z_0.95 x (sigma / sqrt(n)), with z_0.95 = 1.645.

Step 3: Standard error: 15 / sqrt(25) = 15 / 5 = 3 lbs.

Step 4: Margin of error: 1.645 x 3 = 4.935 lbs.

Answer: The interval is 100 +/- 4.935, that is, 95.065 < mu < 104.935 lbs.

Q. 5 (a) Suppose that the weights of 100 male students of a university represent a random sample of weights of 1546 students of the university. Find 99% confidence intervals for the mean weight of the students, given x-bar = 67.45 and s-hat = 2.99.

(Book answer: 66.68 < mu < 68.22.)

Step 1: n = 100, x-bar = 67.45, s-hat = 2.99. The sample is large, so the 99% interval is x-bar +/- z_0.995 x (s-hat / sqrt(n)), with z_0.995 = 2.576.

Step 2: Standard error: 2.99 / sqrt(100) = 2.99 / 10 = 0.299.

Step 3: Margin of error: 2.576 x 0.299 = 0.770.

Answer: The interval is 67.45 +/- 0.770, that is, 66.68 < mu < 68.22.

Q. 5 (b) 150 bags of flour of a particular brand are weighed and the mean mass is found to be 748 g, with standard deviation 3.6 g. Find 98% confidence intervals for the mean mass of bags of flour of this brand. (Book answer: 747.316 < mu < 748.684.)

Step 1: n = 150, x-bar = 748 g, s-hat = 3.6 g. The sample is large, so the 98% interval is x-bar +/- z_0.99 x (s-hat / sqrt(n)), with z_0.99 = 2.326.

Step 2: Standard error: 3.6 / sqrt(150) = 3.6 / 12.247 = 0.294 g.

Step 3: Margin of error: 2.326 x 0.294 = 0.684 g.

Answer: The interval is 748 +/- 0.684, that is, 747.316 < mu < 748.684 g.

Q. 6 (a) If the two-sided 100 (1 - alpha)% confidence interval based on random sample taken from X ~ N(mu, sigma-squared) is 12.18 < mu < 20.56, find x-bar.

(Book answer: x-bar = 16.37.)

Step 1: The sample mean x-bar is the midpoint of the confidence interval.

Step 2: Midpoint = (12.18 + 20.56) / 2 = 32.74 / 2 = 16.37.

Answer: x-bar = 16.37.

Q. 6 (b) On the basis of the results obtained from a random sample of 100 men from a particular area, the 95% confidence interval for the mean height of the male population of the area was found to be (177.22 cm, 179.18 cm). Find the value of x-bar, the mean of the sample and sigma, the standard deviation of the normal population from which the sample was drawn. Find 98% confidence interval for the mean height. (Book answers: x-bar = 178.2, sigma = 5, 177.04 < mu < 179.36.)

Step 1: x-bar is the midpoint of the 95% interval: x-bar = (177.22 + 179.18) / 2 = 356.40 / 2 = 178.2 cm.

Step 2: The 95% margin of error is (179.18 - 177.22) / 2 = 1.96 / 2 = 0.98 cm.

Step 3: Margin = z_0.975 x (sigma / sqrt(n)) = 1.960 x (sigma / 10) = 0.98, so sigma / 10 = 0.5, giving sigma = 5 cm.

Step 4: The 98% margin is z_0.99 x (sigma / sqrt(n)) = 2.326 x 0.5 = 1.163 cm.

Answer: The 98% interval is 178.2 +/- 1.163, that is, 177.04 < mu < 179.36 cm.

Q. 7 (a) Explain what is meant by the statement, 'we are 100 (1 - alpha)% confident that our interval estimate contains mu.' (Book answer: In repeated sampling, 100 (1 - alpha)% of all such confidence intervals contain mu.)

Step 1: Before the sample is taken, the interval (L, U) is random, and the probability that it includes the fixed parameter mu is 1 - alpha.

Step 2: After the sample is taken, the particular interval either contains mu or it does not; the probability statement refers to the procedure, not to the one interval.

Answer: In repeated sampling, about 100 (1 - alpha)% of all such confidence intervals will contain mu, and about 100 alpha% will miss it.

Q. 7 (b) Explain what is meant by the statement, 'we are 95% confident that our interval contains mu.' (Book answer: In repeated sampling, 95% of all such confidence intervals contain mu.)

Step 1: The confidence coefficient is 1 - alpha = 0.95.

Step 2: The procedure produces intervals that include mu in 95% of repeated samples.

Answer: We are 95% confident that our interval contains mu means that, in repeated sampling, 95% of all such confidence intervals contain mu.

Q. 7 (c) If an 85% confidence interval is 27.5 < mu < 43.8, what does this statement 85% mean? (Book answer: Intervals so formed would contain mu 85% of the time.)

Step 1: The confidence coefficient is 85%, so 1 - alpha = 0.85.

Step 2: The interval 27.5 < mu < 43.8 is one interval produced by the procedure.

Answer: 85% means that intervals formed in this way would contain mu 85% of the time, in repeated sampling.

Q. 7 (d) If alpha = 0.10, how many intervals would be expected to contain mu?

(Book answer: We would expect about 90% of the intervals to contain mu and 10% to miss mu in the long-run in repeated sampling.)

Step 1: The confidence coefficient is 1 - alpha = 1 - 0.10 = 0.90, that is, 90%.

Answer: We would expect about 90% of the intervals to contain mu and 10% to miss mu, in the long run in repeated sampling.

Q. 8 (a) What role does the sample mean play in a two-sided confidence interval for mu, based on a random sample from X ~ N(mu, sigma-squared)? (Book answer: The sample mean is the midpoint of the confidence interval but has no effect on the length of the interval.)

Step 1: The interval is x-bar +/- z_(1 - alpha/2) x (sigma / sqrt(n)).

Step 2: x-bar fixes the centre of the interval.

Answer: The sample mean is the midpoint of the confidence interval, but it has no effect on the length of the interval, which depends only on z, sigma and n.

Q. 8 (b) When setting a two-sided 100 (1 - alpha)% confidence interval for mu, based on a random sample of size n from a normal population, how will the following changes affect the length of the confidence interval for mu: (Assume all other quantities remain fixed.) (i) increasing n (ii) increasing (1 - alpha) (iii) decreasing n (iv) decreasing (1 - alpha) (v) increasing s-squared (vi) increasing x-bar (vii) increasing alpha (viii) decreasing s-hat. (Book answers: decreased, increased, increased, decreased, increased, no effect, decreased, decreased.)

Step 1: The length of the interval is 2 x z_(1 - alpha/2) x (sigma / sqrt(n)) (or with s-hat in place of sigma).

Step 2: (i) Increasing n makes sigma / sqrt(n) smaller, so the length decreases. (ii) Increasing (1 - alpha) makes z larger, so the length increases.

Step 3: (iii) Decreasing n makes sigma / sqrt(n) larger, so the length increases. (iv) Decreasing (1 - alpha) makes z smaller, so the length decreases.

Step 4: (v) Increasing s-squared (hence s-hat) makes the standard error larger, so the length increases. (vi) Increasing x-bar only shifts the centre, so the length is unchanged (no effect).

Step 5: (vii) Increasing alpha decreases (1 - alpha) and hence z, so the length decreases. (viii) Decreasing s-hat makes the standard error smaller, so the length decreases.

Answer: In order: decreased, increased, increased, decreased, increased, no effect, decreased, decreased.

Q. 9 (a) Define Student's t-statistic. What assumptions are made about the population where the t-distribution is used?

Step 1: Student's t-statistic is T = (X-bar - mu) / (S-hat / sqrt(n)), where S-hat is the sample standard deviation with divisor n - 1.

Step 2: When the population is normal, T has a t-distribution with v = n - 1 degrees of freedom.

Answer: Assumptions: the sample is a random sample from a normal population, the population mean mu is unknown, and the population variance sigma-squared is unknown (so sigma is replaced by S-hat); the t-distribution is used when n is small.

Q. 9 (b) The contents of 10 similar containers of a commercial soap are: 10.2, 9.7, 10.1, 10.3, 10.1, 9.8, 9.9, 10.4, 10.3 and 9.8 litres. Find 99% confidence interval for the mean soap content of all such containers, assuming an approximate normal distribution. (Book answer: 9.807 < mu < 10.313.)

Step 1: n = 10. Sample mean: x-bar = (10.2 + 9.7 + 10.1 + 10.3 + 10.1 + 9.8 + 9.9 + 10.4 + 10.3 + 9.8) / 10 = 100.6 / 10 = 10.06 litres.

Step 2: Sample standard deviation: s-hat = 0.246 litres (computed from the sum of squared deviations divided by n - 1 = 9).

Step 3: The population is normal with sigma unknown and n small, so use the t-distribution with v = n - 1 = 9 degrees of freedom: t_(9; 0.995) = 3.250.

Step 4: Standard error: s-hat / sqrt(n) = 0.246 / sqrt(10) = 0.246 / 3.162 = 0.078 litres.

Step 5: Margin of error: 3.250 x 0.078 = 0.253 litres.

Answer: The interval is 10.06 +/- 0.253, that is, 9.807 < mu < 10.313 litres.

Q. 10 (a) The masses in grams, of thirteen ball bearings taken at random from a batch are 21.4, 23.1, 25.9, 24.7, 23.4, 21.5, 25.0, 22.5, 26.9, 26.4, 25.8, 23.2, 21.9.

Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the mean mass of the population, supposed normal, from which these masses were drawn. (Book answer: 22.82 < mu < 25.14.)

Step 1: n = 13. Sample mean: x-bar = 311.7 / 13 = 23.977 g.

Step 2: Sample standard deviation: s-hat = 1.914 g.

Step 3: The population is normal with sigma unknown and n small, so use the t-distribution with v = 12 degrees of freedom: t_(12; 0.975) = 2.179.

Step 4: Standard error: 1.914 / sqrt(13) = 1.914 / 3.606 = 0.531 g.

Step 5: Margin of error: 2.179 x 0.531 = 1.157 g.

Answer: The interval is 23.977 +/- 1.157, that is, 22.82 < mu < 25.14 g.

Q. 10 (b) A random sample of seven independent observations of a normal variable gave sum x = 35.9, sum x-squared = 186.19. Calculate a 90% confidence interval for the population mean. (Book answer: 4.70 < mu < 5.56.)

Step 1: n = 7. Sample mean: x-bar = 35.9 / 7 = 5.129.

Step 2: Sample variance: s-hat-squared = (sum x-squared - n x-bar-squared) / (n - 1) = (186.19 - 7 x 26.306) / 6 = (186.19 - 184.14) / 6 = 0.342, so s-hat = 0.588.

Step 3: Use the t-distribution with v = 6 degrees of freedom: t_(6; 0.95) = 1.943.

Step 4: Standard error: 0.588 / sqrt(7) = 0.588 / 2.646 = 0.222.

Step 5: Margin of error: 1.943 x 0.222 = 0.432.

Answer: The interval is 5.129 +/- 0.432, that is, 4.70 < mu < 5.56.

Q. 11 (a) A random sample of eight observations of a normal variable gave sum x = 261.2, sum (x - x-bar)-squared = 3.22. Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the population mean. (Book answer: 32.08 < mu < 33.22.)

Step 1: n = 8. Sample mean: x-bar = 261.2 / 8 = 32.65.

Step 2: Sample standard deviation: s-hat = sqrt(3.22 / 7) = sqrt(0.460) = 0.678.

Step 3: Use the t-distribution with v = 7 degrees of freedom: t_(7; 0.975) = 2.365.

Step 4: Standard error: 0.678 / sqrt(8) = 0.678 / 2.828 = 0.240.

Step 5: Margin of error: 2.365 x 0.240 = 0.567.

Answer: The interval is 32.65 +/- 0.567, that is, 32.08 < mu < 33.22.

Q. 11 (b) A sample of 12 measurements of the breaking strength of cotton threads gave a mean x-bar = 209 grams and a standard deviation s-hat = 35 grams. Find 95% and 99% confidence limits for the actual mean breaking strength. (Book answers: 186.76 < mu < 231.24; 177.62 < mu < 240.38.)

Step 1: n = 12, x-bar = 209 g, s-hat = 35 g. Standard error: 35 / sqrt(12) = 35 / 3.464 = 10.104 g.

Step 2: 95% interval: use t_(11; 0.975) = 2.201. Margin of error: 2.201 x 10.104 = 22.24 g.

Step 3: The 95% interval is 209 +/- 22.24, that is, 186.76 < mu < 231.24 g.

Step 4: 99% interval: use t_(11; 0.995) = 3.106. Margin of error: 3.106 x 10.104 = 31.38 g.

Answer: The 99% interval is 209 +/- 31.38, that is, 177.62 < mu < 240.38 g.

Q. 12 (a) A random sample of 16 values from a normal population showed a mean of 41.5 inches and a sum of squares of deviations from this mean equal to 135 (inches)-squared. Show that the 95% confidence limits for this mean are 39.9 and 43.1 inches.

Step 1: n = 16, x-bar = 41.5 inches, sum (x - x-bar)-squared = 135.

Step 2: Sample standard deviation: s-hat = sqrt(135 / 15) = sqrt(9) = 3.0 inches.

Step 3: Use the t-distribution with v = 15 degrees of freedom: t_(15; 0.975) = 2.131.

Step 4: Standard error: 3.0 / sqrt(16) = 3.0 / 4 = 0.75 inches.

Step 5: Margin of error: 2.131 x 0.75 = 1.598 inches.

Answer: The interval is 41.5 +/- 1.598, that is, 39.9 < mu < 43.1 inches, as required.

Q. 12 (b) Find a 99% confidence interval for the mean of normal distribution with sigma = 2.5 and if a sample of size 7 gave the values 9, 16, 10, 14, 8, 13, 14. What would be the confidence interval if sigma were unknown. (Book answers: 9.566 < mu < 14.434; 7.797 < mu < 16.203 when sigma is unknown.)

Step 1: Sample: 9, 16, 10, 14, 8, 13, 14; n = 7. Sample mean: x-bar = 84 / 7 = 12.

Step 2: Sample standard deviation: s-hat = 3.0 (the sum of squared deviations is 54, and 54 / 6 = 9).

Step 3: If sigma = 2.5 is known: standard error = 2.5 / sqrt(7) = 2.5 / 2.646 = 0.945.

Margin of error: z_0.995 x 0.945 = 2.576 x 0.945 = 2.434.

Step 4: The interval with sigma known is 12 +/- 2.434, that is, 9.566 < mu < 14.434.

Step 5: If sigma is unknown: standard error = 3.0 / sqrt(7) = 1.134. Use t_(6; 0.995) = 3.707. Margin of error: 3.707 x 1.134 = 4.204.

Answer: The interval with sigma unknown is 12 +/- 4.204, that is, 7.797 < mu < 16.203.

mcqs.q: Why is an interval estimate more useful than a point estimate?
options: It always gives the exact value of the population parameter
It expresses the estimate together with its measure of variation, while a point estimate alone gives no information about its precision
It is a single number computed from the sample observations
It does not depend on the sample observations at all
mcqs.why: A point estimate alone gives no information about how close it is likely to be to the true value. An interval estimate expresses the estimate together with its measure of variation, so its precision is also reported.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an estimator from an estimate?
options: An estimator is a constant, while an estimate is a random variable
An estimator is the unknown parameter, while an estimate is a sample
An estimator is a statistic used to estimate a parameter and is a random variable; an estimate is its particular numerical value for the observed sample
An estimator and an estimate are both particular numerical values from one sample
mcqs.why: An estimator is a function of the sample observations, so before sampling it is a random variable. Once the sample is observed, the numerical value taken by that estimator is called the estimate.

mcqs.q: The confidence coefficient of a confidence interval (L, U) for a parameter theta is:
options: The probability 1 - alpha that the random interval includes the parameter
The probability alpha that the random interval includes the parameter
The length U - L of the interval
The value of the sample mean x-bar
mcqs.why: By definition P(L < theta < U) = 1 - alpha, so 1 - alpha is the confidence coefficient. Commonly used values given in the notes are 90 percent, 95 percent, 98 percent and 99 percent.

mcqs.q: Find a 90% confidence interval for mu for a normal distribution with sigma = 3, given the sample 2.3, -0.2, -0.4, -0.9.
The standard deviation of amounts poured by a filling machine is sigma = 1.8 ml. A sample of 8 bottles has mean fill 480 ml. Construct a 90% confidence interval for mu.
mcqs.why: x-bar = 3840 / 8 = 480 ml and sigma is known. Standard error = 1.8 / sqrt(8) = 0.636 ml. Margin = 1.645 x 0.636 = 1.047 ml. Interval = 480 +/- 1.047, that is, 478.95 < mu < 481.05 ml.

mcqs.q: A random sample of size 36 from a normal population with sigma-squared = 25 has sample mean 42.6. Find the 95% confidence limits for mu.
For a large sample of 100 male students, x-bar = 67.45 and s-hat = 2.99. Find a 99% confidence interval for mu.
mcqs.why: The sample is large, so use Z with s-hat. Standard error = 2.99 / sqrt(100) = 0.299. Margin = z_0.995 x 0.299 = 2.576 x 0.299 = 0.770. Interval = 67.45 +/- 0.770, that is, 66.68 < mu < 68.22.

mcqs.q: A two-sided confidence interval for mu is 12.18 < mu < 20.56. What is the value of x-bar?
mcqs.why: The sample mean x-bar is the midpoint of a two-sided confidence interval for mu. Midpoint = (12.18 + 20.56) / 2 = 32.74 / 2 = 16.37, so x-bar = 16.37.

mcqs.q: In a two-sided confidence interval for mu, if the sample size n is increased while all other quantities stay fixed, the length of the interval:
mcqs.why: The length is 2 x z x (sigma / sqrt(n)). Increasing n makes sigma / sqrt(n) smaller, so the margin of error and hence the length of the interval decrease.

mcqs.q: The contents of 10 containers have x-bar = 10.06 litres and s-hat = 0.246 litres, from an approximately normal population with sigma unknown. Find a 99% confidence interval for mu.
mcqs.why: Sigma is unknown and n is small, so use t with v = 9: t_(9; 0.995) = 3.250. Standard error = 0.246 / sqrt(10) = 0.078. Margin = 3.250 x 0.078 = 0.253. Interval = 10.06 +/- 0.253, that is, 9.807 < mu < 10.313 litres.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.3 — Confidence Interval for Population Proportion
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) A sample poll of 100 voters chosen at random from all voters in a given district indicated that 55% of them were in favour of a particular candidate. Find (i) 95% and (ii) 99% confidence limits for the proportion of all the voters in favour of this candidate. (Book answers: (i) 0.453 < pi < 0.647, (ii) 0.422 < pi < 0.678.)

Step 1: n = 100, sample proportion p = 0.55.

Step 2: Standard error of P: sqrt(p (1 - p) / n) = sqrt(0.55 x 0.45 / 100) = sqrt(0.002475) = 0.0497.

Step 3: (i) 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.0497 = 0.0975.

Step 4: The 95% interval is 0.55 +/- 0.0975, that is, 0.453 < pi < 0.647.

Step 5: (ii) 99% interval: margin of error = 2.576 x 0.0497 = 0.128.

Answer: The 99% interval is 0.55 +/- 0.128, that is, 0.422 < pi < 0.678.

Q. 1 (b) In a random sample of 1000 houses in a certain city, it is found that 228 own colour television sets. Find 98% confidence interval for the proportion of houses in this city that own coloured sets. (Book answer: 0.197 < pi < 0.259.)

Step 1: n = 1000, x = 228, so p = 228 / 1000 = 0.228.

Step 2: Standard error: sqrt(0.228 x 0.772 / 1000) = sqrt(0.000176) = 0.0133.

Step 3: 98% interval: margin of error = 2.326 x 0.0133 = 0.0309.

Answer: The interval is 0.228 +/- 0.0309, that is, 0.197 < pi < 0.259.

Q. 2 (a) In 40 tosses of a coin 24 heads were obtained. Find (i) 95% and (ii) 99.73% confidence limits for the proportion of heads which would be obtained in an unlimited number of tosses of the coin. (Book answers: (i) 0.448 < pi < 0.752, (ii) 0.368 < pi < 0.832.)

Step 1: n = 40, x = 24, so p = 24 / 40 = 0.60.

Step 2: Standard error: sqrt(0.60 x 0.40 / 40) = sqrt(0.006) = 0.0775.

Step 3: (i) 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.0775 = 0.152.

Step 4: The 95% interval is 0.60 +/- 0.152, that is, 0.448 < pi < 0.752.

Step 5: (ii) 99.73% interval: use z = 3. Margin of error = 3 x 0.0775 = 0.232.

Answer: The 99.73% interval is 0.60 +/- 0.232, that is, 0.368 < pi < 0.832.

Q. 2 (b) A random sample of 200 voters in a constituency included 110 who said they would vote for Mr. A. Assuming all the 15000 voters in the constituency would vote, give an approximate 95% confidence interval for the proportion who would vote for Mr. A. (Book answer: 0.4815 < pi < 0.6185.)

Step 1: n = 200, x = 110, so p = 110 / 200 = 0.55. Population size N = 15000.

Step 2: Standard error with finite population correction: sqrt(p (1 - p) / n) x sqrt((N - n) / (N - 1)) = sqrt(0.55 x 0.45 / 200) x sqrt(14800 / 14999) = 0.0352 x 0.9933 = 0.0349.

Step 3: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.0349 = 0.0685.

Answer: The interval is 0.55 +/- 0.0685, that is, 0.4815 < pi < 0.6185.

Q. 2 (c) A random sample of 500 pineapples was taken from a large consignment and 65 were found to be bad. Show that the percentage of bad pineapples in the consignment almost certainly lies between 8.05 and 17.95. (Book answer: interval 0.0805 < pi < 0.1795.)

Step 1: n = 500, x = 65, so p = 65 / 500 = 0.13.

Step 2: Standard error: sqrt(0.13 x 0.87 / 500) = sqrt(0.000226) = 0.0150.

Step 3: 'Almost certainly' means a 99.9% confidence interval: use z = 3.291. Margin of error: 3.291 x 0.0150 = 0.0495.

Answer: The interval is 0.13 +/- 0.0495, that is, 0.0805 < pi < 0.1795, so the percentage of bad pineapples almost certainly lies between 8.05% and 17.95%.

mcqs.q: In a sample poll of 100 voters, 55% favour a candidate. Find the 95% confidence limits for the proportion pi of all voters in favour.
For the same poll of 100 voters with p = 0.55, find the 99% confidence limits for pi.
In a random sample of 1000 houses, 228 own colour television sets. Find a 98% confidence interval for the proportion pi of houses owning coloured sets.
In 40 tosses of a coin, 24 heads were obtained. Find the 95% confidence limits for the proportion of heads in an unlimited number of tosses.
For the same coin tossed 40 times with 24 heads, find the 99.73% confidence limits for the proportion of heads.
mcqs.why: p = 0.60 and standard error = sqrt(0.60 x 0.40 / 40) = 0.0775. For 99.73% confidence the notes use z = 3, so margin = 3 x 0.0775 = 0.232. Interval = 0.60 +/- 0.232, that is, 0.368 < pi < 0.832.

mcqs.q: A random sample of 200 voters from 15000 voters included 110 who would vote for Mr. A. Using the finite population correction, find the approximate 95% confidence interval for pi.
A random sample of 500 pineapples contained 65 bad ones. The interval showing where the percentage of bad pineapples almost certainly lies is:
mcqs.why: p = 65 / 500 = 0.13. Standard error = sqrt(0.13 x 0.87 / 500) = 0.0150. Almost certainly means 99.9% confidence, z = 3.291, so margin = 3.291 x 0.0150 = 0.0495. Interval = 0.13 +/- 0.0495, that is, 0.0805 < pi < 0.1795.

mcqs.q: In the poll of 100 voters where p = 0.55, the standard error of the sample proportion P is:
mcqs.why: Standard error of P = sqrt(p(1 - p) / n) = sqrt(0.55 x 0.45 / 100) = sqrt(0.002475) = 0.0497. The value 0.002475 is the variance inside the square root, not the standard error itself.

mcqs.q: In the sample of 1000 houses in which 228 own colour television sets, the sample proportion p is:
mcqs.why: The sample proportion is p = x / n = 228 / 1000 = 0.228. This is the point estimate of the population proportion pi used at the centre of the confidence interval in the notes.

mcqs.q: For the television sample (n = 1000, p = 0.228, standard error = 0.0133), the margin of error for a 98% confidence interval is:
mcqs.why: Margin of error = z_0.99 x standard error = 2.326 x 0.0133 = 0.0309. Adding and subtracting this from p = 0.228 gives the 98% interval 0.197 < pi < 0.259 stated in the notes.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.4 — Confidence Interval for Difference Between Two Population Means
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) A test in statistics was given to 50 girls and 75 boys. The girls made an average grade of 76 with a standard deviation of 6, while the boys made an average grade of 82 with a standard deviation of 8. Find a 96% confidence interval for the difference mu_1 - mu_2, where mu_1 is the mean score of all boys and mu_2 is the mean score of all girls who might take this test. (Book answer: 3.42 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 8.58.)

Step 1: Boys: n_1 = 75, x-bar_1 = 82, sigma_1 = 8 (used as known). Girls: n_2 = 50, x-bar_2 = 76, sigma_2 = 6.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: x-bar_1 - x-bar_2 = 82 - 76 = 6.

Step 3: Standard error of the difference: sqrt(sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2) = sqrt(64 / 75 + 36 / 50) = sqrt(0.853 + 0.720) = sqrt(1.573) = 1.254.

Step 4: 96% interval: use z_0.98 = 2.054. Margin of error: 2.054 x 1.254 = 2.576.

Answer: The interval is 6 +/- 2.576, that is, 3.42 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 8.58.

Q. 1 (b) A manufacturing company consists of two departments producing identical products. It is suspected that the hourly outputs in the two departments are different. Two random samples of production hours are respectively selected and the following data are obtained: Department 1: sample size 64, sample mean 100.

Department 2: sample size 49, sample mean 90. The variances of the hourly outputs for the two departments are known to be sigma_1-squared = 256 and sigma_2-squared = 196 respectively. What is the point estimate for the true difference between the mean outputs of the two departments? Find the 95 percent confidence limits for the true difference. (Book answers: x-bar_1 - x-bar_2 = 10; 4.456 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 15.544.)

Step 1: n_1 = 64, x-bar_1 = 100, sigma_1-squared = 256; n_2 = 49, x-bar_2 = 90, sigma_2-squared = 196.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: x-bar_1 - x-bar_2 = 100 - 90 = 10.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(256 / 64 + 196 / 49) = sqrt(4 + 4) = sqrt(8) = 2.828.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 2.828 = 5.544.

Answer: The interval is 10 +/- 5.544, that is, 4.456 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 15.544.

Q. 2 (a) Two independent samples of 100 mechanists and 100 carpenters are taken to estimate the difference between the weekly wages of the two categories of workers. The relevant data are given below: Mechanists: sample mean wages 345, population variance 196. Carpenters: sample mean wages 340, population variance 204. Determine the 95% and the 99% confidence limits for the true difference between the average wages of mechanists and carpenters. (Book answers: 1.08 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 8.92; -0.152 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 10.152.)

Step 1: n_1 = n_2 = 100, x-bar_1 = 345, sigma_1-squared = 196; x-bar_2 = 340, sigma_2-squared = 204.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: 345 - 340 = 5.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(196 / 100 + 204 / 100) = sqrt(1.96 + 2.04) = sqrt(4) = 2.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 2 = 3.92. The interval is 5 +/- 3.92, that is, 1.08 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 8.92.

Step 5: 99% interval: margin of error = 2.576 x 2 = 5.152.

Answer: The 99% interval is 5 +/- 5.152, that is, -0.152 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 10.152.

Q. 2 (b) General Incorporated Mill's packing machinery is known to pour dry cereal into economy-size boxes with a standard deviation of 0.6 ounce. Two samples taken on two machines yield the following information: Machine I: n_1 = 15, x-bar_1 = 18.7 ounces. Machine II: n_2 = 21, x-bar_2 = 21.9 ounces. Assuming machine I packages a content that is N(mu_1, 0.36) and machine II packages a content that is N(mu_2, 0.36), construct a 95% confidence interval estimate of mu_2 - mu_1. (Book answer: 2.8 < mu_2 - mu_1 < 3.6.)

Step 1: n_1 = 15, x-bar_1 = 18.7; n_2 = 21, x-bar_2 = 21.9; sigma-squared = 0.36 for both machines.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: x-bar_2 - x-bar_1 = 21.9 - 18.7 = 3.2.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(0.36 / 15 + 0.36 / 21) = sqrt(0.024 + 0.0171) = sqrt(0.0411) = 0.203.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.203 = 0.398.

Answer: The interval is 3.2 +/- 0.398, that is, 2.8 < mu_2 - mu_1 < 3.6.

Q. 3 (a) A sample of 150 brand A light bulbs showed a mean lifetime of 1400 hours with a standard deviation of 120 hours. A sample of 200 brand B light bulbs showed a mean lifetime of 1200 hours with a standard deviation of 80 hours. Find 95% and 99% confidence limits for the difference between the mean lifetime of the populations of brands A and B. (Book answers: 177.825 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 222.175; 170.856 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 229.144.)

Step 1: Brand A: n_1 = 150, x-bar_1 = 1400, s-hat_1 = 120. Brand B: n_2 = 200, x-bar_2 = 1200, s-hat_2 = 80. Both samples are large, so use the normal approximation.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: 1400 - 1200 = 200 hours.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(120-squared / 150 + 80-squared / 200) = sqrt(96 + 32) = sqrt(128) = 11.314 hours.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 11.314 = 22.175. The interval is 200 +/- 22.175, that is, 177.825 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 222.175.

Step 5: 99% interval: margin of error = 2.576 x 11.314 = 29.144.

Answer: The 99% interval is 200 +/- 29.144, that is, 170.856 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 229.144 hours.

Q. 3 (b) Let two independent random samples, each of size 100, from independent normal distributions N(mu_1, sigma_1-squared) and N(mu_2, sigma_2-squared) yield x-bar_1 = 4.8, s-hat_1-squared = 8.64, x-bar_2 = 5.6, s-hat_2-squared = 7.

Find a 95% confidence interval for (mu_2 - mu_1). (Book answer: 0.025 < mu_2 - mu_1 < 1.575.)

Step 1: n_1 = n_2 = 100, x-bar_1 = 4.8, s-hat_1-squared = 8.64; x-bar_2 = 5.6, s-hat_2-squared = 7.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: x-bar_2 - x-bar_1 = 5.6 - 4.8 = 0.8.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(8.64 / 100 + 7 / 100) = sqrt(0.0864 + 0.07) = sqrt(0.1564) = 0.395.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.395 = 0.775.

Answer: The interval is 0.8 +/- 0.775, that is, 0.025 < mu_2 - mu_1 < 1.575.

Q. 4 (a) In order to ascertain the age distribution of operatives in a certain industry, random samples of 1720 males and 1230 females are drawn. The sample means and standard deviations were 33.93 years and 14.20 years for the males and 27.44 years and 10.79 years for the females. Calculate the 95 percent confidence interval for (i) the mean age of all male operatives, (ii) the mean age of all female operatives, (iii) the difference between their mean ages. (Book answers: 33.259 < mu_1 < 34.601; 26.837 < mu_2 < 28.043; 5.588 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 7.392.)

Step 1: Males: n_1 = 1720, x-bar_1 = 33.93, s-hat_1 = 14.20. Females: n_2 = 1230, x-bar_2 = 27.44, s-hat_2 = 10.79. Both samples are large, so use the normal approximation.

Step 2: (i) Male standard error: 14.20 / sqrt(1720) = 14.20 / 41.473 = 0.342. Margin: 1.960 x 0.342 = 0.671. Interval: 33.93 +/- 0.671, that is, 33.259 < mu_1 < 34.601.

Step 3: (ii) Female standard error: 10.79 / sqrt(1230) = 10.79 / 35.071 = 0.308.

Margin: 1.960 x 0.308 = 0.603. Interval: 27.44 +/- 0.603, that is, 26.837 < mu_2 < 28.043.

Step 4: (iii) Difference: 33.93 - 27.44 = 6.49. Standard error of the difference: sqrt(0.342-squared + 0.308-squared) = sqrt(0.117 + 0.095) = sqrt(0.212) = 0.460.

Margin: 1.960 x 0.460 = 0.902.

Answer: The interval for the difference is 6.49 +/- 0.902, that is, 5.588 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 7.392.

Q. 4 (b) The means and variances in the weekly incomes in rupees of the workers employed in the different factories, from the samples are given below: Factory A: sample size 160, mean 12.80, variance 64. Factory B: sample size 220, mean 11.25, variance 49. (i) What is the maximum likelihood estimate of the difference in mean incomes? (ii) Compute the 95 percent confidence interval estimate for the real differences in the incomes of the workers of the two factories. (Book answers: (i) 1.55, (ii) 0.003 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 3.097.)

Step 1: n_1 = 160, x-bar_1 = 12.80, variance 64; n_2 = 220, x-bar_2 = 11.25, variance 49.

Step 2: (i) The maximum likelihood estimate of mu_1 - mu_2 is x-bar_1 - x-bar_2 = 12.80 - 11.25 = 1.55.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(64 / 160 + 49 / 220) = sqrt(0.40 + 0.2227) = sqrt(0.6227) = 0.789.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.789 = 1.547.

Answer: (ii) The interval is 1.55 +/- 1.547, that is, 0.003 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 3.097.

Q. 5 (a) Let two independent random samples, each of size 100, from two independent normal distributions N(mu_1, sigma_1-squared) and N(mu_2, sigma_2-squared) yield x-bar = 4.8, s-hat_1-squared = 8.64, y-bar = 5.6, s-hat_2-squared = 7.88. Find a 95% confidence interval for (mu_1 - mu_2). (Book answer: -1.6 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 0.)

Step 1: n_1 = n_2 = 100, x-bar_1 = 4.8, s-hat_1-squared = 8.64; x-bar_2 = 5.6, s-hat_2-squared = 7.88.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: 4.8 - 5.6 = -0.8.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(8.64 / 100 + 7.88 / 100) = sqrt(0.0864 + 0.0788) = sqrt(0.1652) = 0.406.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.406 = 0.797.

Answer: The interval is -0.8 +/- 0.797, that is, -1.6 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 0 (to the book's rounding).

Q. 5 (b) Given that x-bar_1 = 75, n_1 = 9, sum (x_i1 - x-bar_1)-squared = 1482; x-bar_2 = 60, n_2 = 16, sum (x_i2 - x-bar_2)-squared = 1830; and assuming that the two samples were randomly selected from two normal populations in which sigma_1-squared = sigma_2-squared (but unknown), calculate an 80% confidence interval for the difference between the two population means. (Book answer: 8.4 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 21.6.)

Step 1: n_1 = 9, x-bar_1 = 75; n_2 = 16, x-bar_2 = 60. The populations are normal with a common unknown variance, so use the pooled estimate and the t-distribution.

Step 2: Pooled variance: s_p-squared = (1482 + 1830) / (9 + 16 - 2) = 3312 / 23 = 144, so s_p = 12.

Step 3: Point estimate of the difference: 75 - 60 = 15.

Step 4: Standard error: s_p x sqrt(1 / n_1 + 1 / n_2) = 12 x sqrt(1 / 9 + 1 / 16) = 12 x sqrt(0.1736) = 12 x 0.4167 = 5.0.

Step 5: Degrees of freedom: v = 9 + 16 - 2 = 23. For an 80% interval, t_(23; 0.90) = 1.319. Margin of error: 1.319 x 5.0 = 6.597.

Answer: The interval is 15 +/- 6.597, that is, 8.4 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 21.6.

Q. 6 (a) Two random samples of size n_1 = 9 and n_2 = 16 from two independent population having normal distributions provide the means and standard deviations; x-bar_1 = 64, x-bar_2 = 59, s-hat_1 = 6 and s-hat_2 = 5. Find a 95% confidence interval for mu_1 - mu_2 assuming sigma_1 = sigma_2. (Book answer: 0.37 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 9.63.)

Step 1: n_1 = 9, x-bar_1 = 64, s-hat_1 = 6; n_2 = 16, x-bar_2 = 59, s-hat_2 = 5. The variances are assumed equal, so use the pooled estimate and the t-distribution.

Step 2: Pooled variance: s_p-squared = ((9 - 1) x 36 + (16 - 1) x 25) / (9 + 16 - 2) = (288 + 375) / 23 = 663 / 23 = 28.826, so s_p = 5.369.

Step 3: Point estimate of the difference: 64 - 59 = 5.

Step 4: Standard error: 5.369 x sqrt(1 / 9 + 1 / 16) = 5.369 x 0.4167 = 2.237.

Step 5: Degrees of freedom: v = 23. For a 95% interval, t_(23; 0.975) = 2.069.

Margin of error: 2.069 x 2.237 = 4.628.

Answer: The interval is 5 +/- 4.628, that is, 0.37 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 9.63.

Q. 6 (b) A course in mathematics is taught to 12 students by the conventional class-room method. A second group of 10 students was given the same course by means of programmed materials. At the end of the course, the same examination was given to each group. The 12 students meeting in the class room made an average grade of 85 with a standard deviation of 4, while the 10 students using programmed materials made an average of 81 with a standard deviation of 5. Find a 90% confidence interval for the difference between the population means, assuming the populations to be approximately normally distributed with equal variance. (Book answer: 0.693 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 7.307.)

Step 1: Class-room: n_1 = 12, x-bar_1 = 85, s-hat_1 = 4. Programmed: n_2 = 10, x-bar_2 = 81, s-hat_2 = 5. Equal variances assumed, so use the pooled estimate and the t-distribution.

Step 2: Pooled variance: s_p-squared = ((12 - 1) x 16 + (10 - 1) x 25) / (12 + 10 - 2) = (176 + 225) / 20 = 401 / 20 = 20.05, so s_p = 4.478.

Step 3: Point estimate of the difference: 85 - 81 = 4.

Step 4: Standard error: 4.478 x sqrt(1 / 12 + 1 / 10) = 4.478 x sqrt(0.1833) = 4.478 x 0.4282 = 1.917.

Step 5: Degrees of freedom: v = 20. For a 90% interval, t_(20; 0.95) = 1.725. Margin of error: 1.725 x 1.917 = 3.307.

Answer: The interval is 4 +/- 3.307, that is, 0.693 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 7.307.

mcqs.q: Boys (n_1 = 75, x-bar_1 = 82, sigma_1 = 8) and girls (n_2 = 50, x-bar_2 = 76, sigma_2 = 6) took a statistics test. Find a 96% confidence interval for mu_1 - mu_2.
mcqs.why: Difference = 82 - 76 = 6. Standard error = sqrt(64/75 + 36/50) = sqrt(1.573) = 1.254. For 96% confidence z_0.98 = 2.054, margin = 2.054 x 1.254 = 2.576. Interval = 6 +/- 2.576, that is, 3.42 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 8.58.

mcqs.q: Department 1 (n_1 = 64, x-bar_1 = 100) and Department 2 (n_2 = 49, x-bar_2 = 90) produce identical products. The point estimate of mu_1 - mu_2 is:
mcqs.why: The point estimate of the difference between the two population means is x-bar_1 - x-bar_2 = 100 - 90 = 10. This value is the centre of the confidence interval for the true difference in mean outputs.

mcqs.q: For the two departments with sigma_1-squared = 256 and sigma_2-squared = 196, find the 95% confidence limits for mu_1 - mu_2.
Mechanists (mean 345, variance 196) and carpenters (mean 340, variance 204), each with n = 100, are compared. Find the 95% confidence limits for mu_1 - mu_2.
mcqs.why: Difference = 345 - 340 = 5. Standard error = sqrt(196/100 + 204/100) = sqrt(4) = 2. Margin = 1.960 x 2 = 3.92. Interval = 5 +/- 3.92, that is, 1.08 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 8.92.

mcqs.q: For the same mechanists and carpenters data, find the 99% confidence limits for mu_1 - mu_2.
mcqs.why: Difference = 5 and standard error = sqrt(196/100 + 204/100) = 2. For 99% confidence, margin = 2.576 x 2 = 5.152. Interval = 5 +/- 5.152, that is, -0.152 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 10.152, which is wider than the 95% interval.

mcqs.q: Two cereal machines both have sigma-squared = 0.36. Machine I: n_1 = 15, x-bar_1 = 18.7; Machine II: n_2 = 21, x-bar_2 = 21.9. Construct a 95% confidence interval for mu_2 - mu_1.
Brand A bulbs (n_1 = 150, mean 1400, s-hat_1 = 120) and Brand B bulbs (n_2 = 200, mean 1200, s-hat_2 = 80) are compared. Find the 95% confidence limits for mu_1 - mu_2.
Two samples of size 100 each give x-bar_1 = 4.8, s-hat_1-squared = 8.64 and x-bar_2 = 5.6, s-hat_2-squared = 7. Find a 95% confidence interval for mu_2 - mu_1.

Two normal samples with equal unknown variances give x-bar_1 = 75 (n_1 = 9, sum of squared deviations 1482) and x-bar_2 = 60 (n_2 = 16, sum of squared deviations 1830). Find an 80% confidence interval for mu_1 - mu_2.
mcqs.why: Pooled variance s_p-squared = (1482 + 1830) / 23 = 144, so s_p = 12. Difference = 15. Standard error = 12 x sqrt(1/9 + 1/16) = 5.0. With v = 23, t_(23; 0.90) = 1.319, margin = 1.319 x 5.0 = 6.597. Interval = 15 +/- 6.597, that is, 8.4 < mu_1 - mu_2 < 21.6.

mcqs.q: A class-room group (n_1 = 12, mean 85, s-hat_1 = 4) and a programmed-materials group (n_2 = 10, mean 81, s-hat_2 = 5) are compared, assuming equal variances. Find a 90% confidence interval for mu_1 - mu_2.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.5 — Confidence Interval for Difference Between Two Population Proportions
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) In a poll of college students in a large state university, 300 out of 400 students living in dormitories approved a certain course of action, whereas 200 out of 300 students living in dormitories approved it. Estimate the difference in the proportions favouring the course of action and compute 90% confidence interval for it. (Book answers: p_1 - p_2 = 0.08; 0.023 < pi_1 - pi_2 < 0.137.)

Step 1: Dormitory group 1: n_1 = 400, x_1 = 300, so p_1 = 300 / 400 = 0.75. Group 2: n_2 = 300, x_2 = 200, so p_2 = 200 / 300 = 0.6667.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: p_1 - p_2 = 0.75 - 0.6667 = 0.0833, given in the book as 0.08.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(p_1 (1 - p_1) / n_1 + p_2 (1 - p_2) / n_2) = sqrt(0.75 x 0.25 / 400 + 0.6667 x 0.3333 / 300) = sqrt(0.000469 + 0.000741) = sqrt(0.001210) = 0.0348.

Step 4: 90% interval: margin of error = 1.645 x 0.0348 = 0.0572.

Answer: The interval is 0.0833 +/- 0.0572, that is, 0.026 < pi_1 - pi_2 < 0.141 by exact arithmetic; the book prints 0.023 < pi_1 - pi_2 < 0.137 (its point estimate is rounded to 0.08 and its margin to 0.057).

Q. 1 (b) In a random sample of 400 adults and 600 teenagers who watched a certain television programme, 100 adults and 300 teenagers indicated that they liked it.

Construct 95% and 99% confidence limits for the difference in proportions of all adults and all teenagers who watched the programme and liked it. (Book answers: 0.19 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.31; 0.17 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.33.)

Step 1: Adults: n_1 = 400, x_1 = 100, so p_1 = 100 / 400 = 0.25. Teenagers: n_2 = 600, x_2 = 300, so p_2 = 300 / 600 = 0.50.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference (teenagers minus adults): p_2 - p_1 = 0.50 - 0.25 = 0.25.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(0.25 x 0.75 / 400 + 0.50 x 0.50 / 600) = sqrt(0.000469 + 0.000417) = sqrt(0.000885) = 0.0298.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.0298 = 0.0583. The interval is 0.25 +/- 0.0583, that is, 0.192 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.308, printed in the book as 0.19 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.31.

Step 5: 99% interval: margin of error = 2.576 x 0.0298 = 0.0767.

Answer: The 99% interval is 0.25 +/- 0.0767, that is, 0.173 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.327, printed in the book as 0.17 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.33.

Q. 2 (a) A poll is taken among the residents of a city and the surrounding country to determine the feasibility of a proposal to construct a civic centre. If 2400 of 5000 city residents favour the proposal and 1200 of 2000 country residents favour it, find a 95% confidence interval for the true difference of the proportions favouring the proposal to construct the civic centre. (Book answer: 0.0945 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.1455.)

Step 1: City: n_1 = 5000, x_1 = 2400, so p_1 = 2400 / 5000 = 0.48. Country: n_2 = 2000, x_2 = 1200, so p_2 = 1200 / 2000 = 0.60.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference (country minus city): p_2 - p_1 = 0.60 - 0.48 = 0.12.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(0.48 x 0.52 / 5000 + 0.60 x 0.40 / 2000) = sqrt(0.0000499 + 0.00012) = sqrt(0.0001699) = 0.0130.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.0130 = 0.0256.

Answer: The interval is 0.12 +/- 0.0256, that is, 0.0945 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.1455.

Q. 2 (b) The population of interest are the voting preferences of all registered voters in the Punjab and the Sind. Two independent random samples were taken from these populations and the values n_1 = n_2 = 1000, p_1 = 0.54 and p_2 = 0.47.

Find a 95% confidence interval for pi_1 - pi_2. (Book answer: 0.026 < pi_1 - pi_2 < 0.114.)

Step 1: n_1 = n_2 = 1000, p_1 = 0.54, p_2 = 0.47.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: p_1 - p_2 = 0.54 - 0.47 = 0.07.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(0.54 x 0.46 / 1000 + 0.47 x 0.53 / 1000) = sqrt(0.000248 + 0.000249) = sqrt(0.000497) = 0.0223.

Step 4: 95% interval: margin of error = 1.960 x 0.0223 = 0.0437.

Answer: The interval is 0.07 +/- 0.0437, that is, 0.026 < pi_1 - pi_2 < 0.114.

Q. 3 (a) A market survey organization carried out a product taste study with consumers in two regions. In one region, a random sample of n_1 = 400 consumers was selected while in the other region an independent random sample of n_2 = 300 consumers was selected. Each person was asked to indicate which of two servings of product had a better taste. Unknown to the subject, one serving was a new high protein breakfast cereal and the other was an existing cereal. In the first region, proportion p_1 = 0.55 of the sample persons preferred the new cereal and in the second region the proportion was p_2 = 0.65. Construct a 90% confidence interval for pi_2 - pi_1. (Book answer: 0.039 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.161.)

Step 1: n_1 = 400, p_1 = 0.55; n_2 = 300, p_2 = 0.65.

Step 2: Point estimate of the difference: p_2 - p_1 = 0.65 - 0.55 = 0.10.

Step 3: Standard error: sqrt(0.55 x 0.45 / 400 + 0.65 x 0.35 / 300) = sqrt(0.000619 + 0.000758) = sqrt(0.001377) = 0.0371.

Step 4: 90% interval: margin of error = 1.645 x 0.0371 = 0.0610.

Answer: The interval is 0.10 +/- 0.0610, that is, 0.039 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.161.

Q. 3 (b) Independent random samples are selected from two populations with fractions of success pi_1 and pi_2. Construct a 95% confidence interval for pi_1 - pi_2 for each of the following cases. (i) n_1 = 100, p_1 = 0.72, n_2 = 100, p_2 = 0.61. (ii) n_1 = 130, p_1 = 0.16, n_2 = 210, p_2 = 0.25. (iii) n_1 = 70, p_1 = 0.53, n_2 = 60, p_2 = 0.48. (Book answers: (i) -0.02 to 0.24, (ii) -0.176 to -0.004, (iii) -0.12 to 0.22.)

Step 1: (i) Difference: 0.72 - 0.61 = 0.11. Standard error: sqrt(0.72 x 0.28 / 100 + 0.61 x 0.39 / 100) = sqrt(0.002016 + 0.002379) = sqrt(0.004395) = 0.0663.

Margin: 1.960 x 0.0663 = 0.130. Interval: 0.11 +/- 0.130, that is, -0.02 to 0.24.

Step 2: (ii) Difference: 0.16 - 0.25 = -0.09. Standard error: sqrt(0.16 x 0.84 / 130 + 0.25 x 0.75 / 210) = sqrt(0.001034 + 0.000893) = sqrt(0.001927) = 0.0439.

Margin: 1.960 x 0.0439 = 0.086. Interval: -0.09 +/- 0.086, that is, -0.176 to -0.004.

Step 3: (iii) Difference: 0.53 - 0.48 = 0.05. Standard error: sqrt(0.53 x 0.47 / 70 + 0.48 x 0.52 / 60) = sqrt(0.003559 + 0.004160) = sqrt(0.007719) = 0.0879. Margin: 1.960 x 0.0879 = 0.172.

Answer: The intervals are: (i) -0.02 to 0.24, (ii) -0.176 to -0.004, (iii) 0.05 +/- 0.172, that is, -0.12 to 0.22.

mcqs.q: In a poll, 300 out of 400 dormitory students in group 1 approved an action, and 200 out of 300 students in group 2 approved it. The point estimate of pi_1 - pi_2 is:
mcqs.why: p_1 = 300 / 400 = 0.75 and p_2 = 200 / 300 = 0.6667, so p_1 - p_2 = 0.75 - 0.6667 = 0.0833. The notes point out that the book rounds this point estimate to 0.08 before working the interval.

mcqs.q: For the same dormitory poll (p_1 = 0.75, n_1 = 400; p_2 = 0.6667, n_2 = 300), the 90% confidence interval for pi_1 - pi_2 by exact arithmetic is:
mcqs.why: Standard error = sqrt(0.75 x 0.25/400 + 0.6667 x 0.3333/300) = sqrt(0.001210) = 0.0348. Margin = 1.645 x 0.0348 = 0.0572. Interval = 0.0833 +/- 0.0572, that is, 0.026 < pi_1 - pi_2 < 0.141. The book prints 0.023 to 0.137 because it rounds the point estimate to 0.08 and the margin to 0.057; exact arithmetic gives the interval shown here.

mcqs.q: In a sample, 100 out of 400 adults and 300 out of 600 teenagers liked a television programme. The point estimate of pi_2 - pi_1 (teenagers minus adults) is:
mcqs.why: For adults p_1 = 100 / 400 = 0.25 and for teenagers p_2 = 300 / 600 = 0.50. The difference teenagers minus adults is p_2 - p_1 = 0.50 - 0.25 = 0.25, the centre of the intervals in the notes.

mcqs.q: For the adults and teenagers television data, the 95% confidence limits for pi_2 - pi_1 are:
mcqs.why: Difference = 0.50 - 0.25 = 0.25. Standard error = sqrt(0.25 x 0.75/400 + 0.50 x 0.50/600) = sqrt(0.000885) = 0.0298. Margin = 1.960 x 0.0298 = 0.0583. Interval = 0.25 +/- 0.0583, that is, 0.192 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.308 (printed rounded in the book as 0.19 to 0.31).

mcqs.q: For the same adults and teenagers data, the 99% confidence limits for pi_2 - pi_1 are:
mcqs.why: Difference = 0.25 and standard error = sqrt(0.25 x 0.75/400 + 0.50 x 0.50/600) = 0.0298. For 99% confidence, margin = 2.576 x 0.0298 = 0.0767. Interval = 0.25 +/- 0.0767, that is, 0.173 < pi_2 - pi_1 < 0.327 (printed rounded in the book as 0.17 to 0.33).

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1 — Elements of Hypothesis Testing
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) Define the following concepts in your own words as fully as you can: (i) Hypothesis testing (ii) Statistical hypothesis (iii) Null hypothesis (iv) Test statistic (v) Level of significance (vi) Critical region.

Step 1: (i) Hypothesis testing: a procedure to determine whether or not an assumption about some parameter of a population is supported by the information obtained from the observed random sample.

Step 2: (ii) Statistical hypothesis: an assertion or conjecture about the distribution of one or more random variables, usually phrased quantitatively in terms of population parameters.

Step 3: (iii) Null hypothesis, denoted H_0: the hypothesis which is tested for possible rejection (or nullification) under the assumption that it is true; it is usually a statement of 'no effect' or 'status quo'.

Step 4: (iv) Test statistic: a sample statistic which provides a basis for deciding whether or not the null hypothesis should be rejected; the most commonly used test statistics are Z, T, chi-squared and F.

Step 5: (v) Level of significance, denoted alpha: the maximum probability with which we are willing to risk a Type-I error; it is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, and is a small pre-assigned value, say 0.05 or 0.01.

Answer: (vi) Critical region (rejection region): the set of values of the test statistic for which the null hypothesis is rejected (and for which the alternative hypothesis is accepted).

Q. 1 (b) Explain with examples the difference between: (i) Estimation and hypothesis testing (ii) Null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis (iii) Simple hypothesis and composite hypothesis (iv) Acceptance region and rejection region (v) Type-I error and Type-II error (vi) One-tailed test and two-tailed test.

Step 1: (i) Estimation makes a judgment about the unknown value of a parameter from the sample; hypothesis testing decides whether an assumption about a parameter is supported by the sample.

Step 2: (ii) The null hypothesis H_0 is the hypothesis tested for possible rejection; the alternative hypothesis H_1 is the hypothesis we are willing to accept when H_0 is rejected (often the research hypothesis).

Step 3: (iii) A simple hypothesis completely specifies the underlying distribution, including the specific values of all its parameters (for example, X has a normal distribution with mean 30 and standard deviation 4); a composite hypothesis does not completely specify it (for example, X has a normal distribution with mean 40 and standard deviation 5, or with mean 50 and standard deviation at least 4).

Step 4: (iv) The acceptance (nonrejection) region is the set of values of the test statistic for which H_0 is not rejected; the rejection (critical) region is the set of values for which H_0 is rejected.

Step 5: (v) A Type-I error is made by rejecting H_0 when H_0 is actually true; a Type-II error is made by accepting (not rejecting) H_0 when H_1 is actually true.

Answer: (vi) A one-tailed (one-sided) test has its critical region in only one tail of the sampling distribution (left-tailed if H_1 is theta < theta_0, right-tailed if H_1 is theta > theta_0); a two-tailed (two-sided) test has its critical region equally in both tails (H_1 is theta not equal to theta_0).

Q. 1 (c) What is the difference between a one-sided and a two-sided test? When should each be used?

Step 1: A one-sided test has its rejection region in only one tail of the sampling distribution of the test statistic; a two-sided test has its rejection region in both tails.

Step 2: The choice depends on the form of the alternative hypothesis H_1.

Step 3: Use a one-sided left-tail test when looking for a definite decrease, that is, when H_1 is given by theta < theta_0.

Step 4: Use a one-sided right-tail test when looking for a definite increase, that is, when H_1 is given by theta > theta_0.

Answer: Use a two-sided test when looking for any change, that is, when H_1 is given by theta not equal to theta_0.

Q. 2 (a) Explain what is meant by: (i) Statistical hypothesis (ii) Test-statistic (iii) Significance level (iv) Test of significance.

Step 1: (i) Statistical hypothesis: an assertion about the distribution of one or more random variables, usually about the value of a population parameter.

Step 2: (ii) Test-statistic: a sample statistic used as the basis for deciding whether the null hypothesis should be rejected.

Step 3: (iii) Significance level: the maximum probability of a Type-I error that we are willing to risk, denoted alpha; it is the size of the critical region.

Answer: (iv) Test of significance: a process of testing a hypothesis to gain a general impression about the parameter, in which no decision is imminent or implied; instead we investigate the values of alpha that would lead to rejection of H_0 as opposed to the values leading to acceptance of H_0.

Q. 2 (b) Distinguish between the following concepts: (i) Statistical estimation and hypothesis testing (ii) Rejection and non-rejection regions (iii) A test at alpha level of significance and at 1 - alpha confidence level.

Step 1: (i) Statistical estimation judges the unknown value of a parameter from the sample; hypothesis testing decides whether an assumption about a parameter is supported by the sample.

Step 2: (ii) The rejection region is the set of values of the test statistic that lead to rejecting H_0; the non-rejection (acceptance) region is the set of values that lead to not rejecting H_0.

Answer: (iii) A test at alpha level of significance rejects a true H_0 with probability alpha; a confidence interval at 1 - alpha confidence level includes the parameter with probability 1 - alpha in repeated sampling. The two are complementary: a two-sided test at level alpha rejects H_0: theta = theta_0 exactly when theta_0 lies outside the 100 (1 - alpha)% confidence interval.

Q. 3 (a) Explain how the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis are formulated.

Step 1: The alternative (or research) hypothesis H_1 is a statement about the value of a population parameter that an investigator attempts to support with the observed random sample.

Step 2: The experiment is conducted to see if there is support for some hypothesis, expressed as an inequality in the form 'less than' or 'greater than' or 'not equal to'; this becomes H_1.

Step 3: The null hypothesis H_0 is then stated with an equality sign as a complement of the alternative hypothesis.

Answer: For example, if H_1 is theta < 40, then H_0 is theta >= 40; if H_1 is theta > 40, then H_0 is theta <= 40; if H_1 is theta not equal to theta_0, then H_0 is theta = theta_0. The basic strategy is to attempt to support the research hypothesis by contradicting the null hypothesis.

Q. 3 (b) State the null and alternative hypotheses to be used in testing the following claims: (i) The mean rainfall at Lake Placid during the month of June is 2.8 inches.

(ii) No more than 20% of the faculty at Highland University contributed to the annual giving fund. (iii) The proportion of voters favouring Senator Foghorn in up coming election is 0.58. (iv) On the average children attend school within 3.8 miles of their homes in suburban San Francisco. (Book answers: (i) H_0: mu = 2.8 inches against H_1: mu not equal to 2.8 inches; (ii) H_0: pi <= 0.20 against H_1: pi > 0.20; (iii) H_0: pi = 0.58 against H_1: pi not equal to 0.58; (iv) H_0: mu <= 3.8 miles against H_1: mu > 3.8 miles.)

Step 1: (i) The claim states a specific value, so H_0: mu = 2.8 inches against H_1: mu not equal to 2.8 inches (two-tailed).

Step 2: (ii) 'No more than 20%' is the null statement, so H_0: pi <= 0.20 against H_1: pi > 0.20 (right-tailed).

Step 3: (iii) The claim states a specific proportion, so H_0: pi = 0.58 against H_1: pi not equal to 0.58 (two-tailed).

Answer: (iv) 'Within 3.8 miles' is the null statement, so H_0: mu <= 3.8 miles against H_1: mu > 3.8 miles (right-tailed).

Q. 4 (a) Indicate Type-I and Type-II errors in the following statements: (i) An innocent driver may be held by a traffic constable. (ii) A judge can acquit a guilty person. (iii) A deserving player may not be selected in the team. (iv) A bad student may be passed by the examiner. (Book answers: (i) Type-I, (ii) Type-II, (iii) Type-I, (iv) Type-II.)

Step 1: (i) Holding an innocent driver rejects the true state 'driver is innocent': Type-I error.

Step 2: (ii) Acquitting a guilty person accepts the false state 'person is innocent': Type-II error.

Step 3: (iii) Not selecting a deserving player rejects the true state 'player is deserving': Type-I error.

Answer: (iv) Passing a bad student accepts the false state 'student is good': Type-II error.

Q. 4 (b) For each of the following situations, indicate the Type-I and Type-II errors and the correct decisions. (i) H_0: New system is no better than the old one. Adopt new system when new one is better. Retain old system when new one is better.

Retain old system when new one is not better. Adopt new system when new one is not better. (ii) H_0: New product is satisfactory. Market new product when unsatisfactory. Do not market new product when unsatisfactory. Do not market new product when satisfactory. Market new product when satisfactory. (Book answers: (i) Correct, Type-II, Correct, Type-I; (ii) Type-II, Correct, Type-I, Correct.)

Step 1: (i) Adopt new system when new one is better: H_0 is false and is rejected, so Correct decision.

Step 2: (i) Retain old system when new one is better: H_0 is false but is accepted, so Type-II error.

Step 3: (i) Retain old system when new one is not better: H_0 is true and is accepted, so Correct decision.

Step 4: (i) Adopt new system when new one is not better: H_0 is true but is rejected, so Type-I error.

Step 5: (ii) Market new product when unsatisfactory: H_0 is false but is accepted (the product is treated as satisfactory), so Type-II error.

Step 6: (ii) Do not market new product when unsatisfactory: H_0 is false and is rejected, so Correct decision.

Step 7: (ii) Do not market new product when satisfactory: H_0 is true but is rejected, so Type-I error.

Answer: (ii) Market new product when satisfactory: H_0 is true and is accepted, so Correct decision.

Q. 4 (c) Suppose that a psychological testing service is asked to check whether an executive is emotionally fit to assume the presidency of a large company. What type of error is committed if the hypothesis that he is fit for the job is erroneously accepted? What type of error is committed if the hypothesis that he is fit for the job is erroneously rejected? (Book answers: Type-II error; Type-I error.)

Step 1: The hypothesis is 'he is fit for the job'. Accepting it erroneously means accepting a false hypothesis.

Answer: Erroneously accepting the hypothesis is a Type-II error, and erroneously rejecting the hypothesis is a Type-I error.

Q. 5 (a) The director of an advertising agency is concerned with the effectiveness of a certain kind of television commercial. (i) What hypothesis is he testing, if he is committing a Type-I error when he says erroneously that the commercial is effective. (ii) What hypothesis is he testing, if he is committing a Type-II error when he says erroneously that the commercial is effective. (Book answers: (i) Commercial is not effective; (ii) Commercial is effective.)

Step 1: (i) A Type-I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis. Saying the commercial is effective rejects the null hypothesis 'commercial is not effective'; if that null hypothesis is true, the rejection is a Type-I error.

Answer: (i) He is testing H_0: Commercial is not effective. (ii) A Type-II error is accepting a false null hypothesis. Saying the commercial is effective accepts the null hypothesis 'commercial is effective'; if that null hypothesis is false, the acceptance is a Type-II error. So he is testing H_0: Commercial is effective.

Q. 5 (b) Outline the fundamental procedure followed in testing a null hypothesis.

Step 1: Identify the population of interest and state the conditions required for the validity of the test procedure being used.

Step 2: Formulate and state the null hypothesis H_0 and the alternative hypothesis H_1.

Step 3: Decide and specify the level of significance, alpha.

Step 4: Select the appropriate test statistic and its sampling distribution if H_0 is assumed to be true.

Step 5: Give the critical value (or values) of the test statistic for the desired value of alpha.

Step 6: Establish the rejection (critical) region.

Step 7: State the decision rule: Reject H_0 if the value of the test statistic from the observed sample falls in the rejection region, otherwise do not reject (or accept) H_0.

Step 8: Calculate the value of the test statistic from the observed sample.

Answer: In the light of the decision rule, draw the conclusion as to whether to reject or accept H_0, and then state the decision in managerial (practical) terms.

A procedure to draw the sampling distribution of a statistic
