options: H0 is stated with an equality sign as a complement of H1; for example, if H1 is theta > 40, then H0 is theta <= 40
H0 is always stated with a 'not equal to' sign
H0 is stated first and H1 is its sample value
H0 and H1 are always exactly the same statement
mcqs.q: How is the null hypothesis formulated from the alternative hypothesis?
mcqs.why: The notes say H1 is expressed as an inequality and H0 is then stated with an equality sign as its complement; for H1: theta > 40, H0 is theta <= 40.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.2 — Test of Hypothesis About a Population Mean
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) Why is the z-test usually inappropriate as a test-statistic when the sample size is small?

Step 1: The z-test statistic Z = (X-bar - mu_0) / (sigma / sqrt(n)) requires the population standard deviation sigma to be known.

Step 2: When sigma is unknown it is replaced by the sample standard deviation S-hat, and the resulting statistic no longer has a standard normal distribution.

Answer: When the sample size is small, this replacement matters: the statistic then has a t-distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom, which has heavier tails than the normal, so using z critical values would give the wrong significance level. The z-test is appropriate when sigma is known, or when n is large (say n > 30) so that the t-distribution is well approximated by the normal.

Q. 1 (b) Define 'Student's t-statistic'. What are its assumptions? Explain briefly its use and importance in statistics.

Step 1: Student's t-statistic is T = (X-bar - mu_0) / (S-hat / sqrt(n)), where S-hat is the sample standard deviation with divisor n - 1.

Step 2: Assumptions: the sample is a random sample from a normal population, and the population variance sigma-squared is unknown.

Step 3: Under H_0, T has a t-distribution with v = n - 1 degrees of freedom.

Answer: Use and importance: the t-statistic lets us test hypotheses about a population mean when sigma is unknown and the sample is small, which is the common practical case; without it, small-sample inference about the mean would not be possible.

Q. 2 For each of the following, a random sample of size n is taken from a normal distribution with mean mu and variance sigma-squared. The sample mean is x-bar.

Test the hypothesis stated, at the level of significance indicated. (i) n = 30, x-bar = 15.2, sigma = 3, H_0: mu = 15.8 against H_1: mu not equal to 15.8, 5%. (ii) n = 10, x-bar = 27, sigma = 1.2, H_0: mu <= 26.3 against H_1: mu > 26.3, 5%. (iii) n = 49, x-bar = 125, sigma = 4.2, H_0: mu <= 123.5 against H_1: mu > 123.5, 1%. (iv) n = 100, x-bar = 4.35, sigma = 0.18, H_0: mu >= 4.40 against H_1: mu < 4.40, 2%. (v) n = 65, x-bar = 100, sum (x_i - x-bar)-squared = 842.4, H_0: mu = 99.2 against H_1: mu not equal to 99.2, 5%. (vi) n = 65, x-bar = 100, sum (x_i - x-bar)-squared = 842.4, H_0: mu <= 99.2 against H_1: mu > 99.2, 5%. (vii) n = 80, x-bar = 85.3, sum (x_i - x-bar)-squared = 2508.8, H_0: mu >= 86.2 against H_1: mu < 86.2, 10%.

(viii) n = 100, x-bar = 6.85, sum (x_i - x-bar)-squared = 36, H_0: mu = 7.0 against H_1: mu not equal to 7.0, 1%.

Step 1: (i) Test statistic: z = (15.2 - 15.8) / (3 / sqrt(30)) = -0.6 / 0.548 = -1.095.

Critical values at 5% two-tailed: +/- 1.960. Since -1.960 < -1.095 < 1.960, we do not reject H_0: mu = 15.8 against H_1: mu not equal to 15.8.

Step 2: (ii) z = (27 - 26.3) / (1.2 / sqrt(10)) = 0.7 / 0.379 = 1.845. Critical value at 5% right-tailed: 1.645. Since 1.845 > 1.645, we reject H_0: mu <= 26.3 in favour of H_1: mu > 26.3.

Step 3: (iii) z = (125 - 123.5) / (4.2 / sqrt(49)) = 1.5 / 0.6 = 2.5. Critical value at 1% right-tailed: 2.326. Since 2.5 > 2.326, we reject H_0: mu <= 123.5 in favour of H_1: mu > 123.5.

Step 4: (iv) z = (4.35 - 4.40) / (0.18 / sqrt(100)) = -0.05 / 0.018 = -2.778. Critical value at 2% left-tailed: -2.054. Since -2.778 < -2.054, we reject H_0: mu >= 4.40 in favour of H_1: mu < 4.40.

Step 5: (v) s-hat = sqrt(842.4 / 64) = 3.628. Standard error: 3.628 / sqrt(65) = 0.450. Test statistic: (100 - 99.2) / 0.450 = 1.778. Critical values at 5% two-tailed (n large, normal approximation): +/- 1.960. Since -1.960 < 1.778 < 1.960, we do not reject H_0: mu = 99.2 against H_1: mu not equal to 99.2.

Step 6: (vi) Same test statistic 1.778. Critical value at 5% right-tailed: 1.645. Since 1.778 > 1.645, we reject H_0: mu <= 99.2 in favour of H_1: mu > 99.2.

Step 7: (vii) s-hat = sqrt(2508.8 / 79) = 5.635. Standard error: 5.635 / sqrt(80) = 0.630. Test statistic: (85.3 - 86.2) / 0.630 = -1.428. Critical value at 10% left-tailed: -1.282. Since -1.428 < -1.282, we reject H_0: mu >= 86.2 in favour of H_1: mu < 86.2.

Answer: (viii) s-hat = sqrt(36 / 99) = 0.603. Standard error: 0.603 / sqrt(100) = 0.0603. Test statistic: (6.85 - 7.0) / 0.0603 = -2.487, given in the book as -2.5.

Critical values at 1% two-tailed: +/- 2.576. Since -2.576 < -2.5 < 2.576, we do not reject H_0: mu = 7.0 against H_1: mu not equal to 7.0.

Q. 3 (a) A random sample of size 36 is taken from a normal population with known variance sigma-squared = 25. If the mean of the sample is x-bar = 42.6, test the null hypothesis mu >= 45 against the alternative hypothesis mu < 45 with alpha = 0.05 (alpha is the probability of committing Type-I error). (Book answer: Since z = -2.88 < -1.645 = z_0.05, we reject H_0: mu >= 45 in favour of H_1: mu < 45.)

Step 1: n = 36, x-bar = 42.6, sigma-squared = 25, so sigma = 5. H_0: mu >= 45 against H_1: mu < 45, alpha = 0.05 (left-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (42.6 - 45) / (5 / sqrt(36)) = -2.4 / 0.833 = -2.88.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.05 = -1.645. Rejection region: Z < -1.645.

Answer: Since z = -2.88 < -1.645, we reject H_0: mu >= 45 in favour of H_1: mu < 45.

Q. 3 (b) Ten dry cells were taken from store and voltage tests gave the following results: 1.52, 1.53, 1.49, 1.48, 1.47, 1.49, 1.51, 1.50, 1.47, 1.48 volts. The mean voltage of the cells when stored was 1.51 V. Assuming the population standard deviation to be 0.02 V, is there reason to believe that the cells have deteriorated?

(Book answer: Since z = -2.53 < -1.645 = z_0.05, we reject H_0: mu >= 1.51 in favour of H_1: mu < 1.51.)

Step 1: n = 10. Sample mean: x-bar = (1.52 + 1.53 + 1.49 + 1.48 + 1.47 + 1.49 + 1.51 + 1.50 + 1.47 + 1.48) / 10 = 14.94 / 10 = 1.494 V.

Step 2: H_0: mu >= 1.51 V (no deterioration) against H_1: mu < 1.51 V (deterioration), at the 5% level. sigma = 0.02 V is known.

Step 3: Test statistic: z = (1.494 - 1.51) / (0.02 / sqrt(10)) = -0.016 / 0.00632 = -2.53.

Step 4: Critical value: z_0.05 = -1.645. Rejection region: Z < -1.645.

Answer: Since z = -2.53 < -1.645, we reject H_0: mu >= 1.51 in favour of H_1: mu < 1.51. Yes, there is reason to believe that the cells have deteriorated.

Q. 4 (a) A sample of 400 male students is found to have a mean height of 67.47 inches. Can it be regarded as a simple random sample from a large population with mean height 67.39 inches with standard deviation of 1.3 inches? (Book answer: Since z_0.025 = -1.96 < z = 1.23 < 1.96 = z_0.975, we do not reject H_0: mu = 67.39 against H_1: mu not equal to 67.39 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: n = 400, x-bar = 67.47 inches, mu_0 = 67.39 inches, sigma = 1.3 inches.

H_0: mu = 67.39 against H_1: mu not equal to 67.39, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (67.47 - 67.39) / (1.3 / sqrt(400)) = 0.08 / 0.065 = 1.23.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 1.960. Rejection region: Z < -1.960 or Z > 1.960.

Answer: Since -1.960 < 1.23 < 1.960, we do not reject H_0. Yes, the sample can be regarded as a simple random sample from the population with mean 67.39 inches.

Q. 4 (b) The mean lifetime of electric light bulbs produced by a company has in the past been 1120 hours with a standard deviation of 125 hours. A sample of 8 electric bulbs recently chosen from a supply of newly manufactured bulbs showed a mean lifetime of 1070 hours. Test the hypothesis that mean lifetime of the bulbs has not changed using a level of significance of 0.05. (Book answer: Since z_0.025 = -1.96 < z = -1.13 < 1.96 = z_0.975, we do not reject H_0: mu = 1120 against H_1: mu not equal to 1120.)

Step 1: n = 8, x-bar = 1070 hours, mu_0 = 1120 hours, sigma = 125 hours. H_0: mu = 1120 against H_1: mu not equal to 1120, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (1070 - 1120) / (125 / sqrt(8)) = -50 / 44.194 = -1.13.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 1.960.

Answer: Since -1.960 < -1.13 < 1.960, we do not reject H_0: mu = 1120. The mean lifetime of the bulbs has not changed, on this evidence.

Q. 5 (a) Suppose that the mean mu of a random variable X is unknown but the variance of X is known to be 144. Should we reject the null hypothesis H_0: mu = 15 in favour of an alternative hypothesis H_1: mu not equal to 15 at a level of significance of alpha = 0.05, if a random sample of 64 observations yields a mean x-bar = 12? What are the 95% confidence limits for mu. (Book answer: Since z = -2 < -1.960 = z_0.025, we reject H_0: mu = 15 in favour of H_1: mu not equal to 15; 9.06 < mu < 14.94.)

Step 1: n = 64, x-bar = 12, sigma-squared = 144, so sigma = 12. H_0: mu = 15 against H_1: mu not equal to 15, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (12 - 15) / (12 / sqrt(64)) = -3 / 1.5 = -2.0.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 1.960. Since -2.0 < -1.960, we reject H_0: mu = 15 in favour of H_1: mu not equal to 15.

Step 4: The 95% confidence interval is x-bar +/- 1.960 x (sigma / sqrt(n)) = 12 +/- 1.960 x 1.5 = 12 +/- 2.94.

Answer: The 95% confidence limits are 9.06 < mu < 14.94. Note that mu_0 = 15 lies outside this interval, which agrees with the rejection of H_0.

Q. 5 (b) In a syrup filling factory the mean weight per bottle is claimed to be mu = 16. A random sample of 100 bottles is taken and a test statistic used is X-bar, the mean weight of the sample. For a 0.05 level of significance, find the critical values for the test statistic and formulate the decision rule. Assume the weights to be normally distributed with sigma-squared = 2.56. (Book answer: Reject H_0 if X-bar < 15.68 or X-bar > 16.32.)

Step 1: mu_0 = 16, n = 100, sigma-squared = 2.56, so sigma = 1.6. H_0: mu = 16 against H_1: mu not equal to 16, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: The standard error of X-bar is sigma / sqrt(n) = 1.6 / 10 = 0.16.

Step 3: The critical values of the test statistic are mu_0 +/- z_0.975 x (sigma / sqrt(n)) = 16 +/- 1.960 x 0.16 = 16 +/- 0.314, that is, 15.69 and 16.31.

Step 4: Decision rule: Reject H_0 if X-bar < 15.69 or X-bar > 16.31, otherwise do not reject H_0.

Answer: The book prints the critical values as 15.68 and 16.32, using z = 2 in place of 1.960 (margin 0.32); the decision rule is the same in substance: reject H_0 if X-bar lies outside the interval about 16.

Q. 6 (a) A random sample of 36 drinks from a soft-drink machine has an average content 7.6 ounces with a standard deviation of 0.48 ounces. Test the hypothesis mu <= 7.5 ounces against the alternative hypothesis mu > 7.5 at the 0.05 level of significance. (Book answer: Since z = 1.25 < 1.645 = z_0.95, we do not reject H_0: mu <= 7.5 against H_1: mu > 7.5.)

Step 1: n = 36, x-bar = 7.6 ounces, s-hat = 0.48 ounces. H_0: mu <= 7.5 against H_1: mu > 7.5, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed). The sample is large, so the normal approximation is used.

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (7.6 - 7.5) / (0.48 / sqrt(36)) = 0.1 / 0.08 = 1.25.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.95 = 1.645. Rejection region: Z > 1.645.

Answer: Since z = 1.25 < 1.645, we do not reject H_0: mu <= 7.5 against H_1: mu > 7.5.

Q. 6 (b) It is claimed that an automobile is driven on the average at most 20000 kilometres per year. To test this claim, a random sample of 100 automobile owners are asked to keep a record of the kilometres they travel. Would you agree with claim if the random sample showed an average of 21500 kilometres and a standard deviation of 3900 kilometres? Use a 0.01 level of significance. (Book answer: Since z = 3.846 > 2.326 = z_0.990, we reject H_0: mu <= 20000 in favour of H_1: mu > 20000.)

Step 1: n = 100, x-bar = 21500 km, s-hat = 3900 km. H_0: mu <= 20000 against H_1: mu > 20000, at alpha = 0.01 (right-tailed). The sample is large, so the normal approximation is used.

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (21500 - 20000) / (3900 / sqrt(100)) = 1500 / 390 = 3.846.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.99 = 2.326. Rejection region: Z > 2.326.

Answer: Since z = 3.846 > 2.326, we reject H_0: mu <= 20000 in favour of H_1: mu > 20000. No, we would not agree with the claim.

Q. 7 (a) A random sample of 100 recorded deaths in the United States during the past year showed an average lifespan of 71.8 years with a standard deviation of 8.9 years. Does this seem to indicate that the average lifespan today is greater than 70 years? Use a 0.05 level of significance. (Book answer: Since z = 2.02 > 1.645 = z_0.95, we reject H_0: mu <= 70 in favour of H_1: mu > 70.)

Step 1: n = 100, x-bar = 71.8 years, s-hat = 8.9 years. H_0: mu <= 70 against H_1: mu > 70, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed). The sample is large, so the normal approximation is used.

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (71.8 - 70) / (8.9 / sqrt(100)) = 1.8 / 0.89 = 2.02.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.95 = 1.645. Rejection region: Z > 1.645.

Answer: Since z = 2.02 > 1.645, we reject H_0: mu <= 70 in favour of H_1: mu > 70. Yes, the average lifespan today seems to be greater than 70 years.

Q. 7 (b) It is claimed that an automobile is driven on the average no more than 12000 miles per year. To test this claim, a random sample of 100 automobile owners are asked to keep a record of the miles they travel. Would you agree with claim if the random sample showed an average of 12500 miles and a standard deviation of 2400 miles? (Book answer: Since z = 2.083 > 1.645, we reject H_0: mu <= 12000 in favour of H_1: mu > 12000 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: n = 100, x-bar = 12500 miles, s-hat = 2400 miles. H_0: mu <= 12000 against H_1: mu > 12000, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed). The sample is large, so the normal approximation is used.

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (12500 - 12000) / (2400 / sqrt(100)) = 500 / 240 = 2.083.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.95 = 1.645. Rejection region: Z > 1.645.

Answer: Since z = 2.083 > 1.645, we reject H_0: mu <= 12000 in favour of H_1: mu > 12000. No, we would not agree with the claim.

Q. 8 Given the following information, what is your conclusion in testing each of the indicated null hypothesis? Assume the populations are normal. (i) Sample size 16, sample mean 11, estimate of variance from sample 81, H_0: mu <= 10 against H_1: mu > 10, level of significance 0.01. (ii) Sample size 25, sample mean 8, estimate of variance from sample 64, H_0: mu >= 10 against H_1: mu < 10, level of significance 0.01. (iii) Sample size 25, sample mean 9, estimate of variance from sample 49, H_0: mu = 10 against H_1: mu not equal to 10, level of significance 0.02. (iv) Sample size 12, sample mean 24.9, sum (x_i - x-bar)-squared = 12.3, H_0: mu <= 24.1 against H_1: mu > 24.1, level of significance 2.5%. (v) Sample size 17, sample mean 35.6, sum (x_i - x-bar)-squared = 1471.8, H_0: mu = 40 against H_1: mu not equal to 40, level of significance 5%. (vi) Sample size 6, sample mean 1505.8, sum (x_i - x-bar)-squared = 50.8, H_0: mu <= 1503 against H_1: mu > 1503, level of significance 5%. (vii) Sample size 10, sample mean 129.8, sum (x_i - x-bar)-squared = 97.6, H_0: mu >= 133.0 against H_1: mu < 133.0, level of significance 1%.

Step 1: (i) s-hat = 9. Test statistic: t = (11 - 10) / (9 / sqrt(16)) = 1 / 2.25 = 0.444, with v = 15 degrees of freedom. Critical value at 1% right-tailed: t_(15; 0.99) = 2.602. Since 0.444 < 2.602, we do not reject H_0: mu <= 10.

Step 2: (ii) s-hat = 8. Test statistic: t = (8 - 10) / (8 / sqrt(25)) = -2 / 1.6 = -1.25, with v = 24. Critical value at 1% left-tailed: t_(24; 0.01) = -2.492. Since -1.25 > -2.492, we do not reject H_0: mu >= 10.

Step 3: (iii) s-hat = 7. Test statistic: t = (9 - 10) / (7 / sqrt(25)) = -1 / 1.4 = -0.714, with v = 24. Critical values at 2% two-tailed: +/- 2.492. Since -2.492 < -0.714 < 2.492, we do not reject H_0: mu = 10.

Step 4: (iv) s-hat = sqrt(12.3 / 11) = 1.057. Standard error: 1.057 / sqrt(12) = 0.305.

Test statistic: t = (24.9 - 24.1) / 0.305 = 2.62, with v = 11. Critical value at 2.5% right-tailed: t_(11; 0.975) = 2.201. Since 2.62 > 2.201, we reject H_0: mu <= 24.1 in favour of H_1: mu > 24.1.

Step 5: (v) s-hat = sqrt(1471.8 / 16) = 9.591. Standard error: 9.591 / sqrt(17) = 2.326. Test statistic: t = (35.6 - 40) / 2.326 = -1.892, with v = 16. Critical values at 5% two-tailed: +/- 2.120. Since -2.120 < -1.892 < 2.120, we do not reject H_0: mu = 40.

Step 6: (vi) s-hat = sqrt(50.8 / 5) = 3.187. Standard error: 3.187 / sqrt(6) = 1.301.

Test statistic: t = (1505.8 - 1503) / 1.301 = 2.152, with v = 5. Critical value at 5% right-tailed: t_(5; 0.95) = 2.015. Since 2.152 > 2.015, we reject H_0: mu <= 1503 in favour of H_1: mu > 1503.

Answer: (vii) s-hat = sqrt(97.6 / 9) = 3.294. Standard error: 3.294 / sqrt(10) = 1.042. Test statistic: t = (129.8 - 133.0) / 1.042 = -3.071, with v = 9. Critical value at 1% left-tailed: t_(9; 0.01) = -2.821. Since -3.071 < -2.821, we reject H_0: mu >= 133.0 in favour of H_1: mu < 133.0.

Q. 8 (b) A random sample of size n is drawn from normal population with mean 5 and variance sigma-squared. (i) If n = 25, x-bar = 3 and s-hat = 2, what is t? (ii) If n = 9, x-bar = 2 and t = -2, what is s-hat? (iii) If n = 25, s-hat = 10 and t = 2, what is x-bar? (iv) If s-hat = 15, x-bar = 14 and t = 3, what is n? (Book answers: t = -5, s-hat = 4.5, x-bar = 9, n = 25.)

Step 1: The t-statistic is t = (x-bar - mu_0) / (s-hat / sqrt(n)), with mu_0 = 5.

Step 2: (i) t = (3 - 5) / (2 / sqrt(25)) = -2 / 0.4 = -5.

Step 3: (ii) -2 = (2 - 5) / (s-hat / sqrt(9)) = -9 / s-hat, so s-hat = 9 / 2 = 4.5.

Step 4: (iii) 2 = (x-bar - 5) / (10 / sqrt(25)) = (x-bar - 5) / 2, so x-bar - 5 = 4, giving x-bar = 9.

Answer: (iv) 3 = (14 - 5) / (15 / sqrt(n)) = 9 sqrt(n) / 15 = 0.6 sqrt(n), so sqrt(n) = 5, giving n = 25.

Q. 9 (a) Injection of a certain kind of hormone into hens is said to increase the mean weight of eggs by 0.3 ounces. A sample of 30 eggs has an arithmetic mean 0.4 ounces above the pre-injection mean and a value of s-hat equal to 0.20 ounces. Is this enough reason to accept the statement that the mean increase is more than 0.3 ounces? (Book answer: Since t = 2.74 > 1.699 = t_(29; 0.95), we reject H_0: mu <= 0.3 in favour of H_1: mu > 0.3 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: n = 30, x-bar = 0.4 ounces (mean increase), s-hat = 0.20 ounces. H_0: mu <= 0.3 against H_1: mu > 0.3, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: t = (0.4 - 0.3) / (0.20 / sqrt(30)) = 0.1 / 0.0365 = 2.74, with v = 29 degrees of freedom.

Step 3: Critical value: t_(29; 0.95) = 1.699. Rejection region: T > 1.699.

Answer: Since t = 2.74 > 1.699, we reject H_0: mu <= 0.3 in favour of H_1: mu > 0.3. Yes, there is enough reason to accept that the mean increase is more than 0.3 ounces.

Q. 9 (b) A random sample of 25 hens from a normal population showed that the average laying is 272 eggs per year with a variance of 625 eggs. The company claimed that the average laying is at least 285 eggs per year. Test the claim of the company at alpha = 0.05. (Book answer: Since t = -2.6 < -1.711 = t_(24; 0.05), we reject H_0: mu >= 285 in favour of H_1: mu < 285.)

Step 1: n = 25, x-bar = 272 eggs, s-hat-squared = 625, so s-hat = 25 eggs. H_0: mu >= 285 against H_1: mu < 285, at alpha = 0.05 (left-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: t = (272 - 285) / (25 / sqrt(25)) = -13 / 5 = -2.6, with v = 24 degrees of freedom.

Step 3: Critical value: t_(24; 0.05) = -1.711. Rejection region: T < -1.711.

Answer: Since t = -2.6 < -1.711, we reject H_0: mu >= 285 in favour of H_1: mu < 285. The company's claim is not supported.

Q. 10 (a) A producer of a certain make of flashlight dry cell batteries claims that its output has a mean life of 750 hours. A random sample of 15 such batteries has been tested and a sample mean of 745 hours and a sample standard deviation of 24 hours have been obtained. Verify that these results are consistent with the null hypothesis mu >= 750 against mu < 750 at alpha = 0.01. (Book answer: Since t = -0.807 > -2.624 = t_(14; 0.01), we do not reject H_0: mu >= 750 against H_1: mu < 750.)

Step 1: n = 15, x-bar = 745 hours, s-hat = 24 hours. H_0: mu >= 750 against H_1: mu < 750, at alpha = 0.01 (left-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: t = (745 - 750) / (24 / sqrt(15)) = -5 / 6.197 = -0.807, with v = 14 degrees of freedom.

Step 3: Critical value: t_(14; 0.01) = -2.624. Rejection region: T < -2.624.

Answer: Since t = -0.807 > -2.624, we do not reject H_0: mu >= 750. The results are consistent with the null hypothesis.

Q. 10 (b) Ten individuals are chosen at random from a normal population and the heights are found to be 63, 63, 66, 67, 67, 69, 70, 70, 71 and 71 inches. In the light of these data, discuss the suggestion that the mean height in the population is 66 inches. (Book answer: Since t_(9; 0.025) = -2.262 < t = 1.78 < 2.262 = t_(9; 0.975), we do not reject H_0: mu = 66 against H_1: mu not equal to 66 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: n = 10. Sample mean: x-bar = 677 / 10 = 67.7 inches. Sample standard deviation: s-hat = 3.02 inches.

Step 2: H_0: mu = 66 against H_1: mu not equal to 66, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (67.7 - 66) / (3.02 / sqrt(10)) = 1.7 / 0.955 = 1.78, with v = 9 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical values: +/- 2.262.

Answer: Since -2.262 < 1.78 < 2.262, we do not reject H_0: mu = 66. The suggestion that the mean height is 66 inches is not contradicted by the data.

Q. 11 (a) Ten cartons are taken at random from an automatic filling machine. The mean net weight of the 10 cartons is 15.90 oz and the sum of squared deviations from this mean is 0.276 (oz)-squared. Does the sample mean differ significantly from intended weight of 16 oz.? (Book answer: Since t_(9; 0.025) = -2.262 <= t = -1.806 <= 2.262 = t_(9; 0.975), we do not reject H_0: mu = 16 against H_1: mu not equal to 16 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: n = 10, x-bar = 15.90 oz, sum (x - x-bar)-squared = 0.276. Sample standard deviation: s-hat = sqrt(0.276 / 9) = 0.175 oz.

Step 2: H_0: mu = 16 against H_1: mu not equal to 16, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (15.90 - 16) / (0.175 / sqrt(10)) = -0.10 / 0.0554 = -1.806, with v = 9 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical values: +/- 2.262.

Answer: Since -2.262 < -1.806 < 2.262, we do not reject H_0: mu = 16. The sample mean does not differ significantly from 16 oz.

Q. 11 (b) In the past a machine has produced washers having thickness of 0.050 inches. To determine whether the machine is in proper working order, a sample of 10 washers is chosen for which the mean thickness is 0.053 inches and the standard deviation is 0.003 inches. Test the hypothesis that the machine is in proper working order using a level of significance of 0.05. (Book answer: Since t = 3.16 > 2.262 = t_(9; 0.975), we reject H_0: mu = 0.050 in favour of H_1: mu not equal to 0.050.)

Step 1: n = 10, x-bar = 0.053 inches, s-hat = 0.003 inches. H_0: mu = 0.050 against H_1: mu not equal to 0.050, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: t = (0.053 - 0.050) / (0.003 / sqrt(10)) = 0.003 / 0.000949 = 3.16, with v = 9 degrees of freedom.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 2.262.

Answer: Since t = 3.16 > 2.262, we reject H_0: mu = 0.050 in favour of H_1: mu not equal to 0.050. The machine is not in proper working order.

Q. 12 (a) A random sample of 16 values from a normal population showed a mean of 41.5 inches and a sum of squares of deviations from this mean equal to 135 (inches)-squared. Show that the assumption of a mean of 43.5 inches for the population is not reasonable and that the 95% confidence limits for this mean are 39.9 and 43.1 inches.

Step 1: n = 16, x-bar = 41.5 inches, sum (x - x-bar)-squared = 135. Sample standard deviation: s-hat = sqrt(135 / 15) = 3.0 inches.

Step 2: Test H_0: mu = 43.5 against H_1: mu not equal to 43.5, at alpha = 0.05. Test statistic: t = (41.5 - 43.5) / (3.0 / sqrt(16)) = -2.0 / 0.75 = -2.667, with v = 15 degrees of freedom.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 2.131. Since t = -2.667 < -2.131, we reject H_0: mu = 43.5. The assumption of a mean of 43.5 inches is not reasonable.

Step 4: The 95% confidence interval is x-bar +/- t_(15; 0.975) x (s-hat / sqrt(n)) = 41.5 +/- 2.131 x 0.75 = 41.5 +/- 1.598.

Answer: The 95% confidence limits are 39.9 and 43.1 inches, which do not include 43.5, in agreement with the rejection of H_0.

Q. 12 (b) A random sample of nine from the men of a large city gave a mean height of 68 inches, and the unbiased estimate of the population variance from sample, s-hat-squared was 4.5 (inches)-squared. Are these data consistent with the assumption of a mean height of 68.5 inches for the men of the city? (Book answer: Since t_(8; 0.025) = -2.306 < t = -0.708 < 2.306 = t_(8; 0.975), so we do not reject H_0: mu = 68.5 against H_1: mu not equal to 68.5 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: n = 9, x-bar = 68 inches, s-hat-squared = 4.5, so s-hat = 2.121 inches. H_0: mu = 68.5 against H_1: mu not equal to 68.5, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: t = (68 - 68.5) / (2.121 / sqrt(9)) = -0.5 / 0.707 = -0.708, with v = 8 degrees of freedom.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 2.306.

Answer: Since -2.306 < -0.708 < 2.306, we do not reject H_0: mu = 68.5. Yes, the data are consistent with the assumption of a mean height of 68.5 inches.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.3 — Test of Hypothesis About a Population Proportion
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) For each of the following sets of data, carry out a significance test for the hypotheses stated. (i) Sample size 50, number of successes 45, H_0: pi <= 0.8 against H_1: pi > 0.8, 5%. (ii) Sample size 60, number of successes 42, H_0: pi = 0.55 against H_1: pi not equal to 0.55, 2%. (iii) Sample size 120, number of successes 21, H_0: pi = 1/4 against H_1: pi not equal to 1/4, 5%. (iv) Sample size 300, number of successes 213, H_0: pi = 0.65 against H_1: pi not equal to 0.65, 1%.

(v) Sample size 90, number of successes 56, H_0: pi >= 0.76 against H_1: pi < 0.76, 1%.

Step 1: The test statistic for a proportion is z = (p - pi_0) / sqrt(pi_0 (1 - pi_0) / n), approximately standard normal for large n.

Step 2: (i) p = 45 / 50 = 0.90. z = (0.90 - 0.80) / sqrt(0.80 x 0.20 / 50) = 0.10 / 0.0566 = 1.768. Critical value at 5% right-tailed: 1.645. Since 1.768 > 1.645, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.8 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.8.

Step 3: (ii) p = 42 / 60 = 0.70. z = (0.70 - 0.55) / sqrt(0.55 x 0.45 / 60) = 0.15 / 0.0642 = 2.335. Critical values at 2% two-tailed: +/- 2.326. Since 2.335 > 2.326, we reject H_0: pi = 0.55 in favour of H_1: pi not equal to 0.55.

Step 4: (iii) p = 21 / 120 = 0.175. z = (0.175 - 0.25) / sqrt(0.25 x 0.75 / 120) = -0.075 / 0.0395 = -1.897. Critical values at 5% two-tailed: +/- 1.960. Since -1.960 < -1.897 < 1.960, we do not reject H_0: pi = 1/4 against H_1: pi not equal to 1/4.

Step 5: (iv) p = 213 / 300 = 0.71. z = (0.71 - 0.65) / sqrt(0.65 x 0.35 / 300) = 0.06 / 0.0275 = 2.179. Critical values at 1% two-tailed: +/- 2.576. Since -2.576 < 2.179 < 2.576, we do not reject H_0: pi = 0.65 against H_1: pi not equal to 0.65.

Answer: (v) p = 56 / 90 = 0.6222. z = (0.6222 - 0.76) / sqrt(0.76 x 0.24 / 90) = -0.1378 / 0.0450 = -3.060. Critical value at 1% left-tailed: -2.326. Since -3.060 < -2.326, we reject H_0: pi >= 0.76 in favour of H_1: pi < 0.76.

Q. 1 (b) A basket ball player has hit on 60% of his shots from the floor. If on the next 100 shots he makes 70 baskets, would you say that his shooting has improved. (Use a 0.05 level of significance). (Book answer: Since z = 2.041 > 1.645 = z_0.95, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.60 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.60; Yes.)

Step 1: n = 100, x = 70, so p = 0.70. H_0: pi <= 0.60 against H_1: pi > 0.60, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (0.70 - 0.60) / sqrt(0.60 x 0.40 / 100) = 0.10 / 0.0490 = 2.041.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.95 = 1.645.

Answer: Since z = 2.041 > 1.645, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.60 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.60. Yes, his shooting has improved.

Q. 2 (a) In a poll of 10000 voters selected at a random from all the voters in a certain district, it is found that 5180 voters are in favour of a particular candidate.

Test the null hypotheses that the proportion of all the voters in the district, who favour the candidate is equal to or less than 50% against the alternative that it is greater than 50%. Use a 0.05 level of significance. (Book answer: Since z = 3.6 > 1.645 = z_0.95, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.5 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.5.)

Step 1: n = 10000, x = 5180, so p = 0.518. H_0: pi <= 0.50 against H_1: pi > 0.50, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (0.518 - 0.50) / sqrt(0.50 x 0.50 / 10000) = 0.018 / 0.005 = 3.6.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.95 = 1.645.

Answer: Since z = 3.6 > 1.645, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.5 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.5.

Q. 2 (b) A retailer places an order for 400 recapped automobile tires with a supplier who claims that no more than 5% of his output is ever returned unsatisfactory. In time, 31 of the 400 tires are unsatisfactory. Should the retailer continue to trust his supplier's word as to the rate of returns? Use 5% level of significance. (Book answer: Since z = 2.524 > 1.645 = z_0.95, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.05 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.05; No.)

Step 1: n = 400, x = 31, so p = 31 / 400 = 0.0775. H_0: pi <= 0.05 against H_1: pi > 0.05, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (0.0775 - 0.05) / sqrt(0.05 x 0.95 / 400) = 0.0275 / 0.0109 = 2.524.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.95 = 1.645.

Answer: Since z = 2.524 > 1.645, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.05 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.05. No, the retailer should not continue to trust the supplier's word.

Q. 2 (c) A commonly prescribed drug on a market for relieving nervous tension is believed to be only 60% effective. Experimental results with a new drug administered to a random sample of 100 adults who were suffering from nervous tension showed that 70 got relief. Is this sufficient evidence that the new drug is superior to the one commonly prescribed? Use 5% level of significance. (Book answer: Since z = 2.041 > 1.645 = z_0.95, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.60 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.60; Yes.)

Step 1: n = 100, x = 70, so p = 0.70. H_0: pi <= 0.60 against H_1: pi > 0.60, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (0.70 - 0.60) / sqrt(0.60 x 0.40 / 100) = 0.10 / 0.0490 = 2.041.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.95 = 1.645.

Answer: Since z = 2.041 > 1.645, we reject H_0: pi <= 0.60 in favour of H_1: pi > 0.60. Yes, there is sufficient evidence that the new drug is superior.

Q. 3 (a) An electrical company claimed that at least 95% of the parts which they supplied on a government contract confirmed to specification. A sample of 400 parts was tested, and 355 meet specification. Can we accept the company's claim at a 0.05 level of significance? (Book answer: Since z = -5.735 < -1.645 = z_0.05, we reject H_0: pi >= 0.95 in favour of H_1: pi < 0.95; No.)

Step 1: n = 400, x = 355, so p = 355 / 400 = 0.8875. H_0: pi >= 0.95 against H_1: pi < 0.95, at alpha = 0.05 (left-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (0.8875 - 0.95) / sqrt(0.95 x 0.05 / 400) = -0.0625 / 0.0109 = -5.735.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.05 = -1.645.

Answer: Since z = -5.735 < -1.645, we reject H_0: pi >= 0.95 in favour of H_1: pi < 0.95. No, we cannot accept the company's claim.

Q. 3 (b) An electric company claimed that at least 85% of the parts which they supplied conformed to specifications. A sample of 400 parts was tested and 75 did not meet specifications. Can we accept the company's claim at 0.05 level of significance? (Book answer: Since z = -2.100 < -1.645 = z_0.05, we reject H_0: pi >= 0.85 in favour of H_1: pi < 0.85; No.)

Step 1: n = 400, 75 did not meet specifications, so 325 met them, and p = 325 / 400 = 0.8125. H_0: pi >= 0.85 against H_1: pi < 0.85, at alpha = 0.05 (left-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (0.8125 - 0.85) / sqrt(0.85 x 0.15 / 400) = -0.0375 / 0.0179 = -2.100.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.05 = -1.645.

Answer: Since z = -2.100 < -1.645, we reject H_0: pi >= 0.85 in favour of H_1: pi < 0.85. No, we cannot accept the company's claim.

mcqs.q: For a test of hypothesis about a population proportion pi, with sample proportion p-hat from a large sample of size n, the test statistic is:
options: Z = (p-hat - pi_0) x sqrt(pi_0 (1 - pi_0) / n)
mcqs.why: The notes give the test statistic for a proportion as z = (p - pi_0) / sqrt(pi_0 (1 - pi_0) / n), where pi_0 is the value of pi under H0. The standard error uses pi_0 (not p-hat), and the statistic is approximately standard normal for large n.

mcqs.q: A sample of size 50 has 45 successes. Test H0: pi <= 0.8 against H1: pi > 0.8 at the 5% level. The value of the test statistic Z is:
mcqs.why: Working: p-hat = 45/50 = 0.90. Z = (0.90 - 0.80) / sqrt(0.80 x 0.20 / 50) = 0.10 / 0.0566 = 1.768. The critical value at 5% right-tailed is 1.645, and since 1.768 > 1.645, H0 is rejected in favour of H1: pi > 0.8.

mcqs.q: A sample of size 60 has 42 successes. Test H0: pi = 0.55 against H1: pi not equal to 0.55 at the 2% level. The correct decision is:

mcqs.q: A sample of size 120 has 21 successes. Test H0: pi = 1/4 against H1: pi not equal to 1/4 at the 5% level. The correct decision is:
options: Reject H0, because Z = -1.897 is less than -1.645
Reject H0, because p-hat = 0.175 differs from 0.25
Do not reject H0, because Z = -3.060 is beyond -1.960
Do not reject H0, because Z = -1.897 lies between -1.960 and 1.960

mcqs.q: A sample of size 300 has 213 successes. Test H0: pi = 0.65 against H1: pi not equal to 0.65 at the 1% level. The value of Z and the decision are:
mcqs.why: Working: p-hat = 213/300 = 0.71. Z = (0.71 - 0.65) / sqrt(0.65 x 0.35 / 300) = 0.06 / 0.0275 = 2.179. The critical values at 1% two-tailed are +/- 2.576. Since -2.576 < 2.179 < 2.576, we do not reject H0: pi = 0.65.

mcqs.q: A sample of size 90 has 56 successes. Test H0: pi >= 0.76 against H1: pi < 0.76 at the 1% level. The correct decision is:
options: Do not reject H0, because Z = -3.060 is greater than -2.326
Reject H0, because Z = -3.060 is less than the critical value -2.326
Reject H0, because Z = -1.897 is less than -1.645
Do not reject H0, because p-hat = 0.6222 is less than 0.76
mcqs.why: Working: p-hat = 56/90 = 0.6222. Z = (0.6222 - 0.76) / sqrt(0.76 x 0.24 / 90) = -0.1378 / 0.0450 = -3.060. The critical value at 1% left-tailed is -2.326. Since -3.060 < -2.326, we reject H0: pi >= 0.76 in favour of H1: pi < 0.76.

mcqs.q: A basketball player has hit 60% of his shots. In his next 100 shots he makes 70 baskets. At alpha = 0.05, has his shooting improved?
options: No, because Z = 2.041 is less than 2.326
No, because 70 baskets out of 100 is not enough evidence
Yes, because Z = 1.645 exactly equals the critical value
Yes, because Z = 2.041 exceeds the critical value 1.645, so H0: pi <= 0.60 is rejected
mcqs.why: Working: n = 100, p-hat = 0.70, H0: pi <= 0.60 against H1: pi > 0.60. Z = (0.70 - 0.60) / sqrt(0.60 x 0.40 / 100) = 0.10 / 0.0490 = 2.041. The critical value z_0.95 = 1.645. Since 2.041 > 1.645, we reject H0; yes, his shooting has improved.

mcqs.q: In a poll of 10000 voters, 5180 favour a candidate. Test H0: pi <= 0.50 against H1: pi > 0.50 at the 0.05 level. The value of the test statistic is:
A supplier claims no more than 5% of his tires are returned unsatisfactory. Of 400 tires, 31 are unsatisfactory. At the 5% level, should the retailer keep trusting the supplier?
options: Yes, because Z = 2.524 is less than 2.576

No, because Z = 2.524 exceeds 1.645, so H0: pi <= 0.05 is rejected

Since -5.735 < -1.645, we reject H0: pi >= 0.95 in favour of H1: pi < 0.95, so the company's claim cannot be accepted.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.4 — Test of Hypothesis About Difference Between Two Population Means
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) For each of the following sets of data, perform a test to decide whether there is a significant difference between the means, mu_1 and mu_2, of the normal populations from which the samples are drawn. (i) n_1 = 100, sum x_1 = 4250, sigma_1-squared = 30; n_2 = 80, sum x_2 = 3544, sigma_2-squared = 35; H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, 5%. (ii) n_1 = 20, sum x_1 = 95, sigma_1-squared = 2.3; n_2 = 25, sum x_2 = 135, sigma_2-squared = 2.5; H_0: mu_1 >= mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 < mu_2, 2%. (iii) n_1 = 50, sum x_1 = 1545, sigma_1-squared = 6.5; n_2 = 50, sum x_2 = 1480, sigma_2-squared = 7.1; H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 > mu_2, 1%. (iv) n_1 = 100, sum x_1 = 12730; n_2 = 100, sum x_2 = 12410; common population standard deviation sigma = 10.9; H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, 5%. (v) n_1 = 30, sum x_1 = 192; n_2 = 45, sum x_2 = 315; common population standard deviation sigma = 1.25; H_0: mu_1 >= mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 < mu_2, 1%. (vi) n_1 = 200, sum x_1 = 18470; n_2 = 300, sum x_2 = 27663; common population standard deviation sigma = 0.86; H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, 10%. (vii) n_1 = 40, sum x_1 = 2128, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)-squared = 810; n_2 = 50, sum x_2 = 2580, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)-squared = 772; H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 > mu_2, 5%. (viii) n_1 = 80, sum x_1 = 6824, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)-squared = 2508; n_2 = 100, sum x_2 = 8740, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)-squared = 3969; H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, 2%. (ix) n_1 = 65, sum x_1 = 5369, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)-squared = 8886; n_2 = 80, sum x_2 = 4672, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)-squared = 5026; H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 20 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 20, 1%.

Step 1: (i) x-bar_1 = 42.5, x-bar_2 = 44.3. z = (42.5 - 44.3) / sqrt(30 / 100 + 35 / 80) = -1.8 / 0.859 = -2.096. Critical values at 5% two-tailed: +/- 1.960. Since -2.096 < -1.960, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.

Step 2: (ii) x-bar_1 = 4.75, x-bar_2 = 5.4. z = (4.75 - 5.4) / sqrt(2.3 / 20 + 2.5 / 25) = -0.65 / 0.464 = -1.402. Critical value at 2% left-tailed: -2.054. Since -1.402 > -2.054, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 >= mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 < mu_2.

Step 3: (iii) x-bar_1 = 30.9, x-bar_2 = 29.6. z = (30.9 - 29.6) / sqrt(6.5 / 50 + 7.1 / 50) = 1.3 / 0.522 = 2.493. Critical value at 1% right-tailed: 2.326. Since 2.493 > 2.326, we reject H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 > mu_2.

Step 4: (iv) x-bar_1 = 127.3, x-bar_2 = 124.1. z = (127.3 - 124.1) / (10.9 x sqrt(1 / 100 + 1 / 100)) = 3.2 / 1.542 = 2.076. Critical values at 5% two-tailed: +/- 1.960.

Since 2.076 > 1.960, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.

Step 5: (v) x-bar_1 = 6.4, x-bar_2 = 7.0. z = (6.4 - 7.0) / (1.25 x sqrt(1 / 30 + 1 / 45)) = -0.6 / 0.295 = -2.036. Critical value at 1% left-tailed: -2.326. Since -2.036 > -2.326, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 >= mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 < mu_2.

Step 6: (vi) x-bar_1 = 92.35, x-bar_2 = 92.21. z = (92.35 - 92.21) / (0.86 x sqrt(1 / 200 + 1 / 300)) = 0.14 / 0.0785 = 1.783. Critical value at 10% two-tailed: 1.645.

Since 1.783 > 1.645, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.

Step 7: (vii) x-bar_1 = 53.2, x-bar_2 = 51.6. Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((810 + 772) / (40 + 50 - 2)) = 4.24. t = (53.2 - 51.6) / (4.24 x sqrt(1 / 40 + 1 / 50)) = 1.6 / 0.899 = 1.78, with v = 88 degrees of freedom. Critical value at 5% right-tailed: 1.645. Since 1.78 > 1.645, we reject H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 > mu_2.

Step 8: (viii) x-bar_1 = 85.3, x-bar_2 = 87.4. Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((2508 + 3969) / (80 + 100 - 2)) = 6.03. t = (85.3 - 87.4) / (6.03 x sqrt(1 / 80 + 1 / 100)) = -2.1 / 0.905 = -2.32, with v = 178 degrees of freedom. Critical values at 2% two-tailed: +/- 2.326. Since -2.326 < -2.32 < 2.326, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.

Answer: (ix) x-bar_1 = 82.6, x-bar_2 = 58.4. Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((8886 + 5026) / (65 + 80 - 2)) = 9.86. t = ((82.6 - 58.4) - 20) / (9.86 x sqrt(1 / 65 + 1 / 80)) = 4.2 / 1.647 = 2.55, with v = 143 degrees of freedom. Critical value at 1% right-tailed: 2.326. Since 2.55 > 2.326, we reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 20 in favour of H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 20. Note: the book prints 1.752, -2.351 and 2.453 for the three statistics in (vii), (viii) and (ix) (from unpooled standard errors); the decisions are the same as here.

Q. 1 (b) A simple sample of heights of 6400 Englishmen has a mean of 67.85 inches and a standard deviation of 2.56 inches, while a simple sample of heights of 6400 Australian has a mean of 68.55 inches and a standard deviation of 2.52 inches. Do the data indicate that Australians are on the average taller than the Englishmen?

(Book answer: Since z = 15.589 > 1.645 = z_0.95, we reject H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1 against H_1: mu_2 > mu_1 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: Englishmen: n_1 = 6400, x-bar_1 = 67.85, s-hat_1 = 2.56. Australians: n_2 = 6400, x-bar_2 = 68.55, s-hat_2 = 2.52. H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1 against H_1: mu_2 > mu_1, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed). The samples are very large, so the normal approximation is used.

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (68.55 - 67.85) / sqrt(2.56-squared / 6400 + 2.52-squared / 6400) = 0.70 / 0.0449 = 15.589.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.95 = 1.645.

Answer: Since z = 15.589 > 1.645, we reject H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1 in favour of H_1: mu_2 > mu_1. Yes, the data indicate that Australians are on the average taller than the Englishmen.

Q. 2 (a) A random sample of 100 professors in private colleges showed an average monthly salary of Rs. 5000 with a standard deviation of Rs. 200. Another random sample of 150 professors in Govt. Colleges showed an average monthly salary of Rs.

5600 with a standard deviation of Rs. 250. Test the hypotheses that the average salary for the professors teaching in Govt. Colleges does not exceed the average salary for professors teaching in private colleges by more than Rs. 500. Use alpha = 0.01. (Book answer: Since z = 3.499 > 2.326 = z_0.99, we reject H_0: mu_2 - mu_1 <= 500 in favour of H_1: mu_2 - mu_1 > 500.)

Step 1: Private: n_1 = 100, x-bar_1 = 5000, s-hat_1 = 200. Govt.: n_2 = 150, x-bar_2 = 5600, s-hat_2 = 250. H_0: mu_2 - mu_1 <= 500 against H_1: mu_2 - mu_1 > 500, at alpha = 0.01 (right-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = ((5600 - 5000) - 500) / sqrt(200-squared / 100 + 250-squared / 150) = 100 / 28.58 = 3.499.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.99 = 2.326.

Answer: Since z = 3.499 > 2.326, we reject H_0: mu_2 - mu_1 <= 500 in favour of H_1: mu_2 - mu_1 > 500. The Govt. salary exceeds the private salary by more than Rs. 500.

Q. 2 (b) A random sample of 80 light bulbs manufactured by company A had an average lifetime of 1258 hours with a standard deviation of 94 hours, while a random sample of 60 light bulbs manufactured by company B had an average lifetime of 1029 hours with a standard deviation of 68 hours. Because of the high cost of bulbs from company A, we are inclined to buy from company B unless the bulbs from company A will last over 200 hours longer on the average than those from company B. Run a test using alpha = 0.01 to determine from whom we should buy our bulbs. (Book answer: Since z = 2.118 < 2.326 = z_0.99, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 200 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 200.)

Step 1: Company A: n_1 = 80, x-bar_1 = 1258, s-hat_1 = 94. Company B: n_2 = 60, x-bar_2 = 1029, s-hat_2 = 68. H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 200 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 200, at alpha = 0.01 (right-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = ((1258 - 1029) - 200) / sqrt(94-squared / 80 + 68-squared / 60) = 29 / 13.70 = 2.118.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.99 = 2.326.

Answer: Since z = 2.118 < 2.326, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 200.

Company A's bulbs do not last over 200 hours longer on the average, so we should buy from company B.

Q. 3 (a) A farmer claims the average yield of corn of variety A exceeds the average yield of variety B by at least 12 bushels per acre. To test this claim, 50 acres of each variety are planted and grown under similar conditions. Variety A yields on the average 86.7 bushels per acre with a standard deviation of 6.28 bushels per acre, while Variety B yields on the average 77.8 bushels per acre with a standard deviation of 5.61 bushels per acre. Test the farmer's claim using a 0.05 level of significance. (Book answer: Since z = -2.603 < -1.645 = z_0.05, we reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 >= 12 in favour of H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 < 12.)

Step 1: Variety A: n_1 = 50, x-bar_1 = 86.7, s-hat_1 = 6.28. Variety B: n_2 = 50, x-bar_2 = 77.8, s-hat_2 = 5.61. H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 >= 12 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 < 12, at alpha = 0.05 (left-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = ((86.7 - 77.8) - 12) / sqrt(6.28-squared / 50 + 5.61-squared / 50) = -3.1 / 1.191 = -2.603.

Step 3: Critical value: z_0.05 = -1.645.

Answer: Since z = -2.603 < -1.645, we reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 >= 12 in favour of H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 < 12. The farmer's claim is not supported.

Q. 3 (b) An examination was taken to two classes of 40 and 50 students respectively. In the first class, mean grade was 74 with a standard deviation of 8, while in the second class the mean grade was 78 with a standard deviation of 7. Is there a significance difference between the mean grades at 1% level. (Book answer: Since z_0.005 = -2.576 < z = 2.490 < 2.576 = z_0.995, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.)

Step 1: Class 1: n_1 = 40, x-bar_1 = 74, s-hat_1 = 8. Class 2: n_2 = 50, x-bar_2 = 78, s-hat_2 = 7. H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.01 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (74 - 78) / sqrt(64 / 40 + 49 / 50) = -4 / 1.606 = -2.490.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 2.576.

Answer: Since -2.576 < -2.490 < 2.576, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2. There is no significant difference between the mean grades at the 1% level.

Q. 4 (a) A random sample of 100 light bulbs manufactured by company A had a mean lifetime of 1230 hours with a standard deviation of 80 hours, while a random sample of 121 light bulbs manufactured by company B had a mean lifetime of 1200 hours with a standard deviation of 66 hours. Are the mean lifetimes of bulbs manufactured by two companies are significantly different? (Book answer: Since z = 3 > 1.960 = z_0.975, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.)

Step 1: Company A: n_1 = 100, x-bar_1 = 1230, s-hat_1 = 80. Company B: n_2 = 121, x-bar_2 = 1200, s-hat_2 = 66. H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (1230 - 1200) / sqrt(80-squared / 100 + 66-squared / 121) = 30 / 10.0 = 3.0.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 1.960.

Answer: Since z = 3.0 > 1.960, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2. Yes, the mean lifetimes are significantly different.

Q. 4 (b) A random sample of 200 villages was taken from Faisalabad District and average population per village was found to be 498 with a standard deviation of 50.

Another sample of 200 villages from the same district gave an average population 510 per village with a standard deviation of 40. Is the difference between the average of the two samples statistically significant? (Book answer: Since z = -2.650 < -1.960 = z_0.025, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.)

Step 1: Sample 1: n_1 = 200, x-bar_1 = 498, s-hat_1 = 50. Sample 2: n_2 = 200, x-bar_2 = 510, s-hat_2 = 40. H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (498 - 510) / sqrt(50-squared / 200 + 40-squared / 200) = -12 / 4.528 = -2.650.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 1.960.

Answer: Since z = -2.650 < -1.960, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2. Yes, the difference is statistically significant.

Q. 4 (c) The means of simple samples of 500 and 400 are 11.5 and 10.9 respectively. Can the samples be regarded as drawn from a population of standard deviation 5? (Book answer: Since z_0.025 = -1.960 < z = 1.789 < 1.960 = z_0.975, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.)

Step 1: n_1 = 500, x-bar_1 = 11.5; n_2 = 400, x-bar_2 = 10.9; common sigma = 5.

H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (11.5 - 10.9) / (5 x sqrt(1 / 500 + 1 / 400)) = 0.6 / 0.335 = 1.789.

Step 3: Critical values: +/- 1.960.

Answer: Since -1.960 < 1.789 < 1.960, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2. Yes, the samples can be regarded as drawn from populations with the same mean.

Q. 5 (a) Describe the procedure for testing the equality of means of two normal populations for: (i) Large samples, (ii) Small samples.

Step 1: (i) Large samples: use the test statistic Z = ((X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) - delta_0) / sqrt(sigma_1-squared / n_1 + sigma_2-squared / n_2), where sigma_1 and sigma_2 are known, or are replaced by s-hat_1 and s-hat_2 when n_1 and n_2 are large. Z is approximately standard normal under H_0.

Step 2: The null hypothesis is H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 = delta_0 (usually delta_0 = 0), and the critical values are taken from the standard normal table at the chosen level of significance.

Answer: (ii) Small samples: when the populations are normal with a common unknown variance, use the pooled estimate s_p-squared = ((n_1 - 1) s-hat_1-squared + (n_2 - 1) s-hat_2-squared) / (n_1 + n_2 - 2) and the test statistic T = ((X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) - delta_0) / (s_p x sqrt(1 / n_1 + 1 / n_2)), which has a t-distribution with v = n_1 + n_2 - 2 degrees of freedom under H_0; critical values are taken from the t-table.

Q. 5 (b) For each of the following sets of data, perform a test to decide whether there is a significant difference between the means, mu_1 and mu_2, of the normal populations from which the samples are drawn. (i) n_1 = 6, sum x_1 = 171, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)-squared = 83; n_2 = 7, sum x_2 = 164.5, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)-squared = 112; H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 > mu_2, 5%. (ii) n_1 = 5, sum x_1 = 678.5, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)-squared = 562.3; n_2 = 7, sum x_2 = 971.6, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)-squared = 308.6; H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, 5%. (iii) n_1 = 8, sum x_1 = 238.4, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)-squared = 296; n_2 = 10, sum x_2 = 206, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)-squared = 145; H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 4 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 4, 1%. (iv) n_1 = 12, sum x_1 = 116.16, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)-squared = 45.1; n_2 = 18, sum x_2 = 156.96, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)-squared = 72; H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, 10%.

Step 1: (i) x-bar_1 = 28.5, x-bar_2 = 23.5. Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((83 + 112) / (6 + 7 - 2)) = 4.21. t = (28.5 - 23.5) / (4.21 x sqrt(1 / 6 + 1 / 7)) = 5.0 / 2.341 = 2.135, with v = 11. Critical value at 5% right-tailed: t_(11; 0.95) = 1.796.

Since 2.135 > 1.796, we reject H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 > mu_2.

Step 2: (ii) x-bar_1 = 135.7, x-bar_2 = 138.8. Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((562.3 + 308.6) / (5 + 7 - 2)) = 9.33. t = (135.7 - 138.8) / (9.33 x sqrt(1 / 5 + 1 / 7)) = -3.1 / 5.464 = -0.567, with v = 10. Critical values at 5% two-tailed: +/- 2.228.

Since -2.228 < -0.567 < 2.228, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.

Step 3: (iii) x-bar_1 = 29.8, x-bar_2 = 20.6. Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((296 + 145) / (8 + 10 - 2)) = 5.25. t = ((29.8 - 20.6) - 4) / (5.25 x sqrt(1 / 8 + 1 / 10)) = 5.2 / 2.491 = 2.088, with v = 16. Critical value at 1% right-tailed: t_(16; 0.99) = 2.583. Since 2.088 < 2.583, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 4 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 4.

Answer: (iv) x-bar_1 = 9.68, x-bar_2 = 8.72. Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((45.1 + 72) / (12 + 18 - 2)) = 2.045. t = (9.68 - 8.72) / (2.045 x sqrt(1 / 12 + 1 / 18)) = 0.96 / 0.762 = 1.260, with v = 28. Critical values at 10% two-tailed: +/- 1.701. Since -1.701 < 1.260 < 1.701, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.

Q. 5 (c) Eight pots, growing three barley plants each, were exposed to a high tension discharge while nine similar pots were enclosed in an earthen wire cage, the number of tillers (shoots) in each pot were as follows: Caged: 17, 18, 25, 27, 29, 27, 23, 17, 28. Electrified: 16, 16, 20, 16, 21, 17, 15, 20. Discuss whether the electrification exercises any real effect on tillering. (Book answer: Since t = 3.058 > 1.753 = t_(15; 0.95), we reject H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 > mu_2 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: Caged: n_1 = 9, sum = 211, x-bar_1 = 23.44. Electrified: n_2 = 8, sum = 141, x-bar_2 = 17.625. H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 > mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed), assuming the populations are normal with a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = 3.92. Standard error: 3.92 x sqrt(1 / 9 + 1 / 8) = 3.92 x 0.486 = 1.903.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (23.44 - 17.625) / 1.903 = 5.819 / 1.903 = 3.058, with v = 9 + 8 - 2 = 15 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical value: t_(15; 0.95) = 1.753.

Answer: Since t = 3.058 > 1.753, we reject H_0: mu_1 <= mu_2 in favour of H_1: mu_1 > mu_2. The caged pots produced significantly more tillers, so electrification does exercise a real effect on tillering (it reduces it).

Q. 6 (a) A random sample of 6 cows of breed A had daily milk yields in lb., as 16, 15, 18, 17, 19, 17 and another random sample of 8 cows of breed B had daily milk yields in lb., as 18, 22, 21, 23, 19, 20, 24 and 21. Test if breed B is better than breed A at alpha = 0.05. (Book answer: Since t = 4.162 > 1.782 = t_(12; 0.95), we reject H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1 in favour of H_1: mu_2 > mu_1.)

Step 1: Breed A: n_1 = 6, x-bar_1 = 17. Breed B: n_2 = 8, x-bar_2 = 21. H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1 against H_1: mu_2 > mu_1, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed), assuming normal populations with a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = 1.78. Standard error: 1.78 x sqrt(1 / 6 + 1 / 8) = 1.78 x 0.540 = 0.961.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (21 - 17) / 0.961 = 4.162, with v = 6 + 8 - 2 = 12 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical value: t_(12; 0.95) = 1.782.

Answer: Since t = 4.162 > 1.782, we reject H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1 in favour of H_1: mu_2 > mu_1. Breed B is better than breed A.

Q. 6 (b) The heights of six randomly selected sailors are in inches: 62, 64, 67, 68, 70 and 71. Those of ten randomly selected soldiers are 62, 63, 65, 66, 69, 69, 70, 71, 72 and 73. Discuss in the light of these data that soldiers are on the average taller than sailors. Assume that the heights are normally distributed. (Book answer: Since t = 0.526 < 1.761 = t_(14; 0.95), we do not reject H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1 against H_1: mu_2 > mu_1 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: Sailors: n_1 = 6, x-bar_1 = 67. Soldiers: n_2 = 10, x-bar_2 = 68. H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1 against H_1: mu_2 > mu_1, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed), assuming normal populations with a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = 3.68. Standard error: 3.68 x sqrt(1 / 6 + 1 / 10) = 3.68 x 0.516 = 1.901.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (68 - 67) / 1.901 = 0.526, with v = 6 + 10 - 2 = 14 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical value: t_(14; 0.95) = 1.761.

Answer: Since t = 0.526 < 1.761, we do not reject H_0: mu_2 <= mu_1. The data do not show that soldiers are on the average taller than sailors.

Q. 7 (a) The weights in grams of 10 male and 10 female juvenile ring-necked pheasants are: Males: 1293, 1380, 1614, 1497, 1340, 1643, 1466, 1627, 1383, 1711. Females: 1061, 1065, 1092, 1017, 1021, 1138, 1143, 1094, 1270, 1028. Test the hypothesis of a difference of 350 grams between population means in favour of the alternative of a greater difference. (Book answer: Since t = 1.007 < 1.734 = t_(18; 0.95), we do not reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 350 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 350 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: Males: n_1 = 10, x-bar_1 = 1495.4 g. Females: n_2 = 10, x-bar_2 = 1092.9 g. Difference: 402.5 g. H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 350 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 350, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed), assuming normal populations with a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = 116.5 g. Standard error: 116.5 x sqrt(1 / 10 + 1 / 10) = 116.5 x 0.447 = 52.1 g.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (402.5 - 350) / 52.1 = 52.5 / 52.1 = 1.007, with v = 18 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical value: t_(18; 0.95) = 1.734.

Answer: Since t = 1.007 < 1.734, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 350. The difference is not significantly greater than 350 grams.

Q. 7 (b) The following data are the gains in weight, measured in pounds, of babies from birth to age six months. All babies in both groups weighed approximately the same at birth. The babies in sample I were fed formula A, and babies in sample II were fed formula B. Sample I: 5, 7, 8, 9, 6, 7, 10, 8, 6. Sample II: 9, 10, 8, 6, 8, 7, 9.

(Assume that the experimenter has no preconceived notions about which formula might be better). Test at the 5% level of significance that the mean of population I equals mean of population II. (Book answer: Since t_(14; 0.025) = -2.145 < t = -1.083 < 2.145 = t_(14; 0.975), we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.)

Step 1: Sample I: n_1 = 9, x-bar_1 = 7.33 lb. Sample II: n_2 = 7, x-bar_2 = 8.14 lb.

H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed), assuming normal populations with a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = 1.485 lb. Standard error: 1.485 x sqrt(1 / 9 + 1 / 7) = 1.485 x 0.504 = 0.749 lb.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (7.33 - 8.14) / 0.749 = -0.81 / 0.749 = -1.083, with v = 9 + 7 - 2 = 14 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical values: +/- 2.145.

Answer: Since -2.145 < -1.083 < 2.145, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2. There is no significant difference between the mean gains of the two formulas.

Q. 8 (a) From the area planted in one variety of value, 54 plants were selected at random. Of these plants, 15 were 'Off-types' and 12 were 'Aberrant'. The rubber percentages for these plants were: Off-types: 6.21, 5.70, 6.04, 4.47, 5.22, 4.45, 4.84, 5.88, 5.82, 6.09, 5.59, 6.06, 5.59, 6.74, 5.55. Aberrants: 4.28, 7.71, 6.48, 7.71, 7.37, 7.20, 7.06, 6.40, 8.93, 5.91, 5.51, 6.36. Test the hypothesis of no difference between the two means. Also compute a 95% confidence interval for the difference of two population means. (Book answers: Since t = -3.120 < -2.060 = t_(25; 0.025), we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2; 0.383 < mu_2 - mu_1 < 1.871.)

Step 1: Off-types: n_1 = 15, x-bar_1 = 5.617. Aberrants: n_2 = 12, x-bar_2 = 6.743.

H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed), assuming normal populations with a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = 0.933. Standard error: 0.933 x sqrt(1 / 15 + 1 / 12) = 0.933 x 0.387 = 0.361.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (5.617 - 6.743) / 0.361 = -1.127 / 0.361 = -3.120, with v = 15 + 12 - 2 = 25 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical values: +/- 2.060. Since t = -3.120 < -2.060, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.

Step 5: The 95% confidence interval for mu_2 - mu_1 is (x-bar_2 - x-bar_1) +/- t_(25; 0.975) x (standard error) = 1.127 +/- 2.060 x 0.361 = 1.127 +/- 0.744.

Answer: The 95% confidence interval is 0.383 < mu_2 - mu_1 < 1.871, which does not include 0, in agreement with the rejection of H_0.

Q. 8 (b) The I.Q.'s of 16 students from one area of a city showed a mean of 107 with a standard deviation of 10, while the I.Q.'s of 14 students from another area of the city showed a mean of 115 with a standard deviation of 8. Is there a significant difference between the I.Q.'s of the two groups at (i) 0.01 and (ii) 0.05 level of significance? (Book answers: (i) Since t_(28; 0.005) = -2.763 < t = -2.395 < 2.763 = t_(28; 0.995), we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2 at alpha = 0.01. (ii) Since t = -2.395 < -2.048 = t_(28; 0.025), we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2; at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: Area 1: n_1 = 16, x-bar_1 = 107, s-hat_1 = 10. Area 2: n_2 = 14, x-bar_2 = 115, s-hat_2 = 8. H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2 (two-tailed), assuming normal populations with a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((15 x 100 + 13 x 64) / (16 + 14 - 2)) = sqrt(2332 / 28) = 9.126. Standard error: 9.126 x sqrt(1 / 16 + 1 / 14) = 9.126 x 0.366 = 3.340.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (107 - 115) / 3.340 = -8 / 3.340 = -2.395, with v = 28 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: (i) At alpha = 0.01, critical values: +/- 2.763. Since -2.763 < -2.395 < 2.763, we do not reject H_0.

Answer: (ii) At alpha = 0.05, critical values: +/- 2.048. Since t = -2.395 < -2.048, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2. There is a significant difference at the 5% level but not at the 1% level.

Q. 9 (a) Means of random samples, each of size 10, from two normal populations with the same standard deviation were found to be 16 and 20 respectively. Further, the sample standard deviations were equal to 5 and 7 respectively. Test the hypotheses that the populations have the same mean, using 0.05 level of significance. (Book answer: Since t_(18; 0.025) = -2.101 < t = -1.47 < 2.101 = t_(18; 0.975), we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.)

Step 1: n_1 = n_2 = 10, x-bar_1 = 16, s-hat_1 = 5; x-bar_2 = 20, s-hat_2 = 7. H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed), assuming a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((9 x 25 + 9 x 49) / 18) = sqrt(666 / 18) = 6.083. Standard error: 6.083 x sqrt(1 / 10 + 1 / 10) = 6.083 x 0.447 = 2.721.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = (16 - 20) / 2.721 = -4 / 2.721 = -1.47, with v = 18 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical values: +/- 2.101.

Answer: Since -2.101 < -1.47 < 2.101, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2. The populations have the same mean, on this evidence.

Q. 9 (b) A random sample of size n_1 = 10, selected from a normal population has a mean x-bar_1 = 20 and a standard deviation s-hat_1 = 5. A second random sample of size n_2 = 12, selected from a different normal population has a mean x-bar_2 = 24 and a standard deviation s-hat_2 = 6. If mu_1 = 22 and mu_2 = 19 and sigma_1-squared and sigma_2-squared are unknown but approximately equal, test whether there is any reason to doubt that mu_1 - mu_2 = 3. (Book answer: Since t = -2.934 < -2.086 = t_(20; 0.025), we reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 = 3 in favour of H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 not equal to 3 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: n_1 = 10, x-bar_1 = 20, s-hat_1 = 5; n_2 = 12, x-bar_2 = 24, s-hat_2 = 6.

H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 = 3 against H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 not equal to 3, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed), assuming a common variance.

Step 2: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((9 x 25 + 11 x 36) / (10 + 12 - 2)) = sqrt(621 / 20) = 5.572. Standard error: 5.572 x sqrt(1 / 10 + 1 / 12) = 5.572 x 0.428 = 2.386.

Step 3: Test statistic: t = ((20 - 24) - 3) / 2.386 = -7 / 2.386 = -2.934, with v = 20 degrees of freedom.

Step 4: Critical values: +/- 2.086.

Answer: Since t = -2.934 < -2.086, we reject H_0: mu_1 - mu_2 = 3 in favour of H_1: mu_1 - mu_2 not equal to 3. Yes, there is reason to doubt that mu_1 - mu_2 = 3.

Q. 10 (a) The following values are obtained by two different samples while sampling a normal population with mu = 3.0 and sigma = 0.5. Using these data solve the following problems: A: 2.7, 3.9, 2.6, 2.8, 3.2, 3.6, 2.7, 3.0, 3.8, 3.1. B: 2.4, 2.8, 3.0, 3.3, 3.7, 3.3, 3.1, 2.7, 2.4, 3.3. (i) Combine the data into one set and test the hypothesis H_0: mu = 3.0 against H_1: mu not equal to 3.0. (ii) Assuming that sigma is unknown test the hypothesis H_0: mu_A <= mu_B against H_1: mu_A > mu_B. Use alpha = 0.05 in both cases. (Book answers: (i) Since z_0.025 = -1.96 < z = 0.626 < 1.96 = z_0.975, we do not reject H_0: mu = 3 against H_1: mu not equal to 3. (ii) Since t = 0.694 < 1.734 = t_(18; 0.95), we do not reject H_0: mu_A <= mu_B against H_1: mu_A > mu_B.)

Step 1: (i) Combined sample: n = 20, x-bar = 3.07. sigma = 0.5 is known. H_0: mu = 3.0 against H_1: mu not equal to 3.0, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: z = (3.07 - 3.0) / (0.5 / sqrt(20)) = 0.07 / 0.112 = 0.626.

Critical values: +/- 1.960. Since -1.960 < 0.626 < 1.960, we do not reject H_0: mu = 3.0.

Step 3: (ii) Sample A: n_A = 10, x-bar_A = 3.14. Sample B: n_B = 10, x-bar_B = 3.00. H_0: mu_A <= mu_B against H_1: mu_A > mu_B, at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed), assuming a common unknown variance.

Step 4: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = 0.451. Standard error: 0.451 x sqrt(1 / 10 + 1 / 10) = 0.451 x 0.447 = 0.202. Test statistic: t = (3.14 - 3.00) / 0.202 = 0.694, with v = 18 degrees of freedom.

Step 5: Critical value: t_(18; 0.95) = 1.734.

Answer: Since t = 0.694 < 1.734, we do not reject H_0: mu_A <= mu_B.

Q. 10 (b) A group of 12 students are found to have the following I.Q.'s: 112, 109, 125, 113, 116, 131, 112, 123, 108, 113, 132, 128. Is it reasonable to assume that these students have come from a large population whose mean I.Q. is 115? Another group of 10 students are found to have the following I.Q.'s: 117, 110, 106, 109, 116, 119, 107, 106, 105, 108. Can we conclude that both the groups of students have come from the same population? (Book answers: (i) Since t_(11; 0.025) = -2.201 < t = 1.386 < 2.201 = t_(11; 0.975), we do not reject H_0: mu = 115 against H_1: mu not equal to 115 at alpha = 0.05. (ii) Since t = 2.608 > 2.086 = t_(20; 0.975), we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2 at alpha = 0.05.)

Step 1: (i) Group 1: n_1 = 12, x-bar_1 = 118.5, s-hat_1 = 8.74. H_0: mu = 115 against H_1: mu not equal to 115, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: t = (118.5 - 115) / (8.74 / sqrt(12)) = 3.5 / 2.523 = 1.386, with v = 11 degrees of freedom. Critical values: +/- 2.201. Since -2.201 < 1.386 < 2.201, we do not reject H_0: mu = 115. Yes, it is reasonable to assume the students have come from a population with mean I.Q. 115.

Step 3: (ii) Group 2: n_2 = 10, x-bar_2 = 110.3. H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed), assuming a common variance.

Step 4: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = 7.35 (from the two sample variances).

Standard error: 7.35 x sqrt(1 / 12 + 1 / 10) = 7.35 x 0.428 = 3.145. Test statistic: t = (118.5 - 110.3) / 3.145 = 8.2 / 3.145 = 2.608, with v = 20 degrees of freedom.

Step 5: Critical value: t_(20; 0.975) = 2.086.

Answer: Since t = 2.608 > 2.086, we reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2. No, we cannot conclude that both groups have come from the same population.

Q. 10 (c) A random sample of 16 values from a normal population gave a mean of 42 inches and a sum of squared deviations from this mean as 135 (inches)-squared.

Test the hypothesis that the mean in the population is 43.5 inches. Another random sample of 9 values from another normal population gave a mean of 41.5 inches and a sum of squares of deviations from this mean as 128 (inches)-squared. Test the hypothesis that the mean of first population equals the mean of the second population. (Book answers: Since t_(15; 0.025) = -2.131 < t = -2 < 2.131 = t_(15; 0.975), we do not reject H_0: mu = 43.5 against H_1: mu not equal to 43.5. Since t_(23; 0.025) = -2.069 < t = 0.355 < 2.069 = t_(23; 0.975), we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.)

Step 1: Sample 1: n_1 = 16, x-bar_1 = 42, sum (x - x-bar)-squared = 135, so s-hat_1 = sqrt(135 / 15) = 3.0. H_0: mu = 43.5 against H_1: mu not equal to 43.5, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed).

Step 2: Test statistic: t = (42 - 43.5) / (3.0 / sqrt(16)) = -1.5 / 0.75 = -2.0, with v = 15 degrees of freedom. Critical values: +/- 2.131. Since -2.131 < -2.0 < 2.131, we do not reject H_0: mu = 43.5.

Step 3: Sample 2: n_2 = 9, x-bar_2 = 41.5, sum (x - x-bar)-squared = 128. H_0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H_1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2, at alpha = 0.05 (two-tailed), assuming a common variance.

Step 4: Pooled standard deviation: s_p = sqrt((135 + 128) / (16 + 9 - 2)) = sqrt(263 / 23) = 3.382. Standard error: 3.382 x sqrt(1 / 16 + 1 / 9) = 3.382 x 0.417 = 1.410.

Test statistic: t = (42 - 41.5) / 1.410 = 0.5 / 1.410 = 0.355, with v = 23 degrees of freedom.

Step 5: Critical values: +/- 2.069.

Answer: Since -2.069 < 0.355 < 2.069, we do not reject H_0: mu_1 = mu_2.

mcqs.q: For small samples from two normal populations with a common unknown variance, the test of H0: mu_1 - mu_2 = delta_0 uses:
options: The Z statistic with the separate sample variances in the denominator
The t statistic with the pooled standard deviation s_p and v = n_1 + n_2 - 2 degrees of freedom
The t statistic with v = n_1 + n_2 degrees of freedom and no pooling
The Z statistic, because the t-distribution is never used for two means
mcqs.why: The notes state that for small samples from normal populations with a common unknown variance, the pooled estimate s_p^2 = ((n_1 - 1) s-hat_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) s-hat_2^2) / (n_1 + n_2 - 2) is used, and T = ((X-bar_1 - X-bar_2) - delta_0) / (s_p x sqrt(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)) has a t-distribution with v = n_1 + n_2 - 2 degrees of freedom under H0.

mcqs.q: n_1 = 100, sum x_1 = 4250, sigma_1^2 = 30; n_2 = 80, sum x_2 = 3544, sigma_2^2 = 35. Test H0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2 at 5%. The value of Z and the decision are:
mcqs.why: Working: x-bar_1 = 4250/100 = 42.5 and x-bar_2 = 3544/80 = 44.3. Z = (42.5 - 44.3) / sqrt(30/100 + 35/80) = -1.8 / 0.859 = -2.096. The critical values at 5% two-tailed are +/- 1.960. Since -2.096 < -1.960, we reject H0: mu_1 = mu_2 in favour of H1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2.

mcqs.q: n_1 = 20, sum x_1 = 95, sigma_1^2 = 2.3; n_2 = 25, sum x_2 = 135, sigma_2^2 = 2.5. Test H0: mu_1 >= mu_2 against H1: mu_1 < mu_2 at 2%. The correct decision is:
options: Reject H0, because Z = -1.402 is less than -1.645
Reject H0, because x-bar_1 = 4.75 is less than x-bar_2 = 5.4
Do not reject H0, because Z = -2.096 is less than -2.054
Do not reject H0, because Z = -1.402 is greater than the critical value -2.054
mcqs.why: Working: x-bar_1 = 95/20 = 4.75 and x-bar_2 = 135/25 = 5.4. Z = (4.75 - 5.4) / sqrt(2.3/20 + 2.5/25) = -0.65 / 0.464 = -1.402. The critical value at 2% left-tailed is -2.054. Since -1.402 > -2.054, we do not reject H0: mu_1 >= mu_2 against H1: mu_1 < mu_2.

mcqs.q: n_1 = 50, sum x_1 = 1545, sigma_1^2 = 6.5; n_2 = 50, sum x_2 = 1480, sigma_2^2 = 7.1. Test H0: mu_1 <= mu_2 against H1: mu_1 > mu_2 at 1%. The correct decision is:
options: Reject H0, because Z = 2.493 exceeds the critical value 2.326
Do not reject H0, because Z = 2.493 is less than 2.576
Do not reject H0, because Z = 1.783 is less than 2.326
Reject H0, because Z = 2.493 exceeds the critical value 1.645
mcqs.why: Working: x-bar_1 = 1545/50 = 30.9 and x-bar_2 = 1480/50 = 29.6. Z = (30.9 - 29.6) / sqrt(6.5/50 + 7.1/50) = 1.3 / 0.522 = 2.493. The critical value at 1% right-tailed is 2.326. Since 2.493 > 2.326, we reject H0: mu_1 <= mu_2 in favour of H1: mu_1 > mu_2.

mcqs.q: n_1 = 100, sum x_1 = 12730; n_2 = 100, sum x_2 = 12410; common population standard deviation sigma = 10.9. Test H0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2 at 5%. The value of Z is:
mcqs.why: Working: x-bar_1 = 12730/100 = 127.3 and x-bar_2 = 12410/100 = 124.1. With a common sigma, Z = (127.3 - 124.1) / (10.9 x sqrt(1/100 + 1/100)) = 3.2 / 1.542 = 2.076. The critical values at 5% two-tailed are +/- 1.960, and since 2.076 > 1.960, H0: mu_1 = mu_2 is rejected.

mcqs.q: n_1 = 30, sum x_1 = 192; n_2 = 45, sum x_2 = 315; common population standard deviation sigma = 1.25. Test H0: mu_1 >= mu_2 against H1: mu_1 < mu_2 at 1%. The correct decision is:
options: Reject H0, because Z = -2.036 is less than -1.645
Do not reject H0, because Z = -2.036 is greater than the critical value -2.326
Reject H0, because x-bar_1 = 6.4 is less than x-bar_2 = 7.0
Do not reject H0, because Z = -2.326 exactly equals the critical value
mcqs.why: Working: x-bar_1 = 192/30 = 6.4 and x-bar_2 = 315/45 = 7.0. Z = (6.4 - 7.0) / (1.25 x sqrt(1/30 + 1/45)) = -0.6 / 0.295 = -2.036. The critical value at 1% left-tailed is -2.326. Since -2.036 > -2.326, we do not reject H0: mu_1 >= mu_2 against H1: mu_1 < mu_2.

mcqs.q: n_1 = 40, sum x_1 = 2128, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)^2 = 810; n_2 = 50, sum x_2 = 2580, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)^2 = 772. Test H0: mu_1 <= mu_2 against H1: mu_1 > mu_2 at 5% using the pooled t-test. The value of t, its degrees of freedom and the decision are:
options: t = 1.78, v = 90; do not reject H0
t = 1.26, v = 88; do not reject H0
mcqs.why: Working: x-bar_1 = 53.2, x-bar_2 = 51.6. Pooled s_p = sqrt((810 + 772) / (40 + 50 - 2)) = sqrt(1582/88) = 4.24. t = (53.2 - 51.6) / (4.24 x sqrt(1/40 + 1/50)) = 1.6 / 0.899 = 1.78, with v = 88 degrees of freedom. The critical value at 5% right-tailed is 1.645; since 1.78 > 1.645, we reject H0. (The book prints 1.752 from an unpooled standard error; the notes use the pooled value 1.78, and the decision is the same.)

mcqs.q: n_1 = 80, sum x_1 = 6824, sum (x_1 - x-bar_1)^2 = 2508; n_2 = 100, sum x_2 = 8740, sum (x_2 - x-bar_2)^2 = 3969. Test H0: mu_1 = mu_2 against H1: mu_1 not equal to mu_2 at 2% using the pooled t-test. The correct decision is:
options: Reject H0, because t = -2.32 is less than -1.960
Reject H0, because t = -2.55 is less than -2.326
Do not reject H0, because t = -2.32 lies between -2.326 and 2.326
Do not reject H0, because t = -0.567 lies between -2.326 and 2.326
mcqs.why: Working: x-bar_1 = 85.3, x-bar_2 = 87.4. Pooled s_p = sqrt((2508 + 3969) / (80 + 100 - 2)) = sqrt(6477/178) = 6.03. t = (85.3 - 87.4) / (6.03 x sqrt(1/80 + 1/100)) = -2.1 / 0.905 = -2.32, with v = 178 degrees of freedom. The critical values at 2% two-tailed are +/- 2.326. Since -2.326 < -2.32 < 2.326, we do not reject H0: mu_1 = mu_2. (The book prints -2.351 from an unpooled standard error; the notes use the pooled value -2.32.)

mcqs.q: Samples of 6400 Englishmen (mean height 67.85 in, s = 2.56 in) and 6400 Australians (mean height 68.55 in, s = 2.52 in) are taken. At alpha = 0.05, do the data indicate that Australians are on the average taller?
options: No, because Z = 15.589 is too large to be reliable
No, because the difference of 0.70 inches is too small
Yes, because Z = 15.589 exceeds the critical value 1.645, so H0: mu_2 <= mu_1 is rejected
mcqs.why: Working: H0: mu_2 <= mu_1 against H1: mu_2 > mu_1, right-tailed at alpha = 0.05; the samples are very large so the normal approximation is used. Z = (68.55 - 67.85) / sqrt(2.56^2/6400 + 2.52^2/6400) = 0.70 / 0.0449 = 15.589. The critical value z_0.95 = 1.645. Since 15.589 > 1.645, we reject H0; yes, Australians are on the average taller than Englishmen.

mcqs.q: Company A's bulbs (n = 80) average 1258 hours with s = 94 hours; company B's bulbs (n = 60) average 1029 hours with s = 68 hours. We buy from B unless A's bulbs last over 200 hours longer on average. Test H0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 200 against H1: mu_1 - mu_2 > 200 at alpha = 0.01. From whom should we buy?
options: Buy from A, because Z = 3.499 exceeds 2.326
Buy from B, because Z = 2.118 is less than 2.326, so H0 is not rejected
Buy from A, because 1258 - 1029 = 229 hours is more than 200 hours
Buy from B, because Z = -2.603 is less than -1.645
mcqs.why: Working: Z = ((1258 - 1029) - 200) / sqrt(94^2/80 + 68^2/60) = 29 / 13.70 = 2.118. The critical value z_0.99 = 2.326. Since 2.118 < 2.326, we do not reject H0: mu_1 - mu_2 <= 200. Company A's bulbs are not shown to last over 200 hours longer on the average, so we should buy from company B.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.5 — Difference Between Two Population Means, Dependent Samples
lessons.notes_html:
Q. 1 (a) Haemoglobin values were determined on six patients before starting and after three weeks on B_12 Therapy. The following data were obtained: Individual: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Haemoglobin (gm) Before Therapy: 12.2, 11.3, 14.7, 11.4, 11.5, 12.7.

Haemoglobin (gm) After Therapy: 13.0, 13.4, 16.0, 13.6, 14.0, 13.8. Do the data indicate a significant improvement? (Book answer: Since t = 5.927 > 2.015 = t_(5; 0.95), we reject H_0: mu_D <= 0 in favour of H_1: mu_D > 0.)

Step 1: Form the differences D = After - Before: 0.8, 2.1, 1.3, 2.2, 2.5, 1.1. Number of pairs: n = 6.

Step 2: Mean of the differences: d-bar = 10.0 / 6 = 1.667 gm. Standard deviation of the differences: s-hat_D = 0.689 gm.

Step 3: H_0: mu_D <= 0 (no improvement) against H_1: mu_D > 0 (improvement), at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed).

Step 4: Test statistic: t = (1.667 - 0) / (0.689 / sqrt(6)) = 1.667 / 0.281 = 5.927, with v = 5 degrees of freedom.

Step 5: Critical value: t_(5; 0.95) = 2.015.

Answer: Since t = 5.927 > 2.015, we reject H_0: mu_D <= 0 in favour of H_1: mu_D > 0. Yes, the data indicate a significant improvement.

Q. 1 (b) Eleven school boys were given a test in Drawing. They were given one month's further tuition and a second test of equal difficulty was held at the end of it.

Marks in 1st test: 23, 20, 19, 21, 18, 20, 18, 17, 23, 16, 19. Marks in 2nd test: 24, 19, 22, 18, 20, 22, 20, 20, 20, 20, 17. Do the marks give evidence that the students have benefited by the extra coaching? (Book answer: Since t = 0.956 < 1.812 = t_(10; 0.95), so we do not reject H_0: mu_D <= 0 against H_1: mu_D > 0.)

Step 1: Form the differences D = 2nd test - 1st test: 1, -1, 3, -3, 2, 2, 2, 3, -3, 4, -2.

Number of pairs: n = 11.

Step 2: Mean of the differences: d-bar = 8 / 11 = 0.727. Standard deviation of the differences: s-hat_D = 2.533.

Step 3: H_0: mu_D <= 0 (no benefit) against H_1: mu_D > 0 (benefit), at alpha = 0.05 (right-tailed).

Step 4: Test statistic: t = (0.727 - 0) / (2.533 / sqrt(11)) = 0.727 / 0.764 = 0.952, with v = 10 degrees of freedom. (The book prints 0.956.)

Step 5: Critical value: t_(10; 0.95) = 1.812.

Answer: Since t = 0.952 < 1.812, we do not reject H_0: mu_D <= 0. The marks do not give evidence that the students have benefited by the extra coaching.

Q. 2 (a) A taxi company is trying to decide whether the use of radial tires instead of regular belted tires improves fuel economy. Twelve cars were equipped with radial tires and driven over a prescribed test course. Without changing drivers, the same cars were then equipped with regular belted tires and driven once again over the test course. The gasoline consumption in km per litre, was recorded as follows: Radial tires: 4.2, 4.7, 6.6, 7.0, 6.7, 4.5, 5.7, 6.0, 7.4, 4.9, 6.1, 5.2. Belted tires: 4.1, 4.9, 6.2, 6.9, 6.8, 4.4, 5.7, 5.8, 6.9, 4.7, 6.0, 4.9. At the 0.025 level of significance, can we conclude, that cars equipped with radial tires give better fuel economy than those equipped with belted tires? Assume the population to be normally distributed.

(Book answer: Since t = 2.490 > 2.201 = t_(11; 0.975), we reject H_0: mu_D <= 0 in favour of H_1: mu_D > 0.)

Step 1: Form the differences D = Radial - Belted: 0.1, -0.2, 0.4, 0.1, -0.1, 0.1, 0.0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.3. Number of pairs: n = 12.

Step 2: Mean of the differences: d-bar = 1.7 / 12 = 0.142 km per litre. Standard deviation of the differences: s-hat_D = 0.198.

Step 3: H_0: mu_D <= 0 (no improvement) against H_1: mu_D > 0 (improvement), at alpha = 0.025 (right-tailed).

Step 4: Test statistic: t = (0.142 - 0) / (0.198 / sqrt(12)) = 0.142 / 0.0572 = 2.485, with v = 11 degrees of freedom. (The book prints 2.490.)

Step 5: Critical value: t_(11; 0.975) = 2.201.

Answer: Since t = 2.485 > 2.201, we reject H_0: mu_D <= 0 in favour of H_1: mu_D > 0. Yes, cars equipped with radial tires give better fuel economy.

Q. 2 (b) A certain stimulus administered to each of the nine patients resulted in the following increase in blood pressure: 5, 1, 8, 0, 3, 3, 5, -2, 4.
